entry.title: Discover The Palm Beaches to host 2-day hospitality and tourism job fair in Lake Worth Beach & Greenacres
entry.summary: Residents looking for work in Palm Beach County's tourism and hospitality industry will have two opportunities this month to connect with employers ahead of the busy tourism season. Discover The Palm Beaches (DTPB), the county's destination marketing organization, announced it will host its 5th Annual Hospitality and Tourism Job Fair on Oct. 9 and Oct. 15, bringing together employers from across the region. The free event is open to everyone and will feature full-time and part-time job opportunities in hotels, restaurants, attractions, entertainment venues, retail businesses and other tourism-related organizations. The first job fair will be held from 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. on Friday, Oct. 9, at Palm Beach State College's Lake Worth campus Public Safety Building, located at 4200 S. Congress Ave. The second event is scheduled for 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. on Thursday, Oct. 15, at the City of Greenacres Community Center, 501 Swain Blvd. According to DTPB, Palm Beach County's tourism industry supports nearly 95,000 local jobs and continues to be one of the area's largest economic drivers. 'A strong tourism industry depends on a strong workforce,' said Heather Andrews, senior vice president of commercial strategy and destination stewardship for DTPB. 'This job fair brings together leading employers and talented local residents, creating connections that strengthen careers, support businesses and contribute to the continued success of The Palm Beaches.' Available positions include front desk, food and beverage, operations, sales, marketing and management roles. Many employers are offering competitive benefits, paid time off and opportunities for advancement, organizers said. The job fair comes amid continued growth in Palm Beach County's tourism sector. DTPB said The Palm Beaches welcomed a record 6.09 million visitors during the first half of 2026, a 6.4% increase compared to the same period last year. Spanish and Creole translators will be available at both events to help job seekers connect with prospective employers. Applicants can pre-register for the event on the Palm Beach's website and are encouraged to dress professionally and bring their resume. entry.title: New I-95 Oslo Road interchange opens in Indian River County over a year ahead of schedule
entry.summary: Governor Ron DeSantis was in Indian River County on Monday to celebrate the completion of a new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road, a $100 million project state officials say will improve traffic flow, emergency response times and freight movement. The interchange, which opened about a year ahead of schedule , marks the first new I-95 interchange built in Indian River County in nearly 50 years. DeSantis said the project will provide a new direct connection to I-95 while easing congestion at nearby interchanges at Indrio Road and State Road 60. 'This is going to bring a new critical connection to I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit,' DeSantis said. According to the governor, drivers using Oslo Road to access I-95 can expect travel times to be cut roughly in half. State transportation officials also project traffic along the corridor will continue growing through 2045. DeSantis said the project is expected to have significant public safety benefits as well. The state estimates emergency response times in the area could be reduced by as much as 56%, allowing first responders to reach crashes and other emergencies more quickly. 'This will ultimately save some lives because time is of the essence in some of these situations,' DeSantis said. Florida Department of Transportation Secretary Jared Perdue said improved access to I-95 for first responders was one of the project's most important features. 'Every single second counts when it comes to saving lives, and this is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially,' Perdue said. The new interchange is also expected to improve freight movement for businesses in southern Indian River County by providing a more direct route to the interstate for trucks and commercial traffic. State officials said the project was accelerated through Florida's Moving Florida Forward initiative, a transportation funding program launched by the DeSantis administration to speed up major road projects across the state. Perdue said FDOT worked with contractors through a 'voluntary acceleration' program that rewarded construction teams for finding ways to complete projects more quickly. entry.article_text: Indiantown residents remain concerned about flooding after heavy rain left streets covered in water last week, with more rain and storms in the forecast for this week. CBS12 crews captured video of vehicles driving through standing water on roadways in parts of the village. Residents say flooding can quickly become expensive when water affects homes and property. The sad part is, if you don’t have insurance or anything like that you’re just stuck, your stuck with the bill, said Mary Brown, a Booker Park resident. The flooding has renewed questions about the more than $2 million drainage and roadway project in Booker Park. The project began in 2022 to help reduce flooding, but residents say heavy rain is still leaving some streets underwater. Village leaders have said they are working with Martin County on longer-term drainage solutions, including the possible repair or replacement of broken pipes. The next Indiantown Village Council meeting is Thursday night. With more rain possible this week, Martin County Fire Rescue and the Florida Department of Health in Martin County have tips available online for residents to plan ahead and avoid driving or walking through floodwater. You can CLICK HERE to view the entire list. Officials say water on a roadway may be deeper or more contaminated than it appears. Drivers who encounter a flooded road should turn around rather than attempt to drive through it. Martin County Fire Rescue responds to flooding-related emergencies, including when a vehicle becomes stuck in floodwater. Residents should call 911 during an emergency. For ongoing drainage problems or flooded roadways, residents can submit a report through Martin County’s online Request for Service system . The county asks residents to include the specific address or location and details about the issue, such as standing water, a blockage or a low spot near a drainage structure. CLICK HERE to submit a request. Health officials also advise residents whose wells flood to use bottled or boiled water until the well can be tested.

entry.title: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County - some just doors apart - WPEC
entry.summary: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County - some just doors apart    WPEC
entry.article_text: Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

entry.title: Gov. DeSantis to hold press conference in Vero Beach - WPBF
entry.summary: Gov. DeSantis to hold press conference in Vero Beach    WPBF
entry.article_text: The new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road is now open for drivers in Indian River County, a year ahead of schedule. Ron DeSantis, joined by Florida Department of Transportation Secretary Jared Perdue, held a press conference at 11 a.m. in Vero Beach on Monday announcing the completion of the nearly $100 million project. "This is the first new interchange built in this area, in almost 50 years, so this is going to bring new critical connection to I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit," DeSantis said. DeSantis said the new interchange is expected to reduce congestion on nearby interchanges like Indrio Road and State Road 60, cutting drive times in half. It also aims to improve emergency response efforts and movement along Florida's supply chain. "With the number of daily vehicles on the corridor still expected to grow between now and 2045 significantly, the Oslo Road interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future," DeSantis said. According to FDOT, work began back in August 2023 and was projected to be completed by spring 2027. "We actually implemented voluntary acceleration on this project," Perdue said. "Thank you to Halley Engineering Contractors and team for bringing an idea forward that actually enabled us to finish this project an entire year — to be exact, 400 days — ahead of schedule." While this new interchange is now complete, Perdue said work isn't done just yet on the Treasure Coast, as there are nearly a billion dollars of transportation investment planned for the area that FDOT will continue to work on and finish as quickly as possible. entry.article_text: Parents, students and grandparents gathered outside the Okeechobee County School Board on Monday, demanding greater accountability over bullying concerns after a 14-year-old student said relentless harassment pushed her to a breaking point.Signs lined the street as protesters chanted "no more bullying" and "hold bullies accountable," rallying around 14-year-old Estrella Ventura Meras, a student at Okeechobee Achievement Academy.Last week, WPTV reported on a video showing Estrella jumping from the window of a moving school bus. WPTV is not showing the video.Estrella told WPTV she jumped to escape students who had been bullying her since the start of the school year. She said she later went home and attempted to take her own life."I thank God he gave me another chance to live," Estrella said, holding back tears.Her mother, Estela Meras, said she found her daughter pale and lying next to a pill bottle. She said Estrella had left behind a note saying she was tired."What if I hadn't found her there lying in bed?" Meras said as she became emotional. Now, Estrella and her mother are calling for change."I just hope there's justice and the students responsible," said Estela Meras. "Everybody was on the bus laughing about her instead of helping her. If it was me, I would have been helping somebody."Estrella told WPTV she repeatedly reported the alleged bullying to teachers and administrators at Okeechobee Achievement Academy but said nothing changed. Her mother said she also previously raised concerns about bullying involving her daughter and now wants the district to reevaluate how it handles those reports.Other families at Monday's protest told WPTV they have also raised concerns about bullying at Okeechobee Achievement Academy and believe more needs to be done. "Somebody has to take some accountability somewhere," protester Maria Rodriguez said. Okeechobee County Schools said it shares parents' belief that "bullying has no place in our schools" and that every student deserves to feel safe, supported and heard.The district said the allegations involving Estrella remain under investigation. Citing federal student privacy law, district officials said they could not publicly discuss details of the investigation, education records or any potential student discipline.The district said schools are responsible for investigating bullying allegations reported by students and parents. If a family believes a school has failed to act on a complaint, district officials said the family should contact the district office so administrators can review both the allegations and the school's response."We take allegations that reports have gone unaddressed seriously," district spokesperson Dr. Joseph Stanley said in a statement to WPTV.Under School Board Policy 5.321, bullying reports can be made verbally, in writing or anonymously, and no specific reporting form is required. The policy calls for separate, confidential interviews and a review of evidence, with investigative procedural steps to be completed within a maximum of 10 school days, according to the district.The district said the policy also requires parents to be promptly notified when an investigation begins and requires a written report and recommendations for corrective action. It also includes provisions for counseling, intervention and follow-up measures intended to protect students.The district told WPTV that Okeechobee Achievement Academy has completed investigations into four other reports of alleged bullying during the current school year. Those cases involved four alleged victims and nine alleged perpetrators.None of the four complaints was substantiated as bullying, according to the district. Those cases are separate from the investigation involving Estrella, which remains open.However, the district stressed that an allegation being unsubstantiated as "bullying" does not necessarily mean no inappropriate behavior occurred. Florida law defines bullying as "systematically and chronically inflicting physical hurt or psychological distress" on one or more students. The district said a single incident generally does not meet that definition on its own, although one incident could reveal a broader pattern. Conduct that does not legally qualify as bullying could also constitute harassment or another violation requiring intervention or discipline.District officials said cooperation from students and parents is important during investigations because details about incidents, witnesses, previous reports and other evidence can help investigators determine what happened. The district said limited participation can restrict the information available to investigators but does not prevent officials from reviewing the evidence they can obtain.Despite calls from some parents for changes, Okeechobee County Schools said it believes its existing policies comply with Florida law and provide a thorough framework for responding to bullying allegations. The district said no procedural, staffing, disciplinary or policy changes are currently under consideration in response to the concerns raised by families.Instead, officials said their focus is on consistently implementing existing requirements, conducting thorough investigations and taking appropriate action based on the evidence.For Estrella's mother and the families who stood alongside her Monday, however, the protest was about making sure their concerns are heard before another child reaches a breaking point."All we want is answers for Estrella," Rodriguez said.

entry.article_text: No arrests have been made in the shooting death of a 17-year-old at a teen meetup near Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County, with a self-defense claim expected in the case, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Monday.WATCH BELOW: Sheriff Eric Flowers give update on shooting death of teen"We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," Flowers said.The shooting occurred late Friday night when approximately 100 teens, ranging in age from 14 to 19, gathered at Garcia's Boat Ramp in the 3700 block of County Road 512, the sheriff said. Deputies had broken up a similar group earlier that evening before the crowd moved to the boat ramp."The 17-year-old, and a group of his friends, are approaching a truck, and there are two people, both 18 years old, inside of that truck. The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch," Flowers said. "He's going to punch on the people that are inside of that truck. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed 17-year-old in this case."The teen's friends drove him away from the scene, east on County Road 512, while calling 911 and a dispatcher told them to stop at Fellsmere City Hall, where emergency crews performed CPR, the sheriff said. He was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he died from his injuries.The two individuals in the truck were identified using the sheriff's office's Flock technology, the sheriff said. Flowers said both have been cooperative with investigators, surrendering the weapon used in the shooting and the truck. Additional individuals involved in the incident have also been identified through Flock, though some remain unidentified. Investigators also recovered other weapons from the vehicle in which the 17-year-old was transported from the scene.WATCH: 17-year-old dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat RampFlowers said a warrant will be submitted in the case, but it will be up to the state to determine whether charges are filed."There have been no arrests on this case at this time, because the preliminary investigation shows that the 17-year-old was opening the door to attempt to fight with the two that were inside of the vehicle. They had a history of fighting," Flowers said. "Self defense plays a part in these, and when these kids go out and videotape these fights, and now guns are involved, there's going to be more of this." Names of those involved are not being released as the investigation continues, the sheriff said.Investigators believe at least four fights occurred at the boat ramp on the night of the shooting. Multiple shell casings and rounds were recovered from the scene.During Monday's news conference, Flowers released video of the shooting, noting the footage had already circulated widely on social media and that the victim's mother had seen it. One of the 18-year-olds involved in the shooting attends Vero Beach High School.The sheriff said teen meetups like the one at Garcia's Boat Ramp are coordinated through Snapchat, making them difficult for law enforcement to track in advance."When it's Snapchat, it's basically a private conversation," Flowers said. "But it quickly can escalate to over 100, 150, 200 people there."Flowers said the meetups, which have included alcohol, fighting, and firearms, have been taking place for years across Indian River County, Okeechobee, and surrounding areas, but that social media has intensified the danger."Now we're adding guns and alcohol into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix, and so what we're seeing is an escalation of each one of these," Flowers said. There's guns, and those two just don't mix. And now add in the fuel of the fire of social media, and now we have a 17-year-old dead."The sheriff said teens at these gatherings are motivated in part by a desire for online attention."The kids like to fight, and they like to videotape it, and they like to get their likes and shares because of that," Flowers said. Parents, you see these videos. You do not want your teens out at these meetups."With Vero Beach High School's homecoming game scheduled for Friday and the dance on Saturday, Flowers said additional deputies will be on duty. Meanwhile, the sheriff urged parents to monitor their children's whereabouts and report any information about planned meetups to the sheriff's office."Parents, if your kids are telling you that they're headed out to one of these meetups, ask them where they're going. Ask, find out the details. Share that with us," Flowers said.He recommended parents use location-sharing apps such as Life360 to track their children and said a child appearing to be in a remote or unusual location can be an indicator that a meetup is taking place.The investigation remains active. Flowers said anyone who witnessed any of the events that night, including the shooting itself, and has not yet spoken to investigators is urged to come forward."I can tell you, our investigation is not even remotely over, and if we are able to identify people that were involved in this, from underage drinking to fighting, hurting other people," Flowers said. " If they did something wrong, they're going to have to be accountable for that."Anyone with information is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff's Office at 772-569-6700 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS.

entry.title: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County - some just doors apart - WPEC
entry.summary: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County - some just doors apart    WPEC
entry.article_text: Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

entry.article_text: Ron DeSantis opened the new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road in Indian River County on Monday, calling it a critical connection for drivers, emergency crews and the region’s growing population. The roughly $100 million project opened one year ahead of schedule , according to the governor’s office and the Florida Department of Transportation. This is the first new interchange built in this area in almost 50 years, DeSantis said. It’s going to bring [a] new critical connection [to] I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit. The new exit is expected to ease congestion at nearby Indrio Road and State Road 60 interchanges, DeSantis said. Drivers traveling from Oslo Road to I-95 can expect their travel times to be cut in half, he added. With the number of daily vehicles on the corridor still expected to grow between now and 2045 significantly, the Oslo Road interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future, DeSantis said. The governor also said the direct interstate connection will help emergency crews respond faster in southern Indian River County. See also: Two killed, including 10th-grade girl, after rollover school bus crash in Polk County We anticipate that just for the local community on a normal basis, for local, like non-hurricane-type emergencies, that the emergency response time will be reduced by up to 56%, DeSantis said. That will ultimately save some lives, of course, because time is of the essence in some of these situations. FDOT Secretary Jared Perdue said the project was completed 400 days early through what the agency calls voluntary acceleration, which lets contractors propose ways to speed construction and share in the savings. This is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially, Perdue said. We’re really excited about that, to include cutting commute time in half and so many other benefits. DeSantis said FDOT also acquired land near the interchange for a dedicated gopher tortoise habitat. He said the site will be the only relocation area of its kind in Southeast Florida. Florida [is] showing that it’s possible to do the projects that we need done while also buttressing environmental stewardship, DeSantis said. Perdue said nearly $1 billion in transportation investment is planned for the Treasure Coast region.

entry.title: Indian River County sheriff investigates whether fatal shooting of teen at boat ramp was self-defense
entry.summary: A 17-year-old was killed in a shooting Friday night at Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County, and investigators are examining whether the shooting was an act of self-defense , according to Sheriff Eric Flowers. WATCH: WPTV'S Coverage of Teen killed in Garcia's Boat Ramp shooting 17-Year-Old Killed at Indian River County Boat Ramp; Sheriff Investigating Self-Defense Claim The shooting happened during a confrontation at the popular waterfront gathering spot, which authorities say has become a frequent meetup location for teenagers. According to Flowers, investigators reviewed video that showed the 17-year-old opening the door of a truck and throwing punches at people inside before a shot was fired. 'The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch. He's going to punch the people that are inside of that truck,' Flowers said during a news conference. 'One shot is fired. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed the 17-year-old in this case.' Video released by the Indian River County Sheriff's Office shows the confrontation moments before the shooting. Flowers said social media has played a role in drawing large groups of teens to locations like Garcia's Boat Ramp and warned that the presence of firearms is increasing the risks associated with those gatherings. 'We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media,' Flowers said. 'Now we're adding guns into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix, and so what we're seeing is an escalation of each one of these.' Authorities said both the shooter and the driver of the truck have cooperated with investigators, turning over the firearm and the vehicle involved in the incident. As of Monday, no arrests had been made. 'It's gonna be up to the state on whether charges are ultimately filed, but I can tell you, self-defense plays a part in these,' Flowers said. The investigation remains active. The sheriff is asking anyone with video footage or information about the shooting, as well as future teen meetup events, to contact investigators. Flowers also urged parents to know where their children are and suggested location-tracking tools as one way to help keep them safe.

entry.title: No arrests after 17-year-old shot, killed at meetup in Indian River County, self-defense claim expected - WFLX
entry.summary: No arrests after 17-year-old shot, killed at meetup in Indian River County, self-defense claim expected    WFLX
entry.article_text: No arrests have been made in the shooting death of a 17-year-old at a teen meetup near Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County, with a self-defense claim expected in the case, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Monday. WATCH BELOW: Sheriff Eric Flowers give update on shooting death of teen "We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," Flowers said. The shooting occurred late Friday night when approximately 100 teens, ranging in age from 14 to 19, gathered at Garcia's Boat Ramp in the 3700 block of County Road 512, the sheriff said. Deputies had broken up a similar group earlier that evening before the crowd moved to the boat ramp. "The 17-year-old, and a group of his friends, are approaching a truck, and there are two people, both 18 years old, inside of that truck. The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch," Flowers said. "He's going to punch on the people that are inside of that truck. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed 17-year-old in this case." The teen's friends drove him away from the scene, east on County Road 512, while calling 911 and a dispatcher told them to stop at Fellsmere City Hall, where emergency crews performed CPR, the sheriff said. He was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he died from his injuries. The two individuals in the truck were identified using the sheriff's office's Flock technology, the sheriff said. Flowers said both have been cooperative with investigators, surrendering the weapon used in the shooting and the truck. Additional individuals involved in the incident have also been identified through Flock, though some remain unidentified. Investigators also recovered other weapons from the vehicle in which the 17-year-old was transported from the scene. WATCH: 17-year-old dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat Ramp Flowers said a warrant will be submitted in the case, but it will be up to the state to determine whether charges are filed. "There have been no arrests on this case at this time, because the preliminary investigation shows that the 17-year-old was opening the door to attempt to fight with the two that were inside of the vehicle. They had a history of fighting," Flowers said. "Self defense plays a part in these, and when these kids go out and videotape these fights, and now guns are involved, there's going to be more of this." Names of those involved are not being released as the investigation continues, the sheriff said. Investigators believe at least four fights occurred at the boat ramp on the night of the shooting. Multiple shell casings and rounds were recovered from the scene. During Monday's news conference, Flowers released video of the shooting, noting the footage had already circulated widely on social media and that the victim's mother had seen it. One of the 18-year-olds involved in the shooting attends Vero Beach High School. The sheriff said teen meetups like the one at Garcia's Boat Ramp are coordinated through Snapchat, making them difficult for law enforcement to track in advance. "When it's Snapchat, it's basically a private conversation," Flowers said. "But it quickly can escalate to over 100, 150, 200 people there." Flowers said the meetups, which have included alcohol, fighting, and firearms, have been taking place for years across Indian River County, Okeechobee, and surrounding areas, but that social media has intensified the danger. "Now we're adding guns and alcohol into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix, and so what we're seeing is an escalation of each one of these," Flowers said. There's guns, and those two just don't mix. And now add in the fuel of the fire of social media, and now we have a 17-year-old dead." Region Indian River County The sheriff said teens at these gatherings are motivated in part by a desire for online attention. "The kids like to fight, and they like to videotape it, and they like to get their likes and shares because of that," Flowers said. Parents, you see these videos. You do not want your teens out at these meetups." With Vero Beach High School's homecoming game scheduled for Friday and the dance on Saturday, Flowers said additional deputies will be on duty. Meanwhile, the sheriff urged parents to monitor their children's whereabouts and report any information about planned meetups to the sheriff's office. "Parents, if your kids are telling you that they're headed out to one of these meetups, ask them where they're going. Ask, find out the details. Share that with us," Flowers said. He recommended parents use location-sharing apps such as Life360 to track their children and said a child appearing to be in a remote or unusual location can be an indicator that a meetup is taking place. The investigation remains active. Flowers said anyone who witnessed any of the events that night, including the shooting itself, and has not yet spoken to investigators is urged to come forward. "I can tell you, our investigation is not even remotely over, and if we are able to identify people that were involved in this, from underage drinking to fighting, hurting other people," Flowers said. " If they did something wrong, they're going to have to be accountable for that." Anyone with information is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff's Office at 772-569-6700 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS.

entry.title: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County - some just doors apart - WPEC
entry.summary: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County - some just doors apart    WPEC
entry.article_text: Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

entry.title: I-Team investigates Florida rules for seatbelts on school buses after fatal crash in Winter Haven
entry.summary: A deadly school bus crash in Polk County is raising new questions about how students are protected inside Florida school buses and why state law still falls short of federal safety recommendations. One student, a 10th grader on her way to Winter Haven High School, was killed Monday morning when a school bus carrying 39 people was involved in a crash. The circumstances surrounding the crash remain under investigation, including what happened outside the bus and what took place inside it. Watch report from Katie Lagrone School bus seatbelts 'We have one fatality of a beautiful high school girl. It's just heartbreaking,' Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said during a morning news briefing. Investigators have not released details about how many students were wearing seat belts, what type of restraints were in use, or whether the belts played a role in the outcome of the crash. Florida requires seat belts, but not the type federal investigators recommend Florida law requires school buses built since 2001 to be equipped with seat belts. However, students are not required to wear them, and state law does not require the more protective lap-and-shoulder belts recommended by federal safety investigators. Instead, many Florida school buses continue to use standard lap belts. The federal recommendation followed an investigation by investigative reporter Katie LaGrone more than a decade ago. In 2012, a St. Lucie County school bus collided with a semi-truck, killing 9-year-old Aaron Beauchamp. Aaron was wearing the bus's standard lap belt at the time of the crash. Several years later, investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) examined that crash and studied how different types of seat belts affect student safety. The agency's testing showed significant differences between standard lap belts and lap-and-shoulder restraints. Simulations demonstrated that lap-and-shoulder belts provide greater protection by better controlling a passenger's movement during a crash. As a result, the NTSB recommended that all school buses nationwide be equipped with lap-and-shoulder belts. Federal recommendation to Florida went unanswered The NTSB specifically urged Florida to change state law to require lap-and-shoulder belts on new large school buses. Aaron was wearing the bus's standard lap belt at the time of the crash.Several years later, investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) examined that crash and studied how different types of seat belts affect student safety.The agency's testing showed significant differences between standard lap belts and lap-and-shoulder restraints. entry.article_text: Parents, students and grandparents gathered outside the Okeechobee County School Board on Monday, demanding greater accountability over bullying concerns after a 14-year-old student said relentless harassment pushed her to a breaking point.Signs lined the street as protesters chanted "no more bullying" and "hold bullies accountable," rallying around 14-year-old Estrella Ventura Meras, a student at Okeechobee Achievement Academy.WATCH BELOW: Parents demand action after girl jumps from school busLast week, WPTV reported on a video showing Estrella jumping from the window of a moving school bus. WPTV is not showing the video.Estrella told WPTV she jumped to escape students who had been bullying her since the start of the school year. She said she later went home and attempted to take her own life."I thank God he gave me another chance to live," Estrella said, holding back tears.Her mother, Estela Meras, said she found her daughter pale and lying next to a pill bottle. She said Estrella had left behind a note saying she was tired."What if I hadn't found her there lying in bed?" Meras said as she became emotional. Now, Estrella and her mother are calling for change."I just hope there's justice and the students responsible," said Estela Meras. "Everybody was on the bus laughing about her instead of helping her. If it was me, I would have been helping somebody."Estrella told WPTV she repeatedly reported the alleged bullying to teachers and administrators at Okeechobee Achievement Academy but said nothing changed. Her mother said she also previously raised concerns about bullying involving her daughter and now wants the district to reevaluate how it handles those reports.Other families at Monday's protest told WPTV they have also raised concerns about bullying at Okeechobee Achievement Academy and believe more needs to be done. "Somebody has to take some accountability somewhere," protester Maria Rodriguez said. Okeechobee County Schools said it shares parents' belief that "bullying has no place in our schools" and that every student deserves to feel safe, supported and heard.The district said the allegations involving Estrella remain under investigation. Citing federal student privacy law, district officials said they could not publicly discuss details of the investigation, education records or any potential student discipline.The district said schools are responsible for investigating bullying allegations reported by students and parents. If a family believes a school has failed to act on a complaint, district officials said the family should contact the district office so administrators can review both the allegations and the school's response."We take allegations that reports have gone unaddressed seriously," district spokesperson Dr. Joseph Stanley said in a statement to WPTV.Under School Board Policy 5.321, bullying reports can be made verbally, in writing or anonymously, and no specific reporting form is required. The policy calls for separate, confidential interviews and a review of evidence, with investigative procedural steps to be completed within a maximum of 10 school days, according to the district.The district said the policy also requires parents to be promptly notified when an investigation begins and requires a written report and recommendations for corrective action. It also includes provisions for counseling, intervention and follow-up measures intended to protect students.The district told WPTV that Okeechobee Achievement Academy has completed investigations into four other reports of alleged bullying during the current school year. Those cases involved four alleged victims and nine alleged perpetrators.None of the four complaints was substantiated as bullying, according to the district. Those cases are separate from the investigation involving Estrella, which remains open.However, the district stressed that an allegation being unsubstantiated as "bullying" does not necessarily mean no inappropriate behavior occurred. Florida law defines bullying as "systematically and chronically inflicting physical hurt or psychological distress" on one or more students. The district said a single incident generally does not meet that definition on its own, although one incident could reveal a broader pattern. Conduct that does not legally qualify as bullying could also constitute harassment or another violation requiring intervention or discipline.District officials said cooperation from students and parents is important during investigations because details about incidents, witnesses, previous reports and other evidence can help investigators determine what happened. The district said limited participation can restrict the information available to investigators but does not prevent officials from reviewing the evidence they can obtain.Despite calls from some parents for changes, Okeechobee County Schools said it believes its existing policies comply with Florida law and provide a thorough framework for responding to bullying allegations. The district said no procedural, staffing, disciplinary or policy changes are currently under consideration in response to the concerns raised by families.Instead, officials said their focus is on consistently implementing existing requirements, conducting thorough investigations and taking appropriate action based on the evidence.For Estrella's mother and the families who stood alongside her Monday, however, the protest was about making sure their concerns are heard before another child reaches a breaking point."All we want is answers for Estrella," Rodriguez said.

entry.title: Discover The Palm Beaches to host 2-day hospitality and tourism job fair in Lake Worth Beach & Greenacres
entry.summary: Residents looking for work in Palm Beach County's tourism and hospitality industry will have two opportunities this month to connect with employers ahead of the busy tourism season. Discover The Palm Beaches (DTPB), the county's destination marketing organization, announced it will host its 5th Annual Hospitality and Tourism Job Fair on Oct. 9 and Oct. 15, bringing together employers from across the region. WATCH: 2-day hospitality, tourism job fair taking place this month 2-day hospitality, tourism job fair taking place this month in Palm Beach County The free event is open to everyone and will feature full-time and part-time job opportunities in hotels, restaurants, attractions, entertainment venues, retail businesses and other tourism-related organizations. The first job fair will be held from 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. on Friday, Oct. 9, at Palm Beach State College's Lake Worth campus Public Safety Building, located at 4200 S. Congress Ave. The second event is scheduled for 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. on Thursday, Oct. 15, at the City of Greenacres Community Center, 501 Swain Blvd. According to DTPB, Palm Beach County's tourism industry supports nearly 95,000 local jobs and continues to be one of the area's largest economic drivers. 'A strong tourism industry depends on a strong workforce,' said Heather Andrews, senior vice president of commercial strategy and destination stewardship for DTPB. 'This job fair brings together leading employers and talented local residents, creating connections that strengthen careers, support businesses and contribute to the continued success of The Palm Beaches.' Available positions include front desk, food and beverage, operations, sales, marketing and management roles. Many employers are offering competitive benefits, paid time off and opportunities for advancement, organizers said. The job fair comes amid continued growth in Palm Beach County's tourism sector. DTPB said The Palm Beaches welcomed a record 6.09 million visitors during the first half of 2026, a 6.4% increase compared to the same period last year. Spanish and Creole translators will be available at both events to help job seekers connect with prospective employers. Applicants can pre-register for the event on the Palm Beach's website and are encouraged to dress professionally and bring their resume. entry.title: Indian River County sheriff investigates whether fatal shooting of teen at boat ramp was self-defense - WFLX
entry.summary: Indian River County sheriff investigates whether fatal shooting of teen at boat ramp was self-defense    WFLX
entry.article_text: A 17-year-old was killed in a shooting Friday night at Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County, and investigators are examining whether the shooting was an act of self-defense , according to Sheriff Eric Flowers. WATCH: WPTV'S Coverage of Teen killed in Garcia's Boat Ramp shooting The shooting happened during a confrontation at the popular waterfront gathering spot, which authorities say has become a frequent meetup location for teenagers. According to Flowers, investigators reviewed video that showed the 17-year-old opening the door of a truck and throwing punches at people inside before a shot was fired. "The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch. He's going to punch the people that are inside of that truck," Flowers said during a news conference. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed the 17-year-old in this case." Video released by the Indian River County Sheriff's Office shows the confrontation moments before the shooting. Flowers said social media has played a role in drawing large groups of teens to locations like Garcia's Boat Ramp and warned that the presence of firearms is increasing the risks associated with those gatherings. "We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," Flowers said. "Now we're adding guns into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix, and so what we're seeing is an escalation of each one of these." Authorities said both the shooter and the driver of the truck have cooperated with investigators, turning over the firearm and the vehicle involved in the incident. entry.article_text: A 17-year-old was killed in a Fellsmere shooting Friday night after a meetup of more than 100 teens turned violent, according to the sheriff. The shooting happened around 11:24 p.m. at Garcia’s Boat Ramp , where a large crowd had gathered. Sheriff Eric Flowers said the group included teens ages 14 to 19, with drinking and fighting reported. These have been happening since before I was in high school, since before many of you were in high school. This has been going on for a long time. But now we're adding guns into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix. CBS12 confirmed with the family that the slain 17-year-old was Sulliman Bah, a senior at Sebastian River High School. He and a group of friends approached a pickup truck with two 18-year-olds inside. Detectives say Bah opened the door and attempted to punch someone inside when the passenger fired a single shot at Bah. See also: What Florida voters need to know about the 3 constitutional amendments on the Nov. ballot Bah was taken by friends toward Fellsmere. Deputies and EMS met them at Fellsmere City Hall and performed CPR before he was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later transported to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he succumbed to his injuries. No arrests have been made. Flowers said the driver and passenger inside the truck have cooperated with investigators and turned over the truck and firearm. The sheriff said the preliminary investigation indicates a self-defense claim may apply. We will be submitting a warrant in the case, but at this time it looks as though there will be a self-defense claim as a result, Flowers said. The sheriff said the state will ultimately decide whether charges are filed. Investigators used Flock technology to identify people connected to the truck and shooting. Deputies also recovered additional guns and multiple shell casings. Flowers said investigators believe the meetup was part of a growing trend of teens gathering at remote locations arranged through Snapchat , where fights are recorded and shared online. "We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," he said. "We've got kids out here losing their lives trying to go viral on social media." He said there may have been as many as four fights at the boat ramp that night, and investigators are still working to identify people who were there. "They had a history of fighting," Flowers said. "This has been an ongoing thing." The sheriff urged parents to ask their children whether they attended the meetup and encouraged anyone who witnessed the shooting or recorded it to contact investigators. "It's not safe," Flowers said. There's guns, and those two just don't mix. And now add in the fuel of the fire of social media, and now we have a 17-year-old dead." In a statement, the Indian River School District gave its condolences to the teen's family: The School District of Indian River County is heartbroken by this young person’s death. Our hearts are with his family, friends, and the students and staff who knew and cared about him. Grief support was in place over the weekend, including counselors at Sebastian River High School’s Homecoming Dance, and continues today as students and staff return to school. Our teams will remain available in the days ahead, offering care and responding to the needs of those affected. A spokesperson for SDIRC said the student had recently withdrawn from Sebastian River High School to be home schooled.

entry.article_text: The mother of a 17-year-old boy shot and killed during a party Friday night at a boat ramp in Indian River County said she believes her son was protecting others when he was killed. She has identified her son as Sulliman Bah. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers held a news conference about the shooting Monday afternoon. He said there were about 1,000 teenagers gathered at Garcia's Boat Ramp, just south of Fellsmere. Flowers showed two videos of the shooting from different angles. The videos start with Bah approaching a white pickup truck. "Seventeen-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch. He's going to punch on the people that are inside of that truck. One shot is fired," Flowers said. The sheriff said the shot was fired by the passenger in the truck, killing Bah. Flowers stated that Bah had a history with the two 18-year-olds in the truck, noting that they had fought before. The 18-year-olds told investigators they had the gun to protect themselves. "At this time, it looks as though there will be a self-defense claim," Flowers said. Bah’s mother, however, disputes the self-defense claim. In a text message to WPBF 25 News reporter Ari Hait, she said, "Sulliman was a defender of his friends. Always protecting the underdog, and I believe he was trying to save the crowd from that gun that he knew was about to be used...He was there to protect his friends from the thugs that had previously threatened him and many others multiple times." She added that she does not see her son throwing a punch in the video. "If anything, I believe he was attempting to push the gun away," she said. The sheriff has not released the identities of the two 18-year-olds in the truck but said they are cooperating with investigators. No arrests have been made so far. "It's going to be up to the state on whether charges ultimately will be filed. But I can tell you self-defense plays a part in these," Flowers said. The sheriff emphasized that the investigation is ongoing and urged anyone who attended the party to contact his office. entry.summary: Port St. Lucie woman pleads guilty to theft scheme at Palm Beach County apartment complex    WPBF
entry.article_text: Video above: News and weather for Monday, October 5, 2026 A Port St. Lucie resident accused of theft at a Palm Beach County apartment complex more than two years ago entered a plea agreement. According to court documents in Palm Beach County, Ashley R. Clayton, 38, pleaded guilty on Monday, Oct. 5, to money laundering, organized scheme to defraud and making false entry in book of business entity. Clayton agreed to the plea agreement on Sept. Clayton was sentenced to five years of probation for each charge, but will serve the penalties at the same time, credited with 12 days of time served in Palm Beach County jail, ordered to pay court costs and complete community service. As part of the plea agreement, Clayton and the victim will determine the amount of restitution Clayton owes to the property management company of the apartment complex. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Clayton is banned from performing any financial transaction for any business or person and was ordered to complete mental health and substance abuse evaluations. According to a Riviera Beach Police Department report, Clayton was an employee at Berkeley Landing Apartments located at 3100 Broadway for three months. On June 13, 2024, a regional manager for the apartment complex told police that Clayton was the community manager who oversaw payments for rent, deposits, application fees, background checks, credit checks and compliance application process for the apartment complex. It was determined that Clayton was collecting money by having residents use Zelle, which allows users to electronically transfer money. The residents’ money went to Clayton’s banking account. Some residents even gave Clayton blank money orders. The police report said Clayton sent residents a letter on apartment complex letterhead stating, “They are currently working on making sure all payment ledgers are up-to-date. We are asking that rent payments be made in the form of money orders until further notice.” The apartment complex did not give Clayton permission to send the letter. Clayton was fired but returned to the property and returned 20 money orders totaling $14,798.22 to the apartment complex management. The police report noted that Clayton kept three money orders and attempted to cash them at an Amscot in Miami. One of the three money orders was cashed, and the apartment complex was missing at least $11,999.23. Clayton collected $31,249.32 through Zelle, and at least $58,046.77 was stolen. The police report lists five additional individuals from whom Clayton took money from under false terms while working for the apartment complex. entry.title: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County - some just doors apart - WPEC
entry.summary: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County - some just doors apart    WPEC
entry.article_text: Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

entry.title: DeSantis opens new I-95 interchange in Indian River County, a year early - WPEC
entry.summary: DeSantis opens new I-95 interchange in Indian River County, a year early    WPEC
entry.article_text: Ron DeSantis opened the new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road in Indian River County on Monday, calling it a critical connection for drivers, emergency crews and the region’s growing population. The roughly $100 million project opened one year ahead of schedule , according to the governor’s office and the Florida Department of Transportation. This is the first new interchange built in this area in almost 50 years, DeSantis said. It’s going to bring [a] new critical connection [to] I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit. The new exit is expected to ease congestion at nearby Indrio Road and State Road 60 interchanges, DeSantis said. Drivers traveling from Oslo Road to I-95 can expect their travel times to be cut in half, he added. With the number of daily vehicles on the corridor still expected to grow between now and 2045 significantly, the Oslo Road interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future, DeSantis said. The governor also said the direct interstate connection will help emergency crews respond faster in southern Indian River County. See also: Two killed, including 10th-grade girl, after rollover school bus crash in Polk County We anticipate that just for the local community on a normal basis, for local, like non-hurricane-type emergencies, that the emergency response time will be reduced by up to 56%, DeSantis said. That will ultimately save some lives, of course, because time is of the essence in some of these situations. FDOT Secretary Jared Perdue said the project was completed 400 days early through what the agency calls voluntary acceleration, which lets contractors propose ways to speed construction and share in the savings. This is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially, Perdue said. We’re really excited about that, to include cutting commute time in half and so many other benefits. DeSantis said FDOT also acquired land near the interchange for a dedicated gopher tortoise habitat. He said the site will be the only relocation area of its kind in Southeast Florida. Florida [is] showing that it’s possible to do the projects that we need done while also buttressing environmental stewardship, DeSantis said. Perdue said nearly $1 billion in transportation investment is planned for the Treasure Coast region. Indian River County Commissioner Joseph Flescher recounted his reaction when he first heard about the opening. "When I got the phone call, I said, ' We're not near completion. I had been here just two weeks ago. We were nowhere near where we're at.' This team worked an incredible operation, said Flescher. Flescher also highlighted how important this new entrance ot I-95 is to the growing population across the county. This interchange is very much needed in the development of our county. And I don't mean the future development. I mean the current development, Flescher said.

entry.title: SLC seniors demand answers as Fort Pierce center prepares to close
entry.summary: A Fort Pierce senior center is expected to close, leaving some of the older adults who rely on it worried about losing a gathering place in their own community. The Council on Aging of St. Lucie confirmed the senior center at 1505 Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce is expected to close in the near future. The property is currently listed for sale for $2.2 million. The news came as a surprise to some seniors who use the center regularly, including 77-year-old Sandy Pietrewicz. She has relied on the center for nearly a decade. That's the community center that I go to for lunch and friendship and social activities with other elderly women, said Pietrewicz. After hearing the center could be closing, Pietrewicz said she and other seniors were left with questions about what would happen to the services they depend on. We were all talking about who we could contact, and I thought of WPTV immediately, she said. WPTV reporter Brooke Chau went to the center to get answers and hear directly from the seniors who use it. The Council on Aging said the closure will not mean an end to the services provided to seniors. You're going to get the same treatment. You're going to get the same love. You're going to get the same meals, said Trekina Smith with the Council on Aging. Once the property sells, seniors who currently use the Orange Avenue location are expected to transition to the Council on Aging's facility on Bayshore Boulevard in Port St. Lucie. The organization said transportation will be provided to help seniors get to the new location. But some seniors say the location itself is important. That makes us even angrier. We can't have something in our own community, Pietrewicz said. Geneira Lovett, who also uses the center, told WPTV that seniors in Fort Pierce want to be able to access services close to where they live.
