entry.summary: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County - some just doors apart    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

entry.summary: DeSantis opens new I-95 interchange in Indian River County, a year early    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Ron DeSantis opened the new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road in Indian River County on Monday, calling it a critical connection for drivers, emergency crews and the region’s growing population. The roughly $100 million project opened one year ahead of schedule , according to the governor’s office and the Florida Department of Transportation. This is the first new interchange built in this area in almost 50 years, DeSantis said. It’s going to bring [a] new critical connection [to] I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit. The new exit is expected to ease congestion at nearby Indrio Road and State Road 60 interchanges, DeSantis said. Drivers traveling from Oslo Road to I-95 can expect their travel times to be cut in half, he added. With the number of daily vehicles on the corridor still expected to grow between now and 2045 significantly, the Oslo Road interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future, DeSantis said. The governor also said the direct interstate connection will help emergency crews respond faster in southern Indian River County. See also: Two killed, including 10th-grade girl, after rollover school bus crash in Polk County We anticipate that just for the local community on a normal basis, for local, like non-hurricane-type emergencies, that the emergency response time will be reduced by up to 56%, DeSantis said. That will ultimately save some lives, of course, because time is of the essence in some of these situations. FDOT Secretary Jared Perdue said the project was completed 400 days early through what the agency calls voluntary acceleration, which lets contractors propose ways to speed construction and share in the savings. This is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially, Perdue said. We’re really excited about that, to include cutting commute time in half and so many other benefits. DeSantis said FDOT also acquired land near the interchange for a dedicated gopher tortoise habitat. He said the site will be the only relocation area of its kind in Southeast Florida. Florida [is] showing that it’s possible to do the projects that we need done while also buttressing environmental stewardship, DeSantis said. Perdue said nearly $1 billion in transportation investment is planned for the Treasure Coast region. Indian River County Commissioner Joseph Flescher recounted his reaction when he first heard about the opening. "When I got the phone call, I said, ' We're not near completion. I had been here just two weeks ago. We were nowhere near where we're at.' This team worked an incredible operation, said Flescher. Flescher also highlighted how important this new entrance ot I-95 is to the growing population across the county. This interchange is very much needed in the development of our county. And I don't mean the future development. I mean the current development, Flescher said.

entry.article_text: WPTV is working to get answers to questions residents raised about a controversial Islamic center approved in Palm Beach County's Agricultural Reserve. After Friday's heated public meeting, many viewers reached out asking who is behind the project, how it was approved and what happens next.The proposed development would be located off Lyons Road and 152nd Place South in Delray Beach, on what is currently a dirt road and grassy field. The project includes a mosque, school and daycare.WATCH BELOW: Who's behind the Ag Reserve Islamic Center? Residents seek answersDuring Friday's meeting, several residents questioned who is involved with the project and where funding is coming from. One speaker told county leaders, "If credible documented evidence exists connecting specific individuals or organizations associated with this project to extremist organizations, residents deserve to know what authorities have investigated and determined. Who controls this organization? Who is financing this project? Where is the money coming from? And what security review has been conducted?"The project also drew protesters outside the meeting."Where are they from, who are they, were they vetted? Build it and they shall come," said a woman pushing back against the Islamic center, calling the developments part of a "Muslim takeover."Sachs pushed through the feedback from the crowd and said places of worship of all faiths go through a review process."Yes, an investigation was made into every house of worship, whether it is Christian, Jewish, Muslim, Hindu and we do have Hindu temples if anybody here is interested," Sachs said. there's an investigation made as to who owns it, who's going to run it, and whether or not they're going to abide by the rules of the county and the United States Constitution."Inside the meeting, a woman who identified herself as a Latina Muslim convert questioned the nature of the concerns being raised. Her comments drew a strong reaction from the crowd as some wanted to focus on traffic impacts and nearly caused the meeting to be shut down."I want to be safer again; will this development help my community to be safe? My mosque welcomes people of other faith to ask questions," she said.Questions about who is behind the project have remained a focal point for residents.The project consists of a 15-acre Islamic center featuring 5 acres for the mosque and 10 for the school and daycare along Lyons Road.County documents reviewed by WPTV appear to identify the applicant as the Islamic Center School of west Delray Beach. The organization also appears to own an additional 5 acres on the north side of 152nd Place South. Plans for that portion are uncertain.Seeking more context on the concerns raised at the meeting, WPTV spoke with former Rabbi David Steinhardt, who retired about 16 months ago after serving for more than 30 years as senior rabbi at B'nai Torah Congregation in Boca Raton. He also served as co-president of the Boca Raton Interfaith Clergy Association.When asked what his message would be to residents expressing concern about a mosque coming into the area and the impacts on the Jewish community, Steinhardt said, "No one's trying to take their place. The issue is how do we live together."He said fear often grows when people lack familiarity with one another."I think that when you don't know people, then you suspect people, and when you're suspicious, you fear people. And so when you fear people, then you don't necessarily act rationally. This is not a new group of people. These are people that have been in town for decades. We have worked together at the hospitals, in the courts, in business, in all different arenas of public uh public uh society. And in our community, we have shared in various efforts to bring peace to the world. And so, I know that community. I have been in conversation with that community and its leadership for decades."Steinhardt said he knows the president of the mosque approved for the site and said they are members of the Islamic Center of Boca Raton seeking a second mosque to provide better access for members."I don't know if it's a need, if it's a desire; that should be enough. Is there a need for the number of synagogues we have in our Community? I'm not sure, but there's a desire for more, and we all have the right to do that."WPTV also learned the project is represented by Brian Seymour with the Gunster law firm. A request for additional details has been sent, and WPTV is working to hear back.Another issue repeatedly raised Friday involved notification requirements. Several residents questioned why people living more than 500 feet from the site were not notified.The county's Planning and Zoning Division told WPTV that only property owners within 500 feet were notified because the project is located within the U/S, AGR and Glades tiers. Had the project been located within the Exurban and Rural tiers, a 1,000-foot notification radius would have applied.To see which growth tier a property falls under, open the Palm Beach County GIS Map Viewer. Once you're in the map, click the menu icon (the "pancake" in the upper corner), then use the "Search Layers" tool and type in "Managed Growth Tier System." That layer will show all of the county's designated growth tiers and allow you to see exactly where a property is located within the system.Palm Beach County Commissioner Maria Sachs is planning a second public meeting focused on projects in the Agricultural Reserve following feedback from Friday's meeting. Her staff told WPTV details are still being worked out.Sachs also told WPTV she is working with county staff to find an appropriate date to propose changes to the Unified Land Development Code regarding the Development Review Officer process for places of worship and governmental entities.The issue has become a focal point because several projects residents protested were approved through an administrative review process that has existed for years and allows certain government entities and houses of worship to move forward without direct approval from county commissioners."I think for the most part people had their voices heard, but what they said is they want to have a voice in what comes to development in this county. I respect that I hear them," Sachs said Friday.While the mosque was approved through the administrative process, the proposal for an Islamic school and daycare next door did require a vote by county commissioners.WPTV reviewed records from a 2023 county meeting and learned the project was approved by a 4-3 vote.Sachs, former Commissioner Michael Barnett and then-Commissioner Sara Baxter voted against the proposal, citing concerns that not enough input from residents had been collected.Vice Mayor Marci Woodward, Commissioner Maria Marino, Commissioner Gregg Weiss and former Commissioner Mack Bernard voted in favor of the project.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.article_text: The mother of a 17-year-old boy shot and killed during a party Friday night at a boat ramp in Indian River County said she believes her son was protecting others when he was killed. She has identified her son as Sulliman Bah. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers held a news conference about the shooting Monday afternoon. He said there were about 1,000 teenagers gathered at Garcia's Boat Ramp, just south of Fellsmere. Flowers showed two videos of the shooting from different angles. The videos start with Bah approaching a white pickup truck. "Seventeen-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch. He's going to punch on the people that are inside of that truck. One shot is fired," Flowers said. The sheriff said the shot was fired by the passenger in the truck, killing Bah. Flowers stated that Bah had a history with the two 18-year-olds in the truck, noting that they had fought before. The 18-year-olds told investigators they had the gun to protect themselves. "At this time, it looks as though there will be a self-defense claim," Flowers said. Bah’s mother, however, disputes the self-defense claim. In a text message to WPBF 25 News reporter Ari Hait, she said, "Sulliman was a defender of his friends. Always protecting the underdog, and I believe he was trying to save the crowd from that gun that he knew was about to be used...He was there to protect his friends from the thugs that had previously threatened him and many others multiple times." She added that she does not see her son throwing a punch in the video. "If anything, I believe he was attempting to push the gun away," she said. The sheriff has not released the identities of the two 18-year-olds in the truck but said they are cooperating with investigators. No arrests have been made so far. "It's going to be up to the state on whether charges ultimately will be filed. But I can tell you self-defense plays a part in these," Flowers said. The sheriff emphasized that the investigation is ongoing and urged anyone who attended the party to contact his office. Lucie police responded to reports of multiple gunshots near Southeast Green River Parkway and Southeast Charleston Drive. Police said Gabriella Gina Hanley was driving south on Southeast Green River Parkway in a black Kia Forte with her boyfriend, Darrick Mincey Jr., when another vehicle pulled alongside them and fired multiple rounds into their car. Officers and rescue personnel began life-saving measures after finding Hanley with multiple gunshot wounds. She was pronounced dead Oct. Mincey was also struck by gunfire but survived. Numerous 9mm cartridge casings were recovered, and forensic evidence indicated the bullets were fired from two separate rifles, police said. Five years later, detectives are continuing to conduct interviews and examine forensic and digital evidence. At the time of her death, Hanley left behind a 20-month-old baby. CBS12 reported in 2022 that investigators had identified three people of interest, but no charges were filed against them. entry.title: DeSantis opens new I-95 interchange in Indian River County, a year early - WPEC
entry.summary: DeSantis opens new I-95 interchange in Indian River County, a year early    WPEC
entry.article_text: Ron DeSantis opened the new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road in Indian River County on Monday, calling it a critical connection for drivers, emergency crews and the region’s growing population. The roughly $100 million project opened one year ahead of schedule , according to the governor’s office and the Florida Department of Transportation. This is the first new interchange built in this area in almost 50 years, DeSantis said. It’s going to bring [a] new critical connection [to] I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit. The new exit is expected to ease congestion at nearby Indrio Road and State Road 60 interchanges, DeSantis said. Drivers traveling from Oslo Road to I-95 can expect their travel times to be cut in half, he added. With the number of daily vehicles on the corridor still expected to grow between now and 2045 significantly, the Oslo Road interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future, DeSantis said. The governor also said the direct interstate connection will help emergency crews respond faster in southern Indian River County. See also: Two killed, including 10th-grade girl, after rollover school bus crash in Polk County We anticipate that just for the local community on a normal basis, for local, like non-hurricane-type emergencies, that the emergency response time will be reduced by up to 56%, DeSantis said. That will ultimately save some lives, of course, because time is of the essence in some of these situations. FDOT Secretary Jared Perdue said the project was completed 400 days early through what the agency calls voluntary acceleration, which lets contractors propose ways to speed construction and share in the savings. This is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially, Perdue said. We’re really excited about that, to include cutting commute time in half and so many other benefits. DeSantis said FDOT also acquired land near the interchange for a dedicated gopher tortoise habitat. He said the site will be the only relocation area of its kind in Southeast Florida. Florida [is] showing that it’s possible to do the projects that we need done while also buttressing environmental stewardship, DeSantis said. Perdue said nearly $1 billion in transportation investment is planned for the Treasure Coast region. Indian River County Commissioner Joseph Flescher recounted his reaction when he first heard about the opening. "When I got the phone call, I said, ' We're not near completion. I had been here just two weeks ago. We were nowhere near where we're at.' This team worked an incredible operation, said Flescher. Flescher also highlighted how important this new entrance ot I-95 is to the growing population across the county. This interchange is very much needed in the development of our county. And I don't mean the future development. I mean the current development, Flescher said.

entry.title: Westlake considers school zone speed cameras near Seminole Ridge High School to improve student safety
entry.summary: The city of Westlake is considering installing speed enforcement cameras in a school zone near Seminole Ridge High School, a proposal that city leaders say would improve student safety. The topic is expected to come before the Westlake City Council during its meeting Tuesday at 6 p.m., as officials discuss a potential agreement with RedSpeed, the company that would provide the camera technology. WATCH BELOW: Westlake considers speed cameras near Seminole Ridge High Westlake considers speed cameras near Seminole Ridge High School According to Westlake City Manager Howard Brown Jr., the city has been discussing school zone speed cameras for about a year. A speed zone study conducted by the city found a need for additional enforcement in the area surrounding Seminole Ridge High School. 'Seminole Ridge High School will be the target area,' Brown said. City officials say the cameras would serve as an additional tool to address speeding drivers in the school zone. 'Some people are busy, and they are not paying attention that they are going through a school zone,' Brown said. Brown, who has a young child at home, said protecting children is a top priority. 'I have a little one at home. That's an area where we really want to protect our children and provide law enforcement with additional tools,' he said. Under the proposal, drivers caught traveling more than 10 mph over the posted speed limit on Seminole Pratt Whitney Road within the school zone would face a $100 citation. 'We are trying to break some of those bad driving habits,' Brown said. Not everyone is convinced the cameras are necessary. Westlake resident Nicole Haley said she worries speed cameras could worsen existing traffic congestion. 'I think it would back up traffic even more than it already is,' Haley said. Instead of adding cameras, Haley believes roadway improvements may be a better solution. 'I think integrating a roundabout like the one they have on Stribling would be better,' she said. If approved, the cameras could be operational before the end of the year. The city says there would also be a 30-day warning period before citations are issued. At this time, Seminole Ridge High School is the only school in the city being considered for speed camera enforcement. The speed camera discussion is one of several items on Tuesday night's council agenda. City officials have also indicated they will not move forward with license plate reader technology at this time. The meeting will be held at the Lodge

entry.title: Potential 2028 Democratic contenders set to discuss party’s future at post-midterms meeting
entry.summary: A group of potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidates is heading to Denver days after the midterms to discuss the partys future, in one of the partys first major gatherings following the election. Attendees will include former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and former US Ambassador to Japan Rahm Emanuel, as well as Sens. Ruben Gallego of Arizona, Chris Murphy of Connecticut, Raphael Warnock of Georgia and Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, according to an initial lineup shared first with CNN. The group of speakers also includes Govs. Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey and Abigail Spanberger of Virginia, plus several additional members of Congress. The Whats Next summit is being hosted from November 12-14 by Majority Democrats, an organization that launched last year to help Democrats win in more places. RELATED STORY | New midterm polling gives Democrats an edge in battleground states In staging the event less than two weeks after the midterms, where Democrats hope to retake the Senate and the House, the group is looking to move quickly to outline the lessons learned from the election that could be instructive going forward, including in the next White House race. This isnt a policy conference nor a talk shop on tactics, said Massachusetts Rep. Jake Auchincloss, chair of Majority Democrats, in a statement. Whats Next is timed for a unique moment after the midterms and before the presidential to debate a vision for the Democratic Party. Politicians who believe they have that vision should be on that stage. Organizers chose Denver partly because it is one of the cities under consideration to host the 2028 Democratic National Convention. The initial lineup also includes top party strategists such as David Axelrod, former senior adviser to President Barack Obama and a chief political analyst at CNN; Quentin Fulks, former principal deputy campaign manager for Kamala Harris in 2024; and Morris Katz, adviser to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Trump claims Iran is waiting until after midterm elections to strike deal Majority Democrats is not the only organization holding an event in the immediate aftermath of the midterms in a bid to shape the partys future. entry.summary: Teen identified after deadly Fellsmere shooting involving 100-plus teens    WPEC
entry.article_text: A 17-year-old was killed in a Fellsmere shooting Friday night after a meetup of more than 100 teens turned violent, according to the sheriff. The shooting happened around 11:24 p.m. at Garcia’s Boat Ramp , where a large crowd had gathered. Sheriff Eric Flowers said the group included teens ages 14 to 19, with drinking and fighting reported. These have been happening since before I was in high school, since before many of you were in high school. This has been going on for a long time. But now we're adding guns into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix. CBS12 confirmed with the family that the slain 17-year-old was Sulliman Bah, a senior at Sebastian River High School. He and a group of friends approached a pickup truck with two 18-year-olds inside. Detectives say Bah opened the door and attempted to punch someone inside when the passenger fired a single shot at Bah. See also: What Florida voters need to know about the 3 constitutional amendments on the Nov. ballot Bah was taken by friends toward Fellsmere. Deputies and EMS met them at Fellsmere City Hall and performed CPR before he was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later transported to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he succumbed to his injuries. No arrests have been made. Flowers said the driver and passenger inside the truck have cooperated with investigators and turned over the truck and firearm. The sheriff said the preliminary investigation indicates a self-defense claim may apply. We will be submitting a warrant in the case, but at this time it looks as though there will be a self-defense claim as a result, Flowers said. The sheriff said the state will ultimately decide whether charges are filed. Investigators used Flock technology to identify people connected to the truck and shooting. Deputies also recovered additional guns and multiple shell casings. Flowers said investigators believe the meetup was part of a growing trend of teens gathering at remote locations arranged through Snapchat , where fights are recorded and shared online. "We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," he said. "We've got kids out here losing their lives trying to go viral on social media." He said there may have been as many as four fights at the boat ramp that night, and investigators are still working to identify people who were there. "They had a history of fighting," Flowers said. "This has been an ongoing thing." The sheriff urged parents to ask their children whether they attended the meetup and encouraged anyone who witnessed the shooting or recorded it to contact investigators. "It's not safe," Flowers said. There's guns, and those two just don't mix. And now add in the fuel of the fire of social media, and now we have a 17-year-old dead." In a statement, the Indian River School District gave its condolences to the teen's family: The School District of Indian River County is heartbroken by this young person’s death. Our hearts are with his family, friends, and the students and staff who knew and cared about him. Grief support was in place over the weekend, including counselors at Sebastian River High School’s Homecoming Dance, and continues today as students and staff return to school. Our teams will remain available in the days ahead, offering care and responding to the needs of those affected. A spokesperson for SDIRC said the student had recently withdrawn from Sebastian River High School to be home schooled.

entry.article_text: Indiantown residents remain concerned about flooding after heavy rain left streets covered in water last week, with more rain and storms in the forecast for this week. CBS12 crews captured video of vehicles driving through standing water on roadways in parts of the village. Residents say flooding can quickly become expensive when water affects homes and property. The sad part is, if you don’t have insurance or anything like that you’re just stuck, your stuck with the bill, said Mary Brown, a Booker Park resident. The flooding has renewed questions about the more than $2 million drainage and roadway project in Booker Park. The project began in 2022 to help reduce flooding, but residents say heavy rain is still leaving some streets underwater. Village leaders have said they are working with Martin County on longer-term drainage solutions, including the possible repair or replacement of broken pipes. The next Indiantown Village Council meeting is Thursday night. With more rain possible this week, Martin County Fire Rescue and the Florida Department of Health in Martin County have tips available online for residents to plan ahead and avoid driving or walking through floodwater. You can CLICK HERE to view the entire list. Officials say water on a roadway may be deeper or more contaminated than it appears. Drivers who encounter a flooded road should turn around rather than attempt to drive through it. Martin County Fire Rescue responds to flooding-related emergencies, including when a vehicle becomes stuck in floodwater. Residents should call 911 during an emergency. For ongoing drainage problems or flooded roadways, residents can submit a report through Martin County’s online Request for Service system . The county asks residents to include the specific address or location and details about the issue, such as standing water, a blockage or a low spot near a drainage structure. CLICK HERE to submit a request. Health officials also advise residents whose wells flood to use bottled or boiled water until the well can be tested.

entry.summary: A deadly school bus crash in Polk County is raising new questions about how students are protected inside Florida school buses and why state law still falls short of federal safety recommendations. One student, a 10th grader on her way to Winter Haven High School, was killed Monday morning when a school bus carrying 39 people was involved in a crash. The circumstances surrounding the crash remain under investigation, including what happened outside the bus and what took place inside it. It's just heartbreaking,' Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said during a morning news briefing. Investigators have not released details about how many students were wearing seat belts, what type of restraints were in use, or whether the belts played a role in the outcome of the crash. Aaron was wearing the bus's standard lap belt at the time of the crash.Several years later, investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) examined that crash and studied how different types of seat belts affect student safety.The agency's testing showed significant differences between standard lap belts and lap-and-shoulder restraints. entry.title: No arrests after 17-year-old shot, killed at meetup in Indian River County, self-defense claim expected - WPTV
entry.summary: No arrests after 17-year-old shot, killed at meetup in Indian River County, self-defense claim expected    WPTV
entry.article_text: No arrests have been made in the shooting death of a 17-year-old at a teen meetup near Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County, with a self-defense claim expected in the case, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Monday.WATCH BELOW: Sheriff Eric Flowers give update on shooting death of teen"We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," Flowers said.The shooting occurred late Friday night when approximately 100 teens, ranging in age from 14 to 19, gathered at Garcia's Boat Ramp in the 3700 block of County Road 512, the sheriff said. Deputies had broken up a similar group earlier that evening before the crowd moved to the boat ramp."The 17-year-old, and a group of his friends, are approaching a truck, and there are two people, both 18 years old, inside of that truck. The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch," Flowers said. "He's going to punch on the people that are inside of that truck. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed 17-year-old in this case."The teen's friends drove him away from the scene, east on County Road 512, while calling 911 and a dispatcher told them to stop at Fellsmere City Hall, where emergency crews performed CPR, the sheriff said. He was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he died from his injuries.The two individuals in the truck were identified using the sheriff's office's Flock technology, the sheriff said. Flowers said both have been cooperative with investigators, surrendering the weapon used in the shooting and the truck. Additional individuals involved in the incident have also been identified through Flock, though some remain unidentified. Investigators also recovered other weapons from the vehicle in which the 17-year-old was transported from the scene.WATCH: 17-year-old dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat RampFlowers said a warrant will be submitted in the case, but it will be up to the state to determine whether charges are filed."There have been no arrests on this case at this time, because the preliminary investigation shows that the 17-year-old was opening the door to attempt to fight with the two that were inside of the vehicle. They had a history of fighting," Flowers said. "Self defense plays a part in these, and when these kids go out and videotape these fights, and now guns are involved, there's going to be more of this." Names of those involved are not being released as the investigation continues, the sheriff said.Investigators believe at least four fights occurred at the boat ramp on the night of the shooting. Multiple shell casings and rounds were recovered from the scene.During Monday's news conference, Flowers released video of the shooting, noting the footage had already circulated widely on social media and that the victim's mother had seen it. One of the 18-year-olds involved in the shooting attends Vero Beach High School.The sheriff said teen meetups like the one at Garcia's Boat Ramp are coordinated through Snapchat, making them difficult for law enforcement to track in advance."When it's Snapchat, it's basically a private conversation," Flowers said. "But it quickly can escalate to over 100, 150, 200 people there."Flowers said the meetups, which have included alcohol, fighting, and firearms, have been taking place for years across Indian River County, Okeechobee, and surrounding areas, but that social media has intensified the danger."Now we're adding guns and alcohol into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix, and so what we're seeing is an escalation of each one of these," Flowers said. There's guns, and those two just don't mix. And now add in the fuel of the fire of social media, and now we have a 17-year-old dead."The sheriff said teens at these gatherings are motivated in part by a desire for online attention."The kids like to fight, and they like to videotape it, and they like to get their likes and shares because of that," Flowers said. Parents, you see these videos. You do not want your teens out at these meetups."With Vero Beach High School's homecoming game scheduled for Friday and the dance on Saturday, Flowers said additional deputies will be on duty. Meanwhile, the sheriff urged parents to monitor their children's whereabouts and report any information about planned meetups to the sheriff's office."Parents, if your kids are telling you that they're headed out to one of these meetups, ask them where they're going. Ask, find out the details. Share that with us," Flowers said.He recommended parents use location-sharing apps such as Life360 to track their children and said a child appearing to be in a remote or unusual location can be an indicator that a meetup is taking place.The investigation remains active. Flowers said anyone who witnessed any of the events that night, including the shooting itself, and has not yet spoken to investigators is urged to come forward."I can tell you, our investigation is not even remotely over, and if we are able to identify people that were involved in this, from underage drinking to fighting, hurting other people," Flowers said. " If they did something wrong, they're going to have to be accountable for that."Anyone with information is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff's Office at 772-569-6700 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS.

"Parents, if your kids are telling you that they're headed out to one of these meetups, ask them where they're going. Ask, find out the details. Share that with us," Flowers said. He recommended parents use location-sharing apps such as Life360 to track their children and said a child appearing to be in a remote or unusual location can be an indicator that a meetup is taking place. The investigation remains active. Flowers said anyone who witnessed any of the events that night, including the shooting itself, and has not yet spoken to investigators is urged to come forward. "I can tell you, our investigation is not even remotely over, and if we are able to identify people that were involved in this, from underage drinking to fighting, hurting other people," Flowers said. " If they did something wrong, they're going to have to be accountable for that." Anyone with information is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff's Office at 772-569-6700 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS.

entry.summary: Five years later, Port St. Lucie police seek answers in 20-year-old woman’s killing    WPEC
entry.article_text: Five years after the shooting death of a 20-year-old woman, the Port St. Lucie Police Department is still seeking answers. Lucie police responded to reports of multiple gunshots near Southeast Green River Parkway and Southeast Charleston Drive. Police said Gabriella Gina Hanley was driving south on Southeast Green River Parkway in a black Kia Forte with her boyfriend, Darrick Mincey Jr., when another vehicle pulled alongside them and fired multiple rounds into their car. Officers and rescue personnel began life-saving measures after finding Hanley with multiple gunshot wounds. She was pronounced dead Oct. Mincey was also struck by gunfire but survived. See also: Teen identified after deadly Fellsmere shooting involving 100-plus teens Investigators found the Kia had 37 bullet impacts. Numerous 9mm cartridge casings were recovered, and forensic evidence indicated the bullets were fired from two separate rifles, police said. Five years later, detectives are continuing to conduct interviews and examine forensic and digital evidence. At the time of her death, Hanley left behind a 20-month-old baby. CBS12 reported in 2022 that investigators had identified three people of interest, but no charges were filed against them. Anyone with information is asked to call the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS (8477) .

They'll give us a point out; we'll find it with our radar, we'll go check it out, and basically get their intention, what they're looking to do," Olive said. "If they're just a person who doesn't know they're not supposed to be there, then we'll help escort them out of the TFR safely."Despite the number of interceptions, officials said the overwhelming majority involve pilots making mistakes, not people attempting to threaten the restricted airspace."I would say the majority, that is correct," Olive said. "There's also a majority of it where they have the proper code, they have the proper clearance, they just forget to squawk the right code, so they take off, they have a clearance, they're good to go, but they haven't punched in that clearance in their airplane, and then they do so on departure, but we still have to scramble on them because we don't know their intention because they're not squawking the right code."Asked whether any of the interceptions he has handled involved bad intentions, Olive said: "Not, I don't, no, not from my experience, no, they're just people who forget or who have not done the proper flight planning."Officials say most of the aircraft involved are not large commercial jets."The majority would be smaller Cessnas, single-engine planes for sure," said Olive.Palm Beach presents unique challenges, according to NORAD, because of the large amount of general aviation traffic in the area."I'd say Mar-a-Lago is interesting. It's different from up north," one pilot said. "There's more general aviation down here due to the nice weather, the amount of flight schools that are around here, people want to fly up and down the coast, the banner towers, so we get more general aviation traffic down here for sure."The restricted airspace itself consists of two zones."It's a temporary flight restriction," a pilot explained. "It encompasses a 10-mile ring centered at the airfield here, and then there's a 30-mile ring as well that extends beyond that. The 10-mile ring is essentially a no-fly zone."Pilots operating inside the larger ring must follow special FAA procedures."You have to be on a flight plan. You have to be squawking a discrete code, and in comms with ATC."Officials emphasized that while most violations are innocent mistakes, every response is treated seriously."We're always training to take it all the way to the conclusion that, hey, this is a person with bad intentions," Olive said. "Obviously that is a last, last resort. We're not there to hand down the judgment or the punishment; we're just there to enforce the TFR and escort them safely either to land or outside of the TFR."Any penalties are handled by the FAA once the aircraft lands."We'll safely escort them out. We'll make sure that they land. We'll monitor them until they land at their destination," Olive said. "Upon landing, they'll be notified that they have a phone number to call that'll be a phone number that leads them to the FAA and then the FAA will deal with that."Officials also stressed how closely NORAD and the FAA work together."It's imperative. We're completely intertwined," Olive said. "The FAA, they can't do their job without us. We can't do our job without them."For residents wondering why military aircraft may be overhead during presidential visits, officials say the mission comes down to safety."Any time you have the president of the United States travel anywhere, that's a very high visibility movement, and it attracts a lot of attention not only within the United States but nationally as well," one pilot said.And for pilots flying near Palm Beach, NORAD had a straightforward message:"If you're going to fly, if you're an avid flyer, check your NOTAMs before you fly, just so everybody's safe, and you're not where you're not supposed to be."When asked whether he had a message for Trump himself, the pilot smiled."Yeah, sir, we'll be above you, keeping you safe in the sky."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Shooting death of Gabriella Hanley remains unsolved 5 years later, police seeking tips
entry.summary: Five years have passed, but the shooting death of 20-year-old Gabriella Hanley remains unsolved. No one has been charged with her death, and Port St. Lucie police are asking anyone with information to come forward. WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie police investigating deadly shooting Mystery gunman fires shots into car in Port St. Lucie, killing woman On Oct. 5, 2021, at around 11:45 p.m., Port St. Lucie police said they responded to reports of multiple gunshots near Southeast Green River Parkway and Southeast Charleston Drive. Hanley was driving southbound on Southeast Green River Parkway in a black Kia Forte with her boyfriend, 21-year-old Darrick Mincey Jr., when another vehicle pulled alongside them and fired multiple rounds into their car, police said. Hanley was shot multiple times, police said. Officers and rescue personnel immediately attempted lifesaving measures, but she later died in the early morning hours on Oct. 6, 2021. Mincey was also struck by gunfire but survived. Investigators said they determined the Kia sustained 37 bullet impacts during the shooting. Numerous 9mm cartridge casings were recovered from the scene, and subsequent forensic examination determined they had been fired from two different firearms, police said. The suspect vehicle was described as a silver four-door sedan that fled southbound on Southeast Green River Parkway. In the years since Hanley's death, Port St. Lucie Police Department detectives have continued to investigate her death, conducting numerous interviews, examining forensic and digital evidence, and following up on investigative leads. As of Tuesday, no one has been charged with Hanley's death, and police continue to search for answers. If you know something about what happened to Hanley that night, no matter how insignificant you may think it is, Port St. Lucie police are asking you to come forward. You can call Port St. Lucie Police Department Major Crimes Division at 772-871-5000 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS (8477). Tips provided can remain anonymous.

entry.title: Gov. Ron DeSantis announces removal of 220 Medicaid providers amid fraud, abuse investigation

Ron DeSantis announced Tuesday that Florida's intensified effort to root out fraud, waste and abuse in the state's Medicaid program has resulted in more than $1 billion in projected savings and the removal of hundreds of providers from the system. Speaking at the Healthcare District of Palm Beach County alongside Agency for Health Care Administration (AHCA) Secretary Shevaun Harris, DeSantis said the state has expanded oversight and enforcement measures to identify fraudulent billing and improper Medicaid payments. entry.article_text: Ron DeSantis announced Tuesday that Florida's intensified effort to root out fraud, waste and abuse in the state's Medicaid program has resulted in more than $1 billion in projected savings and the removal of hundreds of providers from the system.Speaking at the Healthcare District of Palm Beach County alongside Agency for Health Care Administration (AHCA) Secretary Shevaun Harris, DeSantis said the state has expanded oversight and enforcement measures to identify fraudulent billing and improper Medicaid payments.WATCH BELOW: State targets Medicaid fraud, removes hundreds of providers"We want to make sure that what is being spent is being spent well," DeSantis said. "Medicaid dollars must go to healthcare for eligible Floridians, not to people who are gaming the system."According to state officials, AHCA has conducted more than 400 provider site visits since January and increased the use of data analytics, claims monitoring and background screening to uncover suspicious activity.As part of the crackdown, the state said more than 150 fraud-related referrals have been made to the Florida Attorney General's Office over the past year, more than 250 providers have been placed on payment restrictions or had payments suspended, and more than 220 providers have been terminated from Florida Medicaid due to fraud, waste or abuse.State officials said those terminated providers accounted for more than $230 million in Medicaid billing in 2025.A major focus of the effort has been Applied Behavioral Analysis (ABA) services, commonly used to help children with autism. According to Harris, Florida Medicaid spent approximately $6.57 billion on ABA services between 2023 and 2025, nearly four times more than any other state's Medicaid program. At one point, spending was projected to grow by 30% annually.The state moved ABA services into managed care in 2025, a change officials say has improved oversight and slowed spending growth to less than 10% annually. As a result, the state now projects ABA-related expenditures at roughly $2.8 billion, more than $1 billion lower than previous forecasts."That is where we want our funding going," Harris said. "Not in the pockets of crooks."Investigators uncovered instances in which providers billed Medicaid for impossible service schedules, including claims for more than 24 hours of care in a single day and services allegedly provided continuously through weekends and holidays.To strengthen provider screening, AHCA also partnered with identity verification company SentiLink to help identify synthetic identities, suspicious ownership structures and other potential fraud indicators before providers enter the Medicaid system.In July, WPTV chief investigator Jamie Ostroff spoke with families in Palm Beach County whose access to ABA was abruptly cut off by Medicaid. They told her ABA was a lifeline for their children who were able to learn in school, communicate, use the bathroom and control tantrums thanks to the therapy.Despite the enforcement actions, DeSantis and Harris emphasized that the effort is aimed at fraudulent providers and not families who rely on Medicaid services.When Ostroff asked about concerns from families struggling to access ABA therapy, particularly in Palm Beach County, DeSantis replied, "If you have a provider that is doing some legitimate services and much fraudulent — to the extent that those services get interrupted, that's not AHCA's fault. That's that provider's fault."Harris added that managed care plans are working with affected recipients to connect them with new providers when a provider is removed from the program."If there is a parent watching and they're having any issues, they can contact the agency and we will help them ourselves or connect them with their managed care plan," Harris said.DeSantis said the Medicaid initiative is part of a broader effort to ensure taxpayer dollars are spent responsibly while maintaining Florida's fiscal position. The governor highlighted the state's recent budget reductions, debt repayment efforts and tax relief measures as examples of what he described as responsible financial management.State officials said AHCA will continue conducting site visits, monitoring claims and referring suspected fraud cases for further investigation.Ostroff asked Harris for a list of providers accused of fraud. She said she would provide what she could without jeopardizing any ongoing, potentially criminal, investigations."This is kind of just the opening salvo," DeSantis said. "I would anticipate you will see more results coming in the weeks, months and years ahead."

entry.title: Palm Beach Gardens High School football players excelling on and off the field with a top state GPA
entry.summary: The Palm Beach Gardens High School football team is not only winning on the field the Gators are also setting a high standard in the classroom, carrying a team grade point average between 3.3 and 3.4, one of the best in the state. Following a dominant Monday night football win against Boynton Beach High School, the team is back focused on the game plan, both on the field and in school. WATCH BELOW: Palm Beach Gardens HS football players are excelling on and off the field with a top state GPA Palm Beach Gardens High School football players are excelling on and off the field Two years ago, head coach Phil Norman made academics a central priority when he took over the program. 'One of the first meetings was detailed in the classroom. A lot of these kids do have aspirations to go to college, and the main thing to get there is you have to be accepted into the college programs first,' Norman said. The team's grade point average ranks among the best in not only Palm Beach County, but the entire state. Junior defensive back Ellby Gedeum is one player setting the pace with a near-perfect GPA. 'My GPA is a 3.9 right now,' Gedeum said. Gedeum said he handles the demands of being a student-athlete by staying disciplined after games. 'Just adapting after a long game, I come home, do my homework and stuff,' Gedeum said. Junior running back Rasheen Brooks is also excelling as a student-athlete. 'My GPA is a 3.5 as we speak, and I have 21 credit hours right now as a junior, so I am eligible to graduate as of now, but you know I'm not. I am in a good spot as a student-athlete,' Brooks said. Brooks said he wants to play college football, and he knows academics are the foundation for getting there. 'Without the books there is no college, so you can be the best athlete you are but without books there's nothing,' Brooks said. entry.title: Teen dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County - WPBF
entry.summary: Teen dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County    WPBF
entry.article_text: A 17-year-old boy died after a shooting late Friday close to a boat ramp near Fellsmere and Vero Beach, the Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Saturday. The Indian River School District said the unnamed teen recently withdrew from Sebastian River High School to homeschool and was not enrolled in the district at the time of the shooting. "We are deeply saddened by the loss of this young person, and our hearts are with his family, friends, and the Sebastian River High School community," district spokeswoman Kyra Schafte said in a statement to WPBF. In a follow-up email she wrote: "This remains an active investigation, and we are in constant communication with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office. Please direct questions about the investigation to IRCSO. Our primary focus is supporting our students, staff, families, and community during this difficult time." A dance is scheduled for 7 p.m. Saturday at Sebastian River High. Read more at: https://www.miamiherald.com/news/article317482082.html#storylink=cpy At 11:24 p.m., deputies responded to reports of a juvenile shot in the area of Garcia's Boat Ramp in the 3700 block of County Road 512 and near the Fort Drum Marsh Conservation Area. Deputies located the teen and began lifesaving measures until Indian River County Fire Rescue arrived. He was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he died from his injuries, the sheriff's office said. "At this time, this appears to be an isolated incident, and there is no threat to the public," Lt. Kevin Jaworski wrote in an alert to the media. "This is an active investigation." He told WPBF that investigators have interviewed all parties involved in the case. Anyone with information about this incident is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office (772-569-6700) or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers (1-800-273-TIPS). Detectives from the Criminal Investigations Division and crime scene personnel were processing the scene and interviewing multiple witnesses. The area remains open to the public. entry.article_text: Indiantown residents remain concerned about flooding after heavy rain left streets covered in water last week, with more rain and storms in the forecast for this week. The sad part is, if you don’t have insurance or anything like that you’re just stuck, your stuck with the bill, said Mary Brown, a Booker Park resident. The flooding has renewed questions about the more than $2 million drainage and roadway project in Booker Park. The project began in 2022 to help reduce flooding, but residents say heavy rain is still leaving some streets underwater. Village leaders have said they are working with Martin County on longer-term drainage solutions, including the possible repair or replacement of broken pipes. The next Indiantown Village Council meeting is Thursday night. With more rain possible this week, Martin County Fire Rescue and the Florida Department of Health in Martin County have tips available online for residents to plan ahead and avoid driving or walking through floodwater. You can CLICK HERE to view the entire list. Officials say water on a roadway may be deeper or more contaminated than it appears. Drivers who encounter a flooded road should turn around rather than attempt to drive through it. Martin County Fire Rescue responds to flooding-related emergencies, including when a vehicle becomes stuck in floodwater. Residents should call 911 during an emergency. For ongoing drainage problems or flooded roadways, residents can submit a report through Martin County’s online Request for Service system . The county asks residents to include the specific address or location and details about the issue, such as standing water, a blockage or a low spot near a drainage structure. CLICK HERE to submit a request. Health officials also advise residents whose wells flood to use bottled or boiled water until the well can be tested.

entry.article_text: Five years after the shooting death of a 20-year-old woman, the Port St. Lucie Police Department is still seeking answers. Lucie police responded to reports of multiple gunshots near Southeast Green River Parkway and Southeast Charleston Drive. Police said Gabriella Gina Hanley was driving south on Southeast Green River Parkway in a black Kia Forte with her boyfriend, Darrick Mincey Jr., when another vehicle pulled alongside them and fired multiple rounds into their car. Officers and rescue personnel began life-saving measures after finding Hanley with multiple gunshot wounds. She was pronounced dead Oct. Mincey was also struck by gunfire but survived. See also: Teen identified after deadly Fellsmere shooting involving 100-plus teens Investigators found the Kia had 37 bullet impacts. Numerous 9mm cartridge casings were recovered, and forensic evidence indicated the bullets were fired from two separate rifles, police said. Five years later, detectives are continuing to conduct interviews and examine forensic and digital evidence. At the time of her death, Hanley left behind a 20-month-old baby. CBS12 reported in 2022 that investigators had identified three people of interest, but no charges were filed against them. Anyone with information is asked to call the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS (8477) .

entry.title: DeSantis opens new I-95 interchange in Indian River County, a year early - cw34.com
entry.summary: DeSantis opens new I-95 interchange in Indian River County, a year early    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Ron DeSantis opened the new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road in Indian River County on Monday, calling it a critical connection for drivers, emergency crews and the region’s growing population. The roughly $100 million project opened one year ahead of schedule , according to the governor’s office and the Florida Department of Transportation. This is the first new interchange built in this area in almost 50 years, DeSantis said. It’s going to bring [a] new critical connection [to] I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit. The new exit is expected to ease congestion at nearby Indrio Road and State Road 60 interchanges, DeSantis said. Drivers traveling from Oslo Road to I-95 can expect their travel times to be cut in half, he added. With the number of daily vehicles on the corridor still expected to grow between now and 2045 significantly, the Oslo Road interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future, DeSantis said. The governor also said the direct interstate connection will help emergency crews respond faster in southern Indian River County. See also: Two killed, including 10th-grade girl, after rollover school bus crash in Polk County We anticipate that just for the local community on a normal basis, for local, like non-hurricane-type emergencies, that the emergency response time will be reduced by up to 56%, DeSantis said. That will ultimately save some lives, of course, because time is of the essence in some of these situations. FDOT Secretary Jared Perdue said the project was completed 400 days early through what the agency calls voluntary acceleration, which lets contractors propose ways to speed construction and share in the savings. This is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially, Perdue said. We’re really excited about that, to include cutting commute time in half and so many other benefits. DeSantis said FDOT also acquired land near the interchange for a dedicated gopher tortoise habitat. He said the site will be the only relocation area of its kind in Southeast Florida. Florida [is] showing that it’s possible to do the projects that we need done while also buttressing environmental stewardship, DeSantis said. Perdue said nearly $1 billion in transportation investment is planned for the Treasure Coast region. Indian River County Commissioner Joseph Flescher recounted his reaction when he first heard about the opening. "When I got the phone call, I said, ' We're not near completion. I had been here just two weeks ago. We were nowhere near where we're at.' This team worked an incredible operation, said Flescher. Flescher also highlighted how important this new entrance ot I-95 is to the growing population across the county. This interchange is very much needed in the development of our county. And I don't mean the future development. I mean the current development, Flescher said.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie streets flood after downpour, stranding vehicles and disrupting commutes - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie streets flood after downpour, stranding vehicles and disrupting commutes    WPEC
entry.article_text: Heavy rain flooded roads across Port St. Lucie Tuesday afternoon, leaving some vehicles stranded, forcing children to walk through standing water after school and prompting a response from police officers and city crews. According to the City of Port St. Lucie , a large amount of rain fell in a short period of time, leading to temporary road closures and flooding in multiple areas. Public Works crews responded to flooding near Savona Boulevard and California Boulevard, closing the roadway until it was safe for travel. The city also reported high-water conditions near Thornhill Drive and Floresta Drive, where Phase 3 construction is underway. On Southwest Thornhill Drive, school buses continued dropping off students despite flooded streets. CBS12 News saw children step off buses carrying their shoes and walk barefoot through standing water to reach home. Along Southwest Broadview Avenue near Crosstown Parkway, residents watched as water spilled across the roadway, making it difficult for drivers to tell where the street ended and floodwater began. "If you didn't see the grass here, you wouldn't know where the road is," resident Kevin Burke told CBS12 News. "It was steady sheets of rain for a good hour. Non-stop, and I mean heavy, heavy." Police officers directed traffic while Public Works crews set up barricades and monitored conditions during the evening commute. Burke said flooding in the area has become a familiar problem during heavy downpours. "When it rains heavy like it did today, it's like this all the time, from that canal coming up," he said. Burke said standing water presents concerns beyond traffic issues. "We have a pond over there by Crosstown and Bayshore. It's got signs all around it saying there are gators in it. It's a long shot, but it could happen, and that's what worries me, with kids and the animals," he said. For some residents, the flooding disrupted everyday tasks. "She has her elderly brother, who's 83 years old, and she's in her 60s, and she was going to run out and get Chinese food, and now she's still sitting here waiting because she can't get to it," Burke said. Earlier in the day, Port St. Lucie police reported flooding at several intersections, including SE Evans Avenue and SE Airoso Boulevard, SE Eyerly Avenue and SE Airoso Boulevard, SW Bayshore Boulevard and SW Thornhill Drive, and NE Floresta Drive and NE Ardsley Drive. See also: Opponents, supporters clash over Palm Beach County Israel Bonds investments City officials said Public Works crews continued monitoring conditions as water slowly receded Tuesday evening. Officials also reminded residents not to walk or drive through flooded roadways because it can be difficult to determine how deep the water is.

entry.title: U.S Senate candidate Angie Nixon campaigns in Fort Pierce, talks economy and reproductive health - WPBF
entry.summary: U.S Senate candidate Angie Nixon campaigns in Fort Pierce, talks economy and reproductive health    WPBF
entry.article_text: Senate candidate Angie Nixon visited Fort Pierce on Tuesday to speak with voters about reproductive health care, the economy, and other issues as part of her campaign across Florida ahead of the general election. Nixon, who represents a Jacksonville-area district in the Florida House of Representatives and describes herself as a Democratic Socialist, is holding town hall meetings across the state to connect with voters. Planned Parenthood President and CEO Alexis McGill Johnson hosted the Fort Pierce town hall, focusing on reproductive freedom and Florida's maternal mortality crisis. McGill Johnson and Nixon outlined the leadership they believe Florida families need, including protecting abortion access and expanding comprehensive health care services statewide. "Representative Nixon is a true champion for reproductive freedom," McGill Johnson said. "In the Senate, she is going to stand up for affordable health care and our right to make our own decisions about our own bodies." During the event, Nixon addressed a question about a proposed Islamic center approved for construction in Palm Beach County. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "This is a country where folks should have freedom of religion," Nixon said. "I would speak out against that type of opposition and hate if it was directed at a synagogue being built, if it was directed at a church being built, if it was directed at any other spiritual facility." Nixon also discussed the state of reproductive health care in Florida and other issues raised by voters. "Gas is high, people are struggling to get to and from work, and then they can't even afford the food anymore, let alone taking their children to the movies or out to eat, that's null and void now," one voter said. Nixon won the Democratic primary in St. Lucie County with about 54% of the vote. When asked how she plans to close the gap between herself and Republican incumbent Ashley Moody, Nixon said she intends to continue engaging with voters, including those who may disagree with her. "They have someone who is going to put them first," Nixon said when asked about the message she hopes attendees took away from Tuesday's event. She added that her campaign for U.S. Senate is focused on putting money back in people's pockets. Nixon spoke with voters for about an hour. Her next stop is in the Orlando area. entry.summary: Port St. Lucie roads face reroutes as flooding leaves cars partially submerged    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Heavy rain flooded roads across Port St. Lucie Tuesday afternoon, leaving some vehicles stranded, forcing children to walk through standing water after school and prompting a response from police officers and city crews. According to the City of Port St. Lucie , a large amount of rain fell in a short period of time, leading to temporary road closures and flooding in multiple areas. Public Works crews responded to flooding near Savona Boulevard and California Boulevard, closing the roadway until it was safe for travel. The city also reported high-water conditions near Thornhill Drive and Floresta Drive, where Phase 3 construction is underway. On Southwest Thornhill Drive, school buses continued dropping off students despite flooded streets. CBS12 News saw children step off buses carrying their shoes and walk barefoot through standing water to reach home. Along Southwest Broadview Avenue near Crosstown Parkway, residents watched as water spilled across the roadway, making it difficult for drivers to tell where the street ended and floodwater began. "If you didn't see the grass here, you wouldn't know where the road is," resident Kevin Burke told CBS12 News. "It was steady sheets of rain for a good hour. Non-stop, and I mean heavy, heavy." Police officers directed traffic while Public Works crews set up barricades and monitored conditions during the evening commute. Burke said flooding in the area has become a familiar problem during heavy downpours. "When it rains heavy like it did today, it's like this all the time, from that canal coming up," he said. Burke said standing water presents concerns beyond traffic issues. "We have a pond over there by Crosstown and Bayshore. It's got signs all around it saying there are gators in it. It's a long shot, but it could happen, and that's what worries me, with kids and the animals," he said. For some residents, the flooding disrupted everyday tasks. "She has her elderly brother, who's 83 years old, and she's in her 60s, and she was going to run out and get Chinese food, and now she's still sitting here waiting because she can't get to it," Burke said. Earlier in the day, Port St. Lucie police reported flooding at several intersections, including SE Evans Avenue and SE Airoso Boulevard, SE Eyerly Avenue and SE Airoso Boulevard, SW Bayshore Boulevard and SW Thornhill Drive, and NE Floresta Drive and NE Ardsley Drive. See also: Opponents, supporters clash over Palm Beach County Israel Bonds investments City officials said Public Works crews continued monitoring conditions as water slowly receded Tuesday evening. Officials also reminded residents not to walk or drive through flooded roadways because it can be difficult to determine how deep the water is.

entry.title: 5 years after Gabriella Hanley's unsolved killing, family and police still calling on community for answers
entry.summary: Five years after Gabriella 'Gabi' Hanley was shot and killed in an apparent drive-by shooting in Port St. Lucie, no arrests have been made in her case. WATCH BELOW: Family seeks answers 5 years after loved one killed Gabi Hanley cold case: Port St. Lucie family seeks answers 5 years later Hanley, 20, was shot along Green River Parkway in 2021. Her boyfriend, who was in the car at the time, was also hit by gunfire but survived. Hanley left behind a 14-month-old daughter, who is now 6 years old. Port St. Lucie police identified several people of interest at the time of the shooting, but five years later, no one has been arrested. The pain of losing Gabi still lingers for her mother, Nicole Vigilante. 'It is tough, but I gotta be strong for my granddaughter,' Vigilante said. As Gabi's daughter grows older, the family is searching for answers for themselves and for her. 'Now she's getting older, and she has questions,' Vigilante said. 'And we want to be able to give her those answers,' Krystal Benitez, Gabi's cousin, added. For Gabi's loved ones, her daughter is a constant reminder of who she was. 'We're reminded of the situation every single day,' Alexia Perez, Gabi's best friend, said. 'We will never forget Gabi. Her daughter is walking memory of her.' 'Gabi was an amazing, amazing woman,' Benitez added. Port St. Lucie police turned to social media Tuesday, saying information that was not shared at the time of the shooting could make a difference today. They're asking anyone with information to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department's Major Crimes Division at 772-871-5000 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-8477. Gabi's family and friends are doing their part to keep the case alive by sharing her story and raising awareness throughout the community. 'We have been spending the day handing out flyers going to all local businesses just trying to again raise awareness,' Benitez said. They are now calling on the community to come forward with information. 'There's a little girl right now that's being raised without her mother, so be brave for her and come forward,' Benitez said.
