entry.article_text: A 17-year-old was killed in a Fellsmere shooting Friday night after a meetup of more than 100 teens turned violent, according to the sheriff. The shooting happened around 11:24 p.m. at Garcia’s Boat Ramp , where a large crowd had gathered. Sheriff Eric Flowers said the group included teens ages 14 to 19, with drinking and fighting reported. These have been happening since before I was in high school, since before many of you were in high school. This has been going on for a long time. But now we're adding guns into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix. CBS12 confirmed with the family that the slain 17-year-old was Sulliman Bah, a senior at Sebastian River High School. He and a group of friends approached a pickup truck with two 18-year-olds inside. Detectives say Bah opened the door and attempted to punch someone inside when the passenger fired a single shot at Bah. See also: What Florida voters need to know about the 3 constitutional amendments on the Nov. ballot Bah was taken by friends toward Fellsmere. Deputies and EMS met them at Fellsmere City Hall and performed CPR before he was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later transported to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he succumbed to his injuries. No arrests have been made. Flowers said the driver and passenger inside the truck have cooperated with investigators and turned over the truck and firearm. The sheriff said the preliminary investigation indicates a self-defense claim may apply. We will be submitting a warrant in the case, but at this time it looks as though there will be a self-defense claim as a result, Flowers said. The sheriff said the state will ultimately decide whether charges are filed. Investigators used Flock technology to identify people connected to the truck and shooting. Deputies also recovered additional guns and multiple shell casings. Flowers said investigators believe the meetup was part of a growing trend of teens gathering at remote locations arranged through Snapchat , where fights are recorded and shared online. "We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," he said. "We've got kids out here losing their lives trying to go viral on social media." He said there may have been as many as four fights at the boat ramp that night, and investigators are still working to identify people who were there. "They had a history of fighting," Flowers said. "This has been an ongoing thing." The sheriff urged parents to ask their children whether they attended the meetup and encouraged anyone who witnessed the shooting or recorded it to contact investigators. "It's not safe," Flowers said. There's guns, and those two just don't mix. And now add in the fuel of the fire of social media, and now we have a 17-year-old dead." In a statement, the Indian River School District gave its condolences to the teen's family: The School District of Indian River County is heartbroken by this young person’s death. Our hearts are with his family, friends, and the students and staff who knew and cared about him. Grief support was in place over the weekend, including counselors at Sebastian River High School’s Homecoming Dance, and continues today as students and staff return to school. Our teams will remain available in the days ahead, offering care and responding to the needs of those affected. A spokesperson for SDIRC said the student had recently withdrawn from Sebastian River High School to be home schooled.

entry.title: Islamic Center controversy prompts review of Palm Beach County approval process
entry.summary: WPTV is listening to concerns about what could come next following a lot of controversy surrounding a proposed Islamic center, school and daycare in Palm Beach County's Agricultural Reserve near Delray Beach. Now, WPTV's Joel Lopez is getting answers from Palm Beach County Commissioner Maria Sachs, who is asking county staff to review how some projects, including places of worship, receive approval, a move that could affect how similar projects are handled in the future. WATCH BELOW: Islamic Center controversy prompts county review of approval process Islamic Center controversy prompts review of approval process The proposed development near Lyons Road in Delray Beach has sparked public debate for months, with residents raising concerns about the project and whether projects of that nature should receive additional public scrutiny. During a recent county commission meeting, Sachs asked county staff to review portions of the county's land development code involving government facilities and places of worship. 'I would like board direction to staff to research and prepare a presentation on government services and places of worship uses with draft revisions to the ULDC to require their approval as a Class A conditional use approval before the BCC,' Sachs said. Later in the discussion, Sachs explained why she wants staff to take another look at the current process. 'For many years, any government facilities or places of worship were able to get approval through DRO, which is an administrative approval through the zoning staff, and never came before the board for a hearing,' Sachs said. Sachs stressed she is not proposing an immediate change to county rules, but to begin the first steps in the process. 'I'm asking the staff to review that and bring it back to us for a presentation and our consensus on it and what we think about it,' Sachs said. entry.article_text: WPTV is listening to concerns about what could come next following a lot of controversy surrounding a proposed Islamic center, school and daycare in Palm Beach County's Agricultural Reserve near Delray Beach.Now, WPTV's Joel Lopez is getting answers from Palm Beach County Commissioner Maria Sachs, who is asking county staff to review how some projects, including places of worship, receive approval, a move that could affect how similar projects are handled in the future.WATCH BELOW: Islamic Center controversy prompts county review of approval processThe proposed development near Lyons Road in Delray Beach has sparked public debate for months, with residents raising concerns about the project and whether projects of that nature should receive additional public scrutiny.During a recent county commission meeting, Sachs asked county staff to review portions of the county's land development code involving government facilities and places of worship."I would like board direction to staff to research and prepare a presentation on government services and places of worship uses with draft revisions to the ULDC to require their approval as a Class A conditional use approval before the BCC," Sachs said.Later in the discussion, Sachs explained why she wants staff to take another look at the current process."For many years, any government facilities or places of worship were able to get approval through DRO, which is an administrative approval through the zoning staff, and never came before the board for a hearing," Sachs said.Sachs stressed she is not proposing an immediate change to county rules, but to begin the first steps in the process."I'm asking the staff to review that and bring it back to us for a presentation and our consensus on it and what we think about it," Sachs said.The discussion comes as residents continue to question how the proposed Islamic center moved through the approval process."The issue is whether or not we are going to bring all classifications back to the board as opposed to singling out places of worship," said County attorney David Ottey.Lopez has been digging into this project and learned that the school and daycare portion of the project went before county commissioners in 2023. Sachs, then-Commissioner Sara Baxter and former Commissioner Michael Barnett voted against the proposal, but it was ultimately approved in a 4-3 vote.Commissioners Maria Marino, Marci Woodward, Gregg Weiss and then-Commissioner Mack Bernard voted in favor, allowing the project to move forward.The proposed mosque on an adjacent parcel, however, did not come before county commissioners because places of worship can currently be approved administratively by county staff.That process was the focus of several public comments during Tuesday's meeting.One resident urged county commissioners to revisit the issue."Please consider the vote that was made in 2023," said Pamela Higer-Polani, an attorney who lives in the Ag Reserve. "There is precedent that if this body, this esteemed body, reevaluates its decision, you have it within your power to open up the vote again. We are asking you to do so and reconsider."Another resident questioned whether the project has already obtained legal protections that could make changes difficult."My question is whether those approvals have become legally vested and immune from subsequent action from this commission," the resident said.The resident also asked county officials to answer several legal questions publicly, including if the projects will grandfather development rights, and if construction has not commenced and vested rights have not been established, could a moratorium or new Agricultural Reserve development restrictions adopted by the commission legally apply to this project.WPTV got answers from Sachs, who told WPTV that any changes to the approval process would not affect projects that have already received county approval."If we are able to get these amendments passed, do you think that's going to change the projects going forward?" asked Lopez."It won't change any project that's already been approved," answered Sachs.Sachs said changing the status of previously approved projects would likely require legal action. She also said she is considering a moratorium on new applications, and those in the works while county staff reviews the current process and prepares recommendations for commissioners."My message is very clear: I hear your voices, I know that you're upset, and I understand that, and actually I agree," Sachs said. "This has been an issue, and this is something we need to clear up."Not everyone speaking during public comment opposed the project.Rabbi Steve Moss urged county leaders and residents to support religious freedom regardless of faith."As faith leaders and citizens of Delray Beach, we value living in a pluralistic, respectful democracy where faith communities can live side-by-side in peace," Moss said.Moss also defended the ability of religious groups to build facilities in the community."We join communities throughout our country in standing together and defending every faith community's right to build houses of worship and community centers," Moss said.Questions were also raised by commissioners about the legal implications of changing approval standards for houses of worship.Commissioner Maria Marino asked county attorneys whether federal protections could limit what the county can do."Before we go this route, I would like clarification on what we can and can't do when it comes to a religious use or a place of worship," Marino said.County attorneys told commissioners they would return with research and legal analysis, including any federal and state legal considerations.For now, no code changes have been approved, and no action has been taken against previously approved projects. County staff is expected to review the issue and bring findings and recommendations back to commissioners for future discussion.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

entry.title: Trump seeks to turn his Palm Beach Co. golf club into permanent presidential golf club
entry.summary: President Donald Trump is seeking to turn Trump International Golf Club in Palm Beach County into 'the permanent United States Presidential Golf Course,' according to a letter from the golf club's attorney to county commissioners. 'Our client proposes to make the TIGC golf courses and amenities available to all past, current, and future U.S. Presidents regardless of party affiliation and all visiting foreign heads of state, at the discretion of the White House,' the letter said. According to the letter, TIGC would work with the General Services Administration and United States Secret Service 'to design an appropriate Presidential lodging facility.' The Sept. 3 letter touted the course's proximity to the airport, South Florida weather, and in-place security  calling it 'one of the most secure golf courses in the world'  as factors that made it 'the ideal site for such a use' 'Just as Camp David, Windsor Castle, or the Elysee Palace are known worldwide, so too will the Presidential Golf Course in Palm Beach County,' Attorney Harvey E. Oyer wrote in the letter. Oyer said in the letter TIGC would pay the cost of constructing the lodging facility and would provide access to the facilities 'at no cost to the federal government.' 'This is a gift that the President would like to share with his successors, the people of America, and his fellow Palm Beach County residents,' the letter said. 'It should be noted that President Trump will be out of office before this proposed project could be completed so this is a gift to his successors.' The club is located on county-owned land and is leased long term to the club, according to the letter. The letter proposes an agreement in which TIGC 'grants the County a legal right' to the land for the lodging and other structures, with the county entering into a lease agreement with the federal government 'so that the County controls the property as landlord.' The letter said the county would continue to control the asset if the federal government defaulted or no longer wanted to use the premises. This is a developing story that may be updated as WPTV works to learn more. Read the full letter here:

entry.article_text: A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student is in critical condition after being struck by an SUV while walking to school Wednesday morning in Port St. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say the crash happened around 6 a.m. near the intersection of SW Port St. Lucie Boulevard and SW Squirrel Avenue. PSLPD says the freshman was walking northbound along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near the edge of the roadway, alongside construction barrels in the area. The incident occurred on National Walk, Bike, & Roll to School Day . Lucie flooding problem renews focus on city's stormwater spending Officers said the teen was struck from behind by a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man. The driver initially believed he had hit a construction barrel and did not realize he had struck a person, according to investigators. entry.title: Port St. Lucie streets flood after downpour, stranding vehicles and disrupting commutes - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie streets flood after downpour, stranding vehicles and disrupting commutes    WPEC
entry.article_text: Heavy rain flooded roads across Port St. Lucie Tuesday afternoon, leaving some vehicles stranded, forcing children to walk through standing water after school and prompting a response from police officers and city crews. According to the City of Port St. Lucie , a large amount of rain fell in a short period of time, leading to temporary road closures and flooding in multiple areas. Public Works crews responded to flooding near Savona Boulevard and California Boulevard, closing the roadway until it was safe for travel. The city also reported high-water conditions near Thornhill Drive and Floresta Drive, where Phase 3 construction is underway. On Southwest Thornhill Drive, school buses continued dropping off students despite flooded streets. CBS12 News saw children step off buses carrying their shoes and walk barefoot through standing water to reach home. Along Southwest Broadview Avenue near Crosstown Parkway, residents watched as water spilled across the roadway, making it difficult for drivers to tell where the street ended and floodwater began. "If you didn't see the grass here, you wouldn't know where the road is," resident Kevin Burke told CBS12 News. "It was steady sheets of rain for a good hour. Non-stop, and I mean heavy, heavy." Police officers directed traffic while Public Works crews set up barricades and monitored conditions during the evening commute. Burke said flooding in the area has become a familiar problem during heavy downpours. "When it rains heavy like it did today, it's like this all the time, from that canal coming up," he said. Burke said standing water presents concerns beyond traffic issues. "We have a pond over there by Crosstown and Bayshore. It's got signs all around it saying there are gators in it. It's a long shot, but it could happen, and that's what worries me, with kids and the animals," he said. For some residents, the flooding disrupted everyday tasks. "She has her elderly brother, who's 83 years old, and she's in her 60s, and she was going to run out and get Chinese food, and now she's still sitting here waiting because she can't get to it," Burke said. Earlier in the day, Port St. Lucie police reported flooding at several intersections, including SE Evans Avenue and SE Airoso Boulevard, SE Eyerly Avenue and SE Airoso Boulevard, SW Bayshore Boulevard and SW Thornhill Drive, and NE Floresta Drive and NE Ardsley Drive. See also: Opponents, supporters clash over Palm Beach County Israel Bonds investments City officials said Public Works crews continued monitoring conditions as water slowly receded Tuesday evening. Officials also reminded residents not to walk or drive through flooded roadways because it can be difficult to determine how deep the water is.

entry.title: Ex-CIA agent who stole $194M used $102M to buy Palm Beach, Hobe Sound properties - WPEC
entry.summary: Ex-CIA agent who stole $194M used $102M to buy Palm Beach, Hobe Sound properties    WPEC
entry.article_text: A former CIA agent convicted Tuesday of defrauding the government of $194 million reportedly used the majority of the money to acquire properties in Palm Beach and Hobe Sound. According to CBS Miami , court filings say 49-year-old David J. Rush of Virginia, a former high-ranking federal employee, directed $145 million to a holding company he controlled, and that $102 million was used to purchase four Florida properties: Two Palm Beach homes: $21.9 million and $27 million One Palm Beach parcel: $13.65 million One Hobe Sound parcel: $40 million Prosecutors allege Rush intended to eventually resell the properties for a profit. How the scheme unfolded According to the Department of Justice , Rush, of Ashburn, Virginia, pleaded guilty Tuesday, Oct. 6, to wire fraud in federal court in Alexandria, Virginia. According to prosecutors, Rush used his senior-level government position and "Top Secret" clearance to create fictitious government authorities and obtain federal money for his own benefit. Between November 2025 and March 2026, he directed approximately $145 million to a holding company established at his direction, according to court documents. The money was then used to purchase the properties. The Justice Department says Rush fraudulently obtained approximately $193.6 million in government funds. The South Florida real estate was only part of the alleged scheme. Gold bars Prosecutors say Rush separately created a fake "sensitive government activity" to justify acquiring hundreds of gold bars. On May 19, 2026, FBI agents searched Rush's Virginia home and recovered 298 gold bars, approximately $2.1 million in cash, €104,795, and numerous luxury watches. The gold had cost the government approximately $46 million, according to the Justice Department. Rush has agreed to forfeit the gold bars and cash, the Florida properties, luxury watches, and two 2026 BMW Alpina vehicles as part of his plea agreement. What's next Rush is scheduled to be sentenced Jan. He faces a maximum of 20 years in federal prison, along with possible restitution, forfeiture and a fine. The Justice Department said its investigation is continuing. The Director of National Intelligence has also requested an investigation by the Intelligence Community's inspector general. The allegations and admissions are detailed in federal court documents filed as part of Rush's guilty plea.

entry.title: 'Just insanity': Port St. Lucie residents reacting to heavy rain and flooding - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Just insanity': Port St. Lucie residents reacting to heavy rain and flooding    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie residents are dealing with the aftermath of heavy rain that flooded roads and swales Tuesday, leaving vehicles stranded and prompting city officials to prepare for more potential rainfall. Barricades remain in place as a precaution, according to city officials. Resident Tommy Fry shared a video of his flooded driveway, saying, "This is the end of the driveway and, you know, two plus feet of water." "It poured, you know, it came down pretty quick, probably 45 minutes of rain," Fry said, describing the rapid accumulation of water. He also described the extent of the flooding. "Just insanity, you know, it's just water two feet deep in the middle of California Boulevard and a waterline 15 feet up my driveway from the street and, of course, the swale over here that's been like that. I can't mow it," Fry said. Drone footage captured severe flooding near Savona and California boulevards, showing streets covered in water after the afternoon rain. Some vehicles became stranded while attempting to navigate the flooded streets. City officials reported that most of the water had receded by 8 p.m. However, some residents are still seeking relief, and officials acknowledge their concerns. "We're responsible for a very wide network of swales, right, so we try to get to as much as we can," said Scott Samples, the city's strategic communications team leader. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Samples explained that public works crews check drains before storms but noted the challenges of managing heavy rainfall. We try to do as much as we can. We know that Mother Nature sometimes is going to win, and we try to do the best that we can to make sure that first of all, people are safe and the inconvenience lasts as little as possible," Samples said. City officials are also exploring long-term projects to address flooding. "So, we're looking at how can we change some of the stormwater management across the city. These are longer-term projects that, you know, I know people would like to have solutions right now. But again, our goal is to try to do this as well as we possibly can for the long term," Samples said. City officials emphasized that crews and equipment are on standby in case of additional heavy rainfall. entry.article_text: The man accused of crossing state lines and traveling to Indian River County to kill his ex-girlfriend was booked into the Indian River County Jail on Monday. According to Indian River County Jail records, Matthew Waggle, 33, was booked into the Indian River County Jail at around 5:20 a.m. He faces a charge of first-degree murder. CBS12 reported on the August shooting after authorities found the victim's body, identified as Dawn Kriskewic , in a roadway in the southern part of the county. Investigators say Waggle traveled to Vero Beach by bus and Uber before allegedly killing Kriskewic outside her home Sunday morning. See also: FHP: Wrong-way driver caused deadly I-95 crash Sunday near PB Lakes Boulevard Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said surveillance video captured Waggle walking through Kriskewic's neighborhood shortly after an Uber dropped him off. Investigators say Waggle then left the area, taking an Uber back to Orlando before boarding another Greyhound bus. He eventually made his way to West Virginia, where investigators say he hid at a motel. Flowers said at the time that Flock Safety cameras were instrumental in tracking down Waggle. Authorities had later tracked Waggle to a motel in West Virginia and taken him into custody. Authorities said Kriskewic had ended her relationship with Waggle before the shooting and had warned coworkers at the hair salon that she wanted no contact with him.

The fare hike, which took effect Oct. 1 , increases one-way fares by roughly 30 cents to $1, depending on the route. Round-trip costs have increased by about $1 to $2, according to Tri-Rail. entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire Board continues law firm search in effort to create complaint policy amid hazing fallout - WFLX
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire Board continues law firm search in effort to create complaint policy amid hazing fallout    WFLX
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District has hit a snag in its effort to create a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders as fallout continues from a controversial hazing investigation. During a Fire District Board workshop Wednesday morning, board members had hoped to hear from outside law firms about helping draft a new complaint policy. WATCH BELOW: Fire district's new complaint policy effort stalls amid hazing fallout Instead, St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said one of the law firms contacted never returned her calls, while another disclosed a potential conflict of interest. "I appreciated her honesty and forthrightness on that issue," Fowler said of the attorney during the meeting. "That being said, she did provide two references, both on the West Coast." The board discussed now reaching out to additional law firms in hopes of securing outside legal help ahead of its next meeting Oct. "I think we'd be doing ourselves an injustice if we at least we don't have a courtesy conversation with these other firms, so that we're at least prepared just in case these two firms aren't available, non-responsive," Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson said. "I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and and I don't want to delay any further." The effort follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30 , when members publicly acknowledged what they described as a significant gap in district policy: There is no clear process for independently handling complaints made against some of the district's own contract employees. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said during that meeting. "They — being those positions — have essentially been able to investigate themselves." Those positions include the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director. The issue came under increased scrutiny amid fallout from a hazing investigation involving three veteran firefighters. A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing. Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result. Hutchinson and Boudrias previously told WPTV they did not consider the conduct hazing and said there was no intent to hurt anyone. "It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said. "We're all still friends," Boudrias said. "Us and the victims, there was no ill intent." The controversy has also raised questions about how complaints involving district leadership have been handled. Months before the hazing incident came to light, Baldwin and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025. District officials ultimately denied it. Baldwin and Hutchinson later filed additional complaints, including an amended complaint to investigators alleging the hazing investigation and their subsequent terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. Lucie County Fire District told WPTV it is not currently in receipt of any official retaliation complaint from any party involved in this matter. "That's not a good process," Fowler previously told WPTV. Sabol submitted her notice of retirement Sept. 30, just minutes after the special board meeting, effective 90 days from her notice. The District stated she will continue to provide services during that 90-day period. Lee previously acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process and told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey that he welcomed outside scrutiny. "I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," Lee said, adding that he "welcomes any investigation from any agency." Lee also defended Sabol following her notice of retirement, calling it a "sad day" and saying she had been a "tremendous attorney for the district." Meanwhile, firefighters have been casting ballots in a union vote of no confidence in Lee. "It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler previously said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message." Lee previously said he would wait for the results before commenting further on the vote. "We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee said. "I came up on the labor side; I've always fought for our men and women on the line." The union is also continuing its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin. 30 meeting, Fowler questioned whether the fire board itself may have the authority to bring the three firefighters back rather than waiting for the arbitration process to play out. "I think we might actually," Fowler said at the time. Board members are expected to continue searching for an outside law firm to help develop the new policy before the Fire District Board meets again Oct.

entry.article_text: A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student is in critical condition after being struck by an SUV while walking to school Wednesday morning in Port St. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say the crash happened around 6 a.m. near the intersection of SW Port St. Lucie Boulevard and SW Squirrel Avenue. PSLPD says the freshman was walking northbound along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near the edge of the roadway, alongside construction barrels in the area. The incident occurred on National Walk, Bike, & Roll to School Day . Lucie flooding problem renews focus on city's stormwater spending Officers said the teen was struck from behind by a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man. The driver initially believed he had hit a construction barrel and did not realize he had struck a person, according to investigators. Police said the driver made a U-turn at the next available location where he could safely turn around. He returned to the area, activated his hazard lights, and found the teen unconscious on the side of the road. The driver called 911 and has remained cooperative with investigators, police said. Investigators have not observed any apparent signs of impairment involving the driver. Police emphasized that assessment is preliminary and could change as the investigation continues. The teen suffered life-threatening injuries and remains in critical condition. The investigation remains active. Police are asking anyone who witnessed the crash or has dashcam, surveillance, or other video from the area around the time of the crash to contact PSLPD at 772-871-5000 .

entry.summary: Isaias strengthened into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season late Wednesday as it surged towards the U.S. Gulf Coast, the National Hurricane Center said. Forecasters warned that it was on track to make landfall between the Mississippi coast and the Florida Panhandle late Friday or early Saturday and was expected to bring heavy rains and potentially flash flooding. The center of the cyclone was about 460 miles (745 kilometers) south-southwest of the Mississippi River, with maximum sustained winds around 75 mph (120 kph), according to an advisory from the Miami-based hurricane center. The hurricane formed late in the season Isaias is developing more than four months into the Atlantic hurricane season, tying a 121-year-old record for the areas latest-forming hurricane. According to the National Weather Service, the record dates to 1905, when the years first Atlantic hurricane formed on Oct. 8. The Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year because of a strong El Nio, which disrupts storm formation over that ocean. Some Gulf oil wells paused production while governors in Florida and Alabama declared a state of emergency for dozens of counties. Isaias is expected to strike along a wide swath of coastline thats very familiar with major hurricanes. One of the 20th centurys worst storms, Hurricane Camille, killed more than 250 people after hitting land near Waveland, Mississippi, in 1969. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 razed neighborhoods in Mississippi, flooded New Orleans and killed nearly 1,400 people. And Hurricane Michael leveled homes and buildings near Panama City, Florida, in 2018. It said eight of the Gulf's 371 manned oil platforms were evacuated. Kay Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties, saying on the social platform X that, “While I hope for minimal impacts, we must take preparations seriously.”Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared one for 25 counties in the Panhandle and Big Bend regions. The declaration activates the state's emergency management plan for hurricanes, allowing officials to deploy disaster responders and equipment. The state also planned to deploy a Miami-based urban search and rescue task force.In Pensacola, electric utilities were pre-positioning crews to quickly repair any power outages. City officials provided sand for residents to fill sandbags to protect their homes against flooding. Reeves urged people to check on older adult neighbors and others who might need help.“Obviously no need to panic at this point,” Reeves told a news conference. “This is really about preparation.”

According to Donovan, Huntingtons disease is a hereditary and progressive neurological disease that can affect movement and behavior. For Donovan, the diagnosis has become a reason to help others better understand a disease she says affects everyday families. I want to spread awareness. Its not just a disease that goes into the rare disease book. Its something that is affecting everyday people, Donovan said. Proceeds from the event will benefit the Huntingtons Disease Society of America, Donovan said. The fundraising goal is $10,000. Donovan says organizers are already halfway to that goal. The event will take place Saturday at 9 a.m. outside the Spanish River Library in Boca Raton.

entry.article_text: President Donald Trump wants to transform Trump International Golf Club in Palm Beach County into a permanent presidential retreat for U.S. presidents and visiting foreign leaders, a proposal that would involve county-owned land and a new lodging facility paid for by the golf club.The proposal, outlined in a Sept. 3 letter from Trump International Golf Club attorney Harvey E. Oyer to Palm Beach County commissioners, calls for the golf club to partner with the county and the federal government to create what Trump has described as a Camp David-style retreat.Trump announced the idea Wednesday, saying the concept was suggested by the military and U.S. Secret Service.“They could spend the weekend there like a retreat, like sort of a Camp David retreat,” Trump said. But the location presents a significant security question. Trump International Golf Club was the site of an attempted assassination of Trump in September 2024, when he was a presidential candidate. A former FBI agent who spoke with WPTV's Michael Hoffman says the property's location and surrounding roads could make it difficult to secure as a permanent presidential retreat.The golf club's letter asks Palm Beach County to designate Trump International Golf Club as the “permanent United States Presidential Golf Course.”Under the proposal, the club would make its golf courses and amenities available to past, current and future U.S. presidents, regardless of political party, as well as visiting foreign heads of state, at the discretion of the White House.The letter says Trump International Golf Club would work with the U.S. General Services Administration and U.S. Secret Service to design an appropriate presidential lodging facility.The club says it would pay the cost of constructing the lodging facility and provide access to the facilities at no cost to the federal government.Oyer described the proposal as a gift to future presidents and the American people, noting in the letter that Trump would be out of office before the project could be completed.The letter also points to the golf club's proximity to Palm Beach International Airport, South Florida's weather and existing security measures as reasons the property would be well suited for the proposal.The club called Trump International Golf Club “one of the most secure golf courses in the world” and described it as an ideal site for a presidential retreat.The golf course sits on county-owned land that is leased long term to Trump International Golf Club, according to the club's letter.Under the proposed arrangement, Trump International Golf Club would grant the county a legal right to the land needed for the lodging facility and other structures. The county would then lease that property to the federal government, allowing the county to remain the landlord.The proposal says Palm Beach County would retain control of the property if the federal government no longer wanted to use the facility or defaulted on its lease.That means the proposal would require more than simply building a new facility at the golf course. It would create a new arrangement among the golf club, Palm Beach County and the federal government.The proposal remains in its early stages. WPTV is reaching out to Palm Beach County commissioners about whether they support providing county land for the project.The proposal's security claims come with a notable complication: Trump International Golf Club was the scene of an attempted assassination of Trump on Sept. 15, 2024.Federal prosecutors said Ryan Wesley Routh was convicted in 2025 of attempting to assassinate Trump at the golf course. He was sentenced in February 2026 to life in federal prison plus seven years.According to the Justice Department, a Secret Service agent conducting a security sweep at the golf course spotted Routh along the fence line near the sixth hole with a rifle. The agent fired at Routh, who fled before being arrested in Martin County.The incident demonstrated the security challenges posed by the golf course's perimeter, including areas adjacent to public roads.Former FBI agent Stuart Kaplan told WPTV he believes securing the property as a permanent presidential retreat would be extremely difficult.“I think it would be absolutely impossible to secure the Trump International Golf Course,” Kaplan said.Kaplan pointed to the property's location near major thoroughfares and the need to secure both the perimeter and surrounding airspace.“If you're going to secure this type of retreat, it has to be 24 hours a day, seven days a week, all day long, every single day,” Kaplan said.Kaplan also questioned the need for a permanent presidential retreat in South Florida.Trump's proposal would ultimately require coordination between Palm Beach County, Trump International Golf Club and the federal government.The club has proposed paying for the lodging facility and says the arrangement would come at no cost to the federal government. Palm Beach County, however, would play a central role because the golf course sits on county-owned land.For now, the proposal is only that — a proposal. County commissioners have yet to determine whether they support the arrangement, and additional questions remain about the project's design, land agreement and security requirements.WPTV is seeking reaction from Palm Beach County commissioners as the proposal moves forward.Read the full letter here:

entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire Board continues law firm search in effort to create complaint policy amid hazing fallout - WPTV
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire Board continues law firm search in effort to create complaint policy amid hazing fallout    WPTV
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District has hit a snag in its effort to create a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders as fallout continues from a controversial hazing investigation. During a Fire District Board workshop Wednesday morning, board members had hoped to hear from outside law firms about helping draft a new complaint policy.WATCH BELOW: Fire district's new complaint policy effort stalls amid hazing falloutInstead, St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said one of the law firms contacted never returned her calls, while another disclosed a potential conflict of interest."I appreciated her honesty and forthrightness on that issue," Fowler said of the attorney during the meeting. "That being said, she did provide two references, both on the West Coast." The board discussed now reaching out to additional law firms in hopes of securing outside legal help ahead of its next meeting Oct. 21."I think we'd be doing ourselves an injustice if we at least we don't have a courtesy conversation with these other firms, so that we're at least prepared just in case these two firms aren't available, non-responsive," Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson said. "I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and and I don't want to delay any further." The effort follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30, when members publicly acknowledged what they described as a significant gap in district policy: There is no clear process for independently handling complaints made against some of the district's own contract employees. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said during that meeting. "They — being those positions — have essentially been able to investigate themselves."Those positions include the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director.The issue came under increased scrutiny amid fallout from a hazing investigation involving three veteran firefighters.A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing.Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result.Hutchinson and Boudrias previously told WPTV they did not consider the conduct hazing and said there was no intent to hurt anyone."It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said."We're all still friends," Boudrias said. "Us and the victims, there was no ill intent."The controversy has also raised questions about how complaints involving district leadership have been handled.Months before the hazing incident came to light, Baldwin and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025. District officials ultimately denied it. Baldwin and Hutchinson later filed additional complaints, including an amended complaint to investigators alleging the hazing investigation and their subsequent terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. Lucie County Fire District told WPTV it is not currently in receipt of any official retaliation complaint from any party involved in this matter."That's not a good process," Fowler previously told WPTV.Sabol submitted her notice of retirement Sept. 30, just minutes after the special board meeting, effective 90 days from her notice. The District stated she will continue to provide services during that 90-day period. Lee previously acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process and told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey that he welcomed outside scrutiny."I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," Lee said, adding that he "welcomes any investigation from any agency."Lee also defended Sabol following her notice of retirement, calling it a "sad day" and saying she had been a "tremendous attorney for the district."Meanwhile, firefighters have been casting ballots in a union vote of no confidence in Lee."It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler previously said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message."Lee previously said he would wait for the results before commenting further on the vote."We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee said. "I came up on the labor side; I've always fought for our men and women on the line."The union is also continuing its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin.During the Sept. 30 meeting, Fowler questioned whether the fire board itself may have the authority to bring the three firefighters back rather than waiting for the arbitration process to play out."I think we might actually," Fowler said at the time.Board members are expected to continue searching for an outside law firm to help develop the new policy before the Fire District Board meets again Oct.

entry.summary: Treasure Coast HS student critically injured after being struck by SUV on way to school in Port St. Lucie    WPTV
entry.article_text: A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student is in critical condition after being struck by a vehicle while walking to school Wednesday morning, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.Police said the crash happened around 6 a.m. near the intersection of Southwest Port St. Lucie Boulevard and Southwest Squirrel Avenue.WATCH BELOW: Student critically injured after being struck by SUVInvestigators said the freshman was walking northbound along Port St. Lucie Boulevard on his way to school and was near the edge of the roadway alongside construction barrels in the area when he was struck from behind by a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man.According to police, the driver initially believed he had hit a construction barrel and did not realize he had struck a person. Authorities said the driver later made a U-turn at the next location where it was safe to do so and returned to the scene.Once back in the area, the driver activated his hazard lights and found the teen unconscious on the side of the roadway. Police said he immediately called 911 and has remained cooperative throughout the investigation.The student suffered life-threatening injuries and remains hospitalized in critical condition, according to police.Investigators said there were no apparent signs of impairment involving the driver, though they noted the assessment is preliminary and could change as the investigation continues.The crash remains under investigation.Police are asking anyone who witnessed the incident or who may have dash camera, surveillance or other video footage from the area around the time of the crash to come forward.Anyone with information is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000.Howard Shapiro lives across the street from where the crash occurred.Shapiro said this stretch of Port St. Lucie Boulevard can be dangerous."I don't walk around here is no lighting outside at nighttime," said Shapiro. "Kids walk along all the time because there's school back there, school down there."Though crews are improving the roadway, Shapiro said lights would make it safer."They are putting in a sidewalk, so that's going to be helpful. But streetlights need to follow," said Shapiro.Celine Gabriel lives off nearby Becker Road and said she avoids Port St. Lucie Boulevard altogether."I don't even come down this road no more," said Gabriel. "I go all the way down to I-95, come up on Gatlin to take my child to school.

The student was walking northbound along Port St. Lucie Boulevard and was near the edge of the roadway in an area marked by construction barrels when he was struck from behind. Investigators said the vehicle involved was a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man. According to police, the driver initially believed he had struck a construction barrel and did not realize he had hit a person. The driver later made a U-turn at the next safe location, returned to the scene, activated his hazard lights and found the teenager unconscious on the side of the roadway. The driver has remained cooperative with investigators, and police said they have not observed any apparent signs of impairment. Authorities noted that the assessment is preliminary and could change as the investigation continues. The student, identified only as a freshman at Treasure Coast High School, suffered life-threatening injuries and remains in critical condition, police said. The investigation is ongoing. Anyone who witnessed the crash or has dash-camera, surveillance or other video footage from the area around the time of the incident is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000. entry.title: UF study finds dengue-linked mosquito common in Indian River County yards - cw34.com
entry.summary: UF study finds dengue-linked mosquito common in Indian River County yards    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Florida has reported nearly 500 dengue cases this year, including more than 250 infections acquired within the state, as new University of Florida research points to residential yards in Indian River County as a key place to understand mosquito-bite exposure. The Florida Department of Health’s latest weekly surveillance report , covering Sept. 20-26, lists 252 locally acquired dengue cases and 245 travel-associated cases statewide 497 total. The locally acquired cases were reported in Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco, Pinellas and Polk counties. Palm Beach County had one locally acquired case and 12 travel-associated cases; St. Lucie County had six travel-associated cases. No locally acquired dengue cases were listed for Indian River County in the report. The state’s locally acquired total includes 223 cases in Hillsborough County, the center of Florida’s outbreak. Health officials also reported 20 mosquito pools testing positive for dengue statewide. Nationally, the CDC’s most recent weekly provisional report counted 690 dengue cases among U.S. Florida accounted for 403 of those cases in the CDC reporting system, though the state’s more current surveillance report lists a higher total because reporting systems update on different schedules. Against that backdrop, researchers at UF/IFAS’ Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory in Vero Beach found a surprising mosquito pattern in suburban Indian River County. The team expected residential yards to be dominated by Aedes albopictus , also known as the Asian tiger mosquito. Instead, researchers found relatively high numbers of Aedes aegypti the yellow fever mosquito and one of the two species most closely associated with dengue transmission worldwide. The finding does not mean dengue is circulating in Indian River County . But it underscores why backyard mosquito control and personal bite prevention matter, researchers said. See also: Florida stages emergency supplies as Tropical Storm Isaias strengthens in Gulf The first-of-its-kind study paired mosquito trapping at homes with a smartphone-based Bite Diary that let residents document when and where they were bitten. Researchers collected 3,788 female mosquitoes from 78 yards. Of 70 reported bites, nearly 93% happened outdoors and nearly 74% happened at home, according to the peer-reviewed study . The number of mosquitoes trapped in a yard was not associated with the number of bites residents reported. Instead, people who spent more time outside during the evening, from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m., reported more bites. Gardening and walking dogs were among activities commonly reported when bites occurred. Dengue is spread when an infected mosquito bites a person; it does not spread directly from person to person. Symptoms can include fever, severe muscle and joint pain, rash, nausea and pain behind the eyes. People with symptoms should contact a health care provider, especially after travel to an area where dengue is common. Health officials urge residents to use EPA-registered insect repellent, wear long sleeves and pants when practical, repair window and door screens, and dump standing water from containers such as buckets, flowerpots, toys, tires and pool covers.

entry.title: Hundreds gather in Vero Beach to remember 17-year-old Sulliman Bah and call for justice - WPBF
entry.summary: Hundreds gather in Vero Beach to remember 17-year-old Sulliman Bah and call for justice    WPBF
entry.article_text: Hundreds of people gathered Wednesday night at the Farm and Flame restaurant in Vero Beach to honor the life of 17-year-old Sulli Bah, who was fatally shot last Friday. "He was just joyful, happy all the time. Contagious smile," said Chelynn Godfrey, Bah’s mother. Godfrey said she was the only one who called her son Sulliman, while everyone else knew him as Sulli, a young man who always had a kind word for strangers. "That was just very important to him, that he made people feel good, that he made people feel seen," Godfrey said. Bah was killed Friday at a party at the Garcia Boat Ramp. Videos released by the sheriff’s office show Bah opening the door of a white pickup truck, and the passenger inside the truck firing one shot, killing him. The vigil, held at the restaurant where Bah worked, began with a prayer, followed by friends sharing memories of the 17-year-old and praying for justice. "Sulli was a kind soul," said one friend, fighting to hold back tears. No arrests have been made in connection with Bah’s death. Sheriff Eric Flowers said the shooter claims he and Bah had fought before and that he fired in self-defense. Bah's mother said she doesn't think that's true. "I believe that my son was murdered. And I believe that the shooter needs to be punished for that," Godfrey said. Flowers said the investigation into the shooting is ongoing, and the state attorney will ultimately decide whether charges will be filed. entry.title: Trump faces hecklers while making high-profile Texas campaign push
entry.summary: President Donald Trump, facing protesters and a poor political climate, fought to rally Texas voters behind Senate candidate Ken Paxton on Wednesday night in a bid to stave off sweeping Democratic victories in the nation's most populous red state. But Trump's remarks were not focused solely on Paxton. Speaking to a packed Freeman Coliseum, Trump also pledged to award retired baseball star Roger Clemens the Presidential Medal of Freedom, restated his support for the death penalty for drug dealers and clarified recent comments in which he talked about the possibility of Iran bombing American cities as part of a recurring riff about how high fuel costs are a small price to pay for the war. You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego, let them hit Los Angeles, Trump said. Were not going to let that happen. We protect our cities. We protect our country. The president's message was interrupted repeatedly by protesters, including by one who appeared to be close to the stage. In all, at least a dozen demonstrators interrupted the president. Some were led away by police. Trump stepped away from the microphone briefly after one interruption. Hes going back home to mom, Trump said. But what he doesnt know is his mom voted for Trump. Texas has become an unexpected battleground for Republicans The Republican Party did not plan to devote so much money and manpower to Texas this midterm season. Texas is the nations most populous reliably Republican state, where Trump won in 2024 by almost 14 percentage points. But with Election Day less than a month away, Trumps poor approval ratings, the Iran war and soaring gas prices have threatened Republicans in virtually every state. Wednesdays appearance marked Trumps third trip to Texas in less than a month, and party officials have devoted more than $300 million to elections in the state so far. Greg Abbott did not attend the evening rally. A three-term Republican governor who won reelection in 2022 by roughly 11 percentage points, even Abbott has been caught in the turbulent national currents. Hes locked in a competitive reelection race against Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa. entry.article_text: Democrats seized on the governor’s absence.“For years, Greg Abbott has never been shy about embracing Donald Trump, calling Trump a ‘great friend’ and championing his agenda every step of the way,” said Texas Democratic Party spokesperson Jacob Long. “But now, as Texas families get crushed by record-high prices driven by Trump’s tariffs and war with Iran, suddenly Greg Abbott has somewhere else to be.”Trump focuses on helping the Senate candidate he endorsed in GOP primaryWhile the race for governor has drawn a sudden influx of cash from Democrats, the state’s U.S. Senate race has drawn the most attention as Democrats fight for the chamber’s majority. The state has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, but candidate James Talarico’s fundraising, Trump’s low approval rating and nagging concerns about Paxton’s character have put the race squarely in play.Trump spent most of his remarks focused on the Senate contest, describing Paxton as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America.”RELATED STORY | Trump holds campaign was being run by operatives in Washington.He repeatedly criticized Talarico, including on the death penalty, a point that would appeal to many conservatives in the state that leads the nation in executions.Trump restated his support for the death penalty for “large scale drug dealers, human traffickers and anyone who kills a police officer,” while acknowledging that Nidal Malik Hasan, a "Sulli was a kind soul," said one friend, fighting to hold back tears. No arrests have been made in connection with Bah’s death. Sheriff Eric Flowers said the shooter claims he and Bah had fought before and that he fired in self-defense. Bah's mother said she doesn't think that's true. "I believe that my son was murdered. And I believe that the shooter needs to be punished for that," Godfrey said. Flowers said the investigation into the shooting is ongoing, and the state attorney will ultimately decide whether charges will be filed. entry.title: 5 years after Gabriella Hanley's unsolved killing, family and police still calling on community for answers
entry.summary: Five years after Gabriella 'Gabi' Hanley was shot and killed in an apparent drive-by shooting in Port St. Lucie, no arrests have been made in her case. WATCH BELOW: Family seeks answers 5 years after loved one killed Gabi Hanley cold case: Port St. Lucie family seeks answers 5 years later Hanley, 20, was shot along Green River Parkway in 2021. Her boyfriend, who was in the car at the time, was also hit by gunfire but survived. Hanley left behind a 14-month-old daughter, who is now 6 years old. Port St. Lucie police identified several people of interest at the time of the shooting, but five years later, no one has been arrested. The pain of losing Gabi still lingers for her mother, Nicole Vigilante. 'It is tough, but I gotta be strong for my granddaughter,' Vigilante said. As Gabi's daughter grows older, the family is searching for answers for themselves and for her. 'Now she's getting older, and she has questions,' Vigilante said. 'And we want to be able to give her those answers,' Krystal Benitez, Gabi's cousin, added. For Gabi's loved ones, her daughter is a constant reminder of who she was. 'We're reminded of the situation every single day,' Alexia Perez, Gabi's best friend, said. 'We will never forget Gabi. Her daughter is walking memory of her.' 'Gabi was an amazing, amazing woman,' Benitez added. Port St. Lucie police turned to social media Tuesday, saying information that was not shared at the time of the shooting could make a difference today. They're asking anyone with information to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department's Major Crimes Division at 772-871-5000 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-8477. Gabi's family and friends are doing their part to keep the case alive by sharing her story and raising awareness throughout the community. 'We have been spending the day handing out flyers going to all local businesses just trying to again raise awareness,' Benitez said. They are now calling on the community to come forward with information. 'There's a little girl right now that's being raised without her mother, so be brave for her and come forward,' Benitez said.

entry.title: Amendments 1 & 2: Lesser-known Florida ballot amendments focus on state reserves, farm tax breaks
entry.summary: While much of the attention surrounding Florida's November election has centered on Amendment 3 , voters will also decide the fate of two other proposed constitutional amendments that could have significant impacts on the state's finances and agricultural industry. Amendment 1 would make major changes to Florida's Budget Stabilization Fund (Read the full text) , often referred to as the state's 'rainy day' fund. WATCH BELOW: Amendments 1 2: What to know about these lesser-known ballot measures Amendments 1 2 on Florida ballot: Budget stabilization, ag tax exemption The proposal would increase the maximum size of the fund from 10% to 25% of net general revenue collections. It would also require annual transfers of up to $750 million into the reserve fund and allow state lawmakers to use the money for certain critical needs. Supporters say the amendment would strengthen Florida's financial position during natural disasters, economic downturns and other emergencies by ensuring the state maintains a larger reserve of available funds. Opponents, however, argue that setting aside additional money in reserves could limit the state's ability to address immediate needs, including public services and infrastructure projects. Voters will also weigh Amendment 2 , which focuses on tax relief for Florida's agriculture sector. ( Read the full text) The measure would exempt agricultural equipment and certain farm-related property from property taxes. Supporters say the change would reduce costs for farmers, strengthen the agriculture industry and help preserve farming operations across the state. Those opposed to the amendment contend the tax exemptions could reduce revenue collected by local governments. Critics argue that loss of tax income could affect funding for public services and other community programs that rely on property tax dollars. Both amendments will appear on Florida's ballot this November, giving voters an opportunity to decide whether the proposed changes should be added to the state constitution. Amendment 3 increases the homestead exemption, for all non-school taxes, to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and adjusts for inflation thereafter. entry.title: WHERE'S WALTER? Taking a spin with the dancers of Paris Ballet
entry.summary: For this week's 'Where's Walter?', I visited Paris Ballet in Jupiter, where students are busy preparing for their upcoming performances of The Nutcracker. As soon as I walked into the studio, I knew I was stepping into a world that requires talent, discipline and plenty of hard work. Of course, I couldn't just stand on the sidelines. WATCH: WHERE'S WALTER? Where's Walter? Taking a spin with the dancers of Paris Ballet The dancers and instructors invited me to join them on the floor, and after a quick warm-up, it was time to learn some ballet basics. Let's just say I quickly discovered there's a reason these students spend so much time training. I teamed up with several dancers, including Maya, who helped teach me a few of the moves from her role as the Sugar Plum Fairy. While she made everything look effortless, my legs had a different opinion. Then it was time to learn part of another routine with dancer Jay. He was kind enough to slow things down for me, but even at a beginner's pace, I realized just how much strength, balance and coordination ballet requires. I'll be honest: I'm no ballet dancer. But spending time with these young performers gave me a whole new appreciation for what they do. Every movement takes focus. Every routine requires practice. And every performance is the result of countless hours spent perfecting their craft. What impressed me most was the dedication of the students. Watching them rehearse, I saw firsthand the commitment and passion they bring to every class and every performance. Their talent shines on stage, but it's the hard work behind the scenes that truly makes it all possible. I also got a special look at preparations for this year's Nutcracker production. Seeing the dancers work together to bring the beloved holiday classic to life made me appreciate just how much effort goes into creating a ballet performance. While I don't think I'll be joining the cast anytime soon, I had an incredible time trying out a few moves and learning from some very talented young dancers. And after seeing their hard work up close, I can tell you one thing: The Nutcracker is in very good hands this holiday season. Tickets are on sale now for the Nutcracker on Nov. 21 at the Duncan Theater in Lake Worth Beach.

entry.article_text: A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student is in critical condition after being struck by an SUV while walking to school Wednesday morning in Port St. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say the crash happened around 6 a.m. near the intersection of SW Port St. Lucie Boulevard and SW Squirrel Avenue. PSLPD says the freshman was walking northbound along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near the edge of the roadway, alongside construction barrels in the area. The incident occurred on National Walk, Bike, & Roll to School Day . Lucie flooding problem renews focus on city's stormwater spending Officers said the teen was struck from behind by a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man. The driver initially believed he had hit a construction barrel and did not realize he had struck a person, according to investigators. Police said the driver made a U-turn at the next available location where he could safely turn around. He returned to the area, activated his hazard lights, and found the teen unconscious on the side of the road. The driver called 911 and has remained cooperative with investigators, police said. Investigators have not observed any apparent signs of impairment involving the driver. Police emphasized that assessment is preliminary and could change as the investigation continues. The teen suffered life-threatening injuries and remains in critical condition. The investigation remains active. Police are asking anyone who witnessed the crash or has dashcam, surveillance, or other video from the area around the time of the crash to contact PSLPD at 772-871-5000 .

entry.title: West Palm Beach woman turns husband's Huntington's diagnosis into awareness mission
entry.summary: A West Palm Beach woman is turning her husbands Huntingtons disease diagnosis into a mission to raise awareness and support families affected by the progressive neurological disease. Madison Donovan says her husband, Brian, was diagnosed with Huntington's disease at age 21, just four years ago. Now, she is helping organize the Hope for HD Walk this weekend outside the Spanish River Library in Boca Raton. The walk is scheduled for Saturday at 9 a.m. and aims to raise both awareness and money for people and families affected by Huntingtons disease. What is Huntingtons disease? According to Donovan, Huntingtons disease is a hereditary and progressive neurological disease that can affect movement and behavior. For Donovan, the diagnosis has become a reason to help others better understand a disease she says affects everyday families. 'I want to spread awareness. Its not just a disease that goes into the rare disease book. It's something that is affecting everyday people,' Donovan said. Hope for HD Walk aims to raise $10,000 Donovan is helping organize the Hope for HD Walk as part of an effort to bring more attention to Huntingtons disease and raise funds for those affected by it. entry.title: Vero Beach remembers 17-year-old Sulli Bah as family seeks justice
entry.summary: Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman Sulli Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. No arrests have been made, and investigators are examining whether the shooting may have involved self-defense. The celebration of life was held at the Vero Beach restaurant where Bah worked. Through tears and memories, those who knew him described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room. Friends remember Sulli as a positive person As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm Flame while people who knew Bah stood together to honor his life. Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. He touched everybodys heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room, Rodriguez said. Bah's close friends told WPTV he was focused on his future and enjoyed spending time with the people closest to him. Alex Cortez said he and Bah boxed together, spent time together and shared many memories. He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future, Cortez said. Friend Xavi Espinosa remembered Bah as someone who could immediately make others feel welcome. Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul, Espinosa said. Family seeks justice as investigation continues The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Bah was at a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired. The sheriff's office said investigators are looking into whether the shooting was self-defense . No arrests have been made. Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his entire life ahead of him. She said she wants investigators to consider all the facts as they determine what happened. I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right, Godfrey said. I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail. Teachers and friends share memories During the celebration, people took turns sharing memories of Bah and the impact he had on their lives. Angela Sanders, one of Bah's former sixth grade teachers, remembered his personality and smile. His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room, Sanders said.

entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District has hit a snag in its effort to create a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders as fallout continues from a controversial hazing investigation. During a Fire District Board workshop Wednesday morning, board members had hoped to hear from outside law firms about helping draft a new complaint policy.WATCH BELOW: Fire district's new complaint policy effort stalls amid hazing falloutInstead, St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said one of the law firms contacted never returned her calls, while another disclosed a potential conflict of interest."I appreciated her honesty and forthrightness on that issue," Fowler said of the attorney during the meeting. "That being said, she did provide two references, both on the West Coast." The board discussed now reaching out to additional law firms in hopes of securing outside legal help ahead of its next meeting Oct. 21."I think we'd be doing ourselves an injustice if we at least we don't have a courtesy conversation with these other firms, so that we're at least prepared just in case these two firms aren't available, non-responsive," Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson said. "I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and and I don't want to delay any further." The effort follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30, when members publicly acknowledged what they described as a significant gap in district policy: There is no clear process for independently handling complaints made against some of the district's own contract employees. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said during that meeting. "They — being those positions — have essentially been able to investigate themselves."Those positions include the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director.The issue came under increased scrutiny amid fallout from a hazing investigation involving three veteran firefighters.A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing.Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result.Hutchinson and Boudrias previously told WPTV they did not consider the conduct hazing and said there was no intent to hurt anyone."It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said."We're all still friends," Boudrias said. "Us and the victims, there was no ill intent."The controversy has also raised questions about how complaints involving district leadership have been handled.Months before the hazing incident came to light, Baldwin and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025. District officials ultimately denied it. Baldwin and Hutchinson later filed additional complaints, including an amended complaint to investigators alleging the hazing investigation and their subsequent terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. Lucie County Fire District told WPTV it is not currently in receipt of any official retaliation complaint from any party involved in this matter."That's not a good process," Fowler previously told WPTV.Sabol submitted her notice of retirement Sept. 30, just minutes after the special board meeting, effective 90 days from her notice. The District stated she will continue to provide services during that 90-day period. Lee previously acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process and told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey that he welcomed outside scrutiny."I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," Lee said, adding that he "welcomes any investigation from any agency."Lee also defended Sabol following her notice of retirement, calling it a "sad day" and saying she had been a "tremendous attorney for the district."Meanwhile, firefighters have been casting ballots in a union vote of no confidence in Lee."It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler previously said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message."Lee previously said he would wait for the results before commenting further on the vote."We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee said. "I came up on the labor side; I've always fought for our men and women on the line."The union is also continuing its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin.During the Sept. 30 meeting, Fowler questioned whether the fire board itself may have the authority to bring the three firefighters back rather than waiting for the arbitration process to play out."I think we might actually," Fowler said at the time.Board members are expected to continue searching for an outside law firm to help develop the new policy before the Fire District Board meets again Oct.

"The generational appeal, the nostalgia and stuff like that."He said the sitcom remains a source of comfort for viewers who return to the familiar characters again and again."Women of a certain age who sometimes can feel forgotten or cast aside, this gives them a voice," Kelley said. "The LGBT community obviously has very strong ties. Everybody can kind of identify with one of the girls, so it's easy to see yourself in the show."Full Interview with CastAlthough the original sitcom was set in Miami, the cast believes its themes resonate throughout South Florida."The lifestyle is born from this area," Kelley said. "We're going to be in West Palm Beach. How many people in West Palm Beach are retirees of a certain age who are maybe living this life, living with friends? They have a timeshare; they're doing this."The actors said audiences across Florida often recognize elements of their own communities in the world created by the television series."It's all South Florida," Kelley said. "The alligators, the humidity, banana leaves."The performers also said Florida audiences have embraced the production since it first began touring in the state."We always look forward to coming to Florida because of how solid the fan base is," Kelley said.The production imagines a continuation of the television series rather than a simple tribute show.According to the cast, Sophia has been arrested for operating a drug ring at Shady Pines, while Blanche and Rose launch a dating app for seniors. Meanwhile, Dorothy is forced into the world of online dating and begins a relationship with the very attorney prosecuting Sophia.The result is a fast-paced comedy that blends modern humor with the personalities fans have loved for decades.The show also embraces some of the continuity quirks that longtime viewers know well.During the interview, the actors laughed about references in the original sitcom that seemingly placed Jupiter's Burt Reynolds Dinner Theatre just a short drive from Miami."None of it makes sense," Graber joked. "You just let it happen."For many fans, The Golden Girls represents more than comedy.The cast said audience members frequently share personal stories during meet-and-greet events, telling them how the show connected them with parents, grandparents and close friends.Others describe finding comfort in the sitcom during difficult periods of their lives.That emotional connection continues to help new generations discover Dorothy, Blanche, Rose and Sophia long after the series left the air.Whether viewers tune in for the one-liners, the friendships, or the nostalgia, the cast believes the secret is simple: everyone can find a little of themselves in one of the four friends.Golden Girls: The Laughs Continue comes to the Kravis Center on Sunday, Oct. 25, with performances at 2 p.m. and 7:30 p.m.Organizers recommend buying tickets directly through Kravis.org to avoid scams and third-party resellers.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI.
