entry.article_text: Jurors are deliberating in the trial of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Mimms, who is accused of bid tampering and official misconduct involving city-owned properties and a nonprofit linked to his niece. Prosecutors said Mimms used his position as city manager to help Lincoln Park Young Professionals, a nonprofit co-founded by his niece, secure a lease to develop two city-owned properties. The defense denied Mimms did anything wrong, arguing that he and his niece, Caleta Scott, have a distant relationship. The prosecution argued there was a conflict of interest, saying Scott was granted special treatment because of her relationship with Mimms. Deliberations began late yesterday after closing arguments from both sides and resumed at 9 a.m. Jurors have broken for lunch but have not yet reached a verdict. entry.title: 'Sully was a kind soul’: Loved ones remember teen killed at large party in Fellsmere - WPEC
entry.summary: 'Sully was a kind soul’: Loved ones remember teen killed at large party in Fellsmere    WPEC
entry.article_text: Family and friends gathered Wednesday night at Farm and Flame restaurant in Vero Beach to remember 17-year-old Sulliman Bah, who was shot and killed last Friday during a teen party at the Garcia boat ramp in Fellsmere. Bah, known to many as Sully, had just finished his shift at the restaurant before going to the large gathering of more than 100 teens. A couple hundred people packed the restaurant, sharing stories about Bah’s kindness and the impact he had on their lives. Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described him as a loving son, brother and kind person. He was just joyful, happy all the time, Godfrey said. Godfrey said her son was the kind of person who made everyone around him feel like they mattered. "We've walked down the street, any stranger he saw, he'd greet them, 'How you doing today?' she said. "That was very important to him that he made people feel good, feel seen." Godfrey said Bah cared deeply about making people feel seen. Friends remembered him as funny and caring and kind. See also: Boynton Beach teen reunites with first responders after surviving lightning strike "He was never mean to nobody, and I hate that this happened to him because he doesn't deserve this," one friend said through tears. "Sully was a kind soul." Investigators say several fights broke out at the teen party before an 18-year-old who knew Bah shot him. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers has said he believes the shooting was in self-defense. "Getting that call on a random Friday night that one of my best friends had just gotten shot...was probably one of the hardest things I've had to go through," another friend said. One of eight children, Bah's mother said he was just a credit and a half away from graduating high school and had big plans for the future. "He wanted to travel," Godfrey said. "He wanted to spend time in a big city. wanted to be an entrepreneur." As she begins to cope with the unimaginable loss of her son, Godfrey said she wants answers about what happened that night and accountability for his death. "His life is not being valued enough, and things are not being looked at seriously enough," she said. "I believe that my son was murdered, and I believe that the shooter needs to be punished for that." The sheriff’s office says the investigation remains open. No arrests have been made, and the State Attorney will decide whether charges will be filed.

entry.title: Delray Beach woman finds purpose as a WPTV Weather Spotter, from rainbows to tornadoes
entry.summary: Julie Wallace Thomas of Delray Beach has been part of the WPTV First Alert Weather Spotters program since it began and a recent visit to the WPTV newsroom gave her a new appreciation for the role she plays. WATCH BELOW: WPTV Weather Spotter: rainbows, tornadoes and making a difference I connected with Thomas and gave her a tour of the station to learn more about what brought her to the team. During the visit, Thomas learned that Weather Spotters have direct communication with the weather service and that their observations actively help the weather service do its job. Our church goes out to Anchor Park in Delray for a beach baptism, and as my husband, the pastor of our church, took this man's wife out into the waters to baptize her, we were rewarded with this brilliant double rainbow,' she said. 'So, I got some great pictures.' Weather Spotters play an important role in the community no matter what weather is headed our way. You can sign up for the program here .

entry.title: Boynton Beach soup kitchen sees increase in demand as rising costs squeeze South Florida families
entry.summary: The Soup Kitchen in Boynton Beach is seeing a surge in demand, with need up about 25% as residents struggle with rising gas prices, medical bills, and other monthly expenses. Marlene Mejia, CEO and executive director of The Soup Kitchen, said the need is increasing. 'I would say it's about 25% higher need,' she said. People are telling the kitchen that tough times are getting tougher. 'They're telling us that the gas prices are killing them, that medication and the bills that they have to pay at the end of the month, it's not enough,' Mejia said. 'So, that's why we're coming in and filling in the gap.' The Soup Kitchen is filling in the gap for every walk of life, including employed residents, who have homes and cars but are still not making ends meet at the end of the month. 'You can see people from all over and we call them the household person, which is asset limited income constrained,' Mejia said. 'But they're employed, so they have cars, they may have a house, they may have an apartment, and it's just not adding up at the end of the month.' Yolanda Marcellus was among the dozens of people standing in a long line and walking through The Soup Kitchen for food. 'I just come here. I pick up the food. They have good food every day. Everybody comes in. So, I'm thank God I'm here,' Marcellus said. The kitchen is able to distribute hundreds of pounds of food every day through faithful volunteers, like Mary Webb. 'You just feel good helping out other people and it comes back to you,' Webb said. 'The goodness comes back to you.' The Soup Kitchen is located at 8655 W. Boynton Beach Blvd. and they can be contacted at 561-732-7595.

I can't be mad at the governor or the decision," Farrington said. "I mean, my uncle did take a life."But Farrington added, "I just want the governor to look at the whole picture."That story stretches back to Sept. 23, 1986.According to court records, Reaves called 911 from a convenience store in Indian River County after he was unable to get a taxi.Raczkowski responded and was attempting to help Reaves call a cab when a gun fell from Reaves' pants. A struggle followed.Reaves shot Raczkowski four times in the back, killing him.For nearly 40 years, Raczkowski's brother, Marc Raczkowski, has lived with the loss."Why? Why?" he said while speaking with WPTV near his brother's gravesite. "It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody." A stretch of road near where the deputy was killed now bears Raczkowski's name — a memorial to a life taken and a crime that continues to reverberate through two families four decades later."The pain will still always be there," Marc Raczkowski said.DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant Sept. 22, scheduling his execution for Oct. 20.Farrington is not asking the governor to pardon his uncle or release him from prison. Instead, he wants DeSantis to commute Reaves' death sentence so the now-77-year-old can spend the rest of his life behind bars.Central to his plea is Reaves' history as a decorated Vietnam War veteran and questions raised during decades of appeals about his mental health, substance abuse and legal representation.Court records show Reaves repeatedly challenged his conviction and death sentence, including claims that his trial attorney failed to adequately investigate and present evidence concerning his drug use and mental health."The attorney wasn't an effective attorney for that type of case," Farrington said. "That was his first death row case."At Reaves' sentencing, testimony described him as suffering from what was then called "Vietnam syndrome," rather than post-traumatic stress disorder.Years later, other experts testified that Reaves suffered from PTSD, substance abuse and other impairments.Farrington said none of that excuses the murder."I'm not going to say that his PTSD, his drug use, his being on cocaine and all the other stuff excuses what he did," Farrington said. "I mean, he's being punished by being in prison, and he's 77. The governor can let him stay in prison for the rest of his life, and still he's being punished without killing him and taking another life."Farrington also acknowledges that his family is not the only one carrying grief into Oct. 20.On the other side is Raczkowski's family, which has spent four decades living with the consequences of Reaves' actions."I mean, trying to understand what he feels — there's no way I could do that," Farrington said of Raczkowski's brother.He said he understands why the deputy's family may want the execution to proceed."I know that the family, the officer ... He has appealed that decision to the Florida Supreme Court.For now, his execution remains scheduled for Oct. 20 unless a court intervenes or DeSantis grants clemency.If carried out, Reaves' execution will mark the 18th in Florida in 2026.

entry.title: Palm Beach County firefighters deploy to Florida Panhandle ahead of Hurricane Isaias
entry.summary: A highly specialized team of firefighters from Palm Beach County is heading to Florida's Panhandle to assist with response efforts as Hurricane Isaias takes aim at the Gulf Coast. Palm Beach County Fire Rescue's Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) team deployed Thursday morning on its first-ever state mission, sending 30 firefighters to areas expected to be impacted by the approaching storm. TRACKING THE TROPICS: Hurricane Center | Hurricane Guide The team specializes in conducting searches and rescues in some of the most dangerous disaster conditions, including collapsed buildings and fast-moving floodwaters. Fire Rescue officials said the crew is transporting multiple boats, search equipment and specialized rescue tools to support emergency operations before and after the hurricane makes landfall. The deployment came after the team was activated overnight by state officials. USAR teams are trained to respond to a wide range of disasters, including structural collapses, severe flooding and other emergencies that require advanced rescue capabilities. Firefighters could remain deployed for up to two weeks, depending on conditions and the level of need in affected communities. Isaias is forecast to make landfall Friday night.

entry.title: Martin County Public Transit riders left without service after transit provider suspends operations
entry.summary: Martin County officials are scrambling to restore public transportation service after the county's contracted transit provider abruptly canceled its services, leaving Martin County Public Transit (MARTY) riders without transportation effective immediately. In a statement Thursday, Martin County said it is aware that its contracted transit service provider has canceled service and that MARTY transit operations are currently interrupted. 'Martin County is actively working to identify solutions to restore transit service as quickly as possible and minimize the impact on our riders,' the county said. 'Additional information will be provided as it becomes available.' Officials did not immediately identify the transit provider or explain why the service was canceled. 'We understand the importance of MARTY services to our community and apologize for the disruption,' the statement said. In response, United Way of Martin County said it is preparing for an increase in transportation assistance requests through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents. 'Transportation isn't a luxury for the people who depend on it. It's how they get to work, receive medical care and put food on the table,' said Carol G. Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County. 'When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn't disappear with it.' United Way officials said the program was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption. The organization is now anticipating an even greater need for transportation assistance. Ashley Capital has committed an initial $2,500 donation to help support Ride United's response to the outage. Since launching in September 2022, Ride United has provided thousands of rides for Martin County residents facing transportation barriers. entry.title: Amendments 1 & 2: Lesser-known Florida ballot amendments focus on state reserves, farm tax breaks
entry.summary: While much of the attention surrounding Florida's November election has centered on Amendment 3 , voters will also decide the fate of two other proposed constitutional amendments that could have significant impacts on the state's finances and agricultural industry. Amendment 1 would make major changes to Florida's Budget Stabilization Fund (Read the full text) , often referred to as the state's 'rainy day' fund. WATCH BELOW: Amendments 1 2: What to know about these lesser-known ballot measures Amendments 1 2 on Florida ballot: Budget stabilization, ag tax exemption The proposal would increase the maximum size of the fund from 10% to 25% of net general revenue collections. It would also require annual transfers of up to $750 million into the reserve fund and allow state lawmakers to use the money for certain critical needs. Supporters say the amendment would strengthen Florida's financial position during natural disasters, economic downturns and other emergencies by ensuring the state maintains a larger reserve of available funds. Opponents, however, argue that setting aside additional money in reserves could limit the state's ability to address immediate needs, including public services and infrastructure projects. Voters will also weigh Amendment 2 , which focuses on tax relief for Florida's agriculture sector. ( Read the full text) The measure would exempt agricultural equipment and certain farm-related property from property taxes. Supporters say the change would reduce costs for farmers, strengthen the agriculture industry and help preserve farming operations across the state. Those opposed to the amendment contend the tax exemptions could reduce revenue collected by local governments. Critics argue that loss of tax income could affect funding for public services and other community programs that rely on property tax dollars. Both amendments will appear on Florida's ballot this November, giving voters an opportunity to decide whether the proposed changes should be added to the state constitution. Amendment 3 increases the homestead exemption, for all non-school taxes, to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and adjusts for inflation thereafter. entry.title: Vero Beach remembers 17-year-old Sulli Bah as family seeks justice - WFLX
entry.summary: Vero Beach remembers 17-year-old Sulli Bah as family seeks justice    WFLX
entry.article_text: Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman “Sulli” Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week, according to the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office. No arrests have been made, and investigators are examining whether the shooting may have involved self-defense. The celebration of life was held at the Vero Beach restaurant where Bah worked. Through tears and memories, those who knew him described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room. As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm Flame while people who knew Bah stood together to honor his life. Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. “He touched everybody’s heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room,” Rodriguez said. Bah’s close friends told WPTV he was focused on his future and enjoyed spending time with the people closest to him. Alex Cortez said he and Bah boxed together, spent time together and shared many memories. “He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future,” Cortez said. Friend Xavi Espinosa remembered Bah as someone who could immediately make others feel welcome. “Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul,” Espinosa said. The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office said Bah was at a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired. The sheriff’s office said investigators are looking into whether the shooting was self-defense . No arrests have been made. Bah’s mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his entire life ahead of him. She said she wants investigators to consider all the facts as they determine what happened. “I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right,” Godfrey said. “I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail.” During the celebration, people took turns sharing memories of Bah and the impact he had on their lives. Angela Sanders, one of Bah’s former sixth grade teachers, remembered his personality and smile. “His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room,” Sanders said. Myan Agosto said Bah was the type of friend who regularly checked on the people around him. “He never failed to make sure everybody was okay,” Agosto said. “He was just a really good friend.” Another friend, Zani Zoutten, remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person. The memories shared Wednesday showed how many people Bah touched during his 17 years. “He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth — look at this room,” another speaker said during the celebration. Bah’s funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County. "When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn't disappear with it." United Way officials said the program was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption. The organization is now anticipating an even greater need for transportation assistance. Ashley Capital has committed an initial $2,500 donation to help support Ride United's response to the outage. Since launching in September 2022, Ride United has provided thousands of rides for Martin County residents facing transportation barriers. However, United Way emphasized that the program cannot fully replace MARTY's fixed-route bus and paratransit services and that its response is only a temporary solution dependent on available funding. WPTV reached out to Martin County Transit who responded with this statement: "We understand that this news may feel sudden to riders and residents. As strong advocates for reliable public transportation, we are disappointed that we are unable to continue to operate the MARTY system." Martin County Transit told WPTV that 29 employees will be losing jobs as a result of the contract termination. Residents seeking transportation assistance can call 772-283-4800 or visit https://www.unitedwaymartin.org/rideunited for more information. Martin County said it will continue providing updates as it works to restore public transit service. Information about MARTY can be found on the county's transit website .

entry.title: 'Sully was a kind soul’: Loved ones remember teen killed at large party in Fellsmere - WPEC
entry.summary: 'Sully was a kind soul’: Loved ones remember teen killed at large party in Fellsmere    WPEC
entry.article_text: Family and friends gathered Wednesday night at Farm and Flame restaurant in Vero Beach to remember 17-year-old Sulliman Bah, who was shot and killed last Friday during a teen party at the Garcia boat ramp in Fellsmere. Bah, known to many as Sully, had just finished his shift at the restaurant before going to the large gathering of more than 100 teens. A couple hundred people packed the restaurant, sharing stories about Bah’s kindness and the impact he had on their lives. Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described him as a loving son, brother and kind person. He was just joyful, happy all the time, Godfrey said. Godfrey said her son was the kind of person who made everyone around him feel like they mattered. "We've walked down the street, any stranger he saw, he'd greet them, 'How you doing today?' she said. "That was very important to him that he made people feel good, feel seen." Godfrey said Bah cared deeply about making people feel seen. Friends remembered him as funny and caring and kind. See also: Boynton Beach teen reunites with first responders after surviving lightning strike "He was never mean to nobody, and I hate that this happened to him because he doesn't deserve this," one friend said through tears. "Sully was a kind soul." Investigators say several fights broke out at the teen party before an 18-year-old who knew Bah shot him. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers has said he believes the shooting was in self-defense. "Getting that call on a random Friday night that one of my best friends had just gotten shot...was probably one of the hardest things I've had to go through," another friend said. One of eight children, Bah's mother said he was just a credit and a half away from graduating high school and had big plans for the future. "He wanted to travel," Godfrey said. "He wanted to spend time in a big city. wanted to be an entrepreneur." As she begins to cope with the unimaginable loss of her son, Godfrey said she wants answers about what happened that night and accountability for his death. "His life is not being valued enough, and things are not being looked at seriously enough," she said. "I believe that my son was murdered, and I believe that the shooter needs to be punished for that." The sheriff’s office says the investigation remains open. No arrests have been made, and the State Attorney will decide whether charges will be filed.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie flooding problem renews focus on city's stormwater spending - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie flooding problem renews focus on city's stormwater spending    WPEC
entry.article_text: After viewer videos showed water covering roads and vehicles struggling through several Port St. Lucie neighborhoods, the city's own budget documents show where it plans to put money to reduce flooding. The city says that work is still in its early stages. Lucie has received about 4 inches of rain over the past 48 hours , and another 2 to 4 inches could fall by the end of the week. City crews are monitoring conditions as water recedes, and officials are reminding drivers and pedestrians to stay out of flooded roads because it is hard to tell how deep the water is. Frank Camarda, who has lived in the area for more than 20 years near SW California Boulevard and SW Plantation Terrace, said Tuesday night's flooding turned his street into a detour. He said drivers piled in while trying to bypass flooded roads, and he believes Savona Boulevard was also underwater. Camarda said he has not seen flooding on his own street before, but he has watched water pool near Oak Hammock a couple of times. He also said city crews used to clean the swale in front of his home about once a month, and he believes that has stopped. "I've been waiting for these guys to clean up. I haven't seen them," Camarda said. City spokesperson Scott Samples said the rain came in too fast for the system to keep up. He said the canals, swales and retention ponds were already full, which makes it harder for water to move. At one location the city monitored, he said, about two feet of water arrived in roughly 30 minutes. Samples said the water had receded from most roadways by about 8:30 p.m. Tuesday, and he described that as the stormwater system doing what it is designed to do. He said Public Works checks drainage before heavy rain and is working to keep swales, drains and canals clear, but there is only so much crews can do when that much water arrives at once. See also: Florida stages emergency supplies as Tropical Storm Isaias strengthens in Gulf Samples said residents who cannot get home should find other accomedations if they can, whether that be another place to stay or carpooling in vehicles that can handle minor flooding. He also said that the city is working closely with police on safety. The city's proposed capital plan for fiscal years 2027 through 2031, submitted to City Council on April 13, includes the Oak Hammock Watershed Improvement Project. It would add new retention ponds, pump systems, and upgraded valves. The plan shows $8 million in each of the first two years and $7 million in each of the next two, for $30 million in all, paid for through stormwater bond financing. Samples said the city has just begun early data analysis for Oak Hammock, which he placed in the California Boulevard area. He said the work will guide the design of a multi-phase project that could include new retention ponds, canal pumps, or even raising the roadway at California and Savona boulevards so water drains off. He said it is hard to predict when residents will see construction or a finished project, because the city must first gather data, settle on a design, and line up funding. He called Oak Hammock a priority for the city. "It will move as fast as it possibly can," Samples said. According to the city, the project covers a large area east of Interstate 95, north of the C-24 Canal and Port St. Lucie Boulevard, and west of Florida's Turnpike. The money would come partly from the $6 increase in the annual stormwater assessment. That went into effect Oct. 1 and raised the assessment from $189 to $195. The city says the assessment helps pay for five projects aimed at flooding and water flow: Oak Hammock, the Elkcam Basin, the E-8 Canal, Hogpen Slough, and faster replacement of swales and culverts. The city says its drainage system includes about 200 miles of canals, 1,200 miles of swales, and more than 6,000 culverts. It also notes that maintaining swales and driveway culverts, from the edge of the pavement to the property line, is the property owner's responsibility under city code.

entry.title: Hurricane deductibles now in effect across Florida as Isaias nears Panhandle
entry.summary: As Hurricane Isaias heads toward the Florida Panhandle, homeowners across the state will see hurricane deductibles go into effect on their insurance policies. 'The trigger in this case for most policies is a (hurricane) watch or (hurricane) warning anywhere in the state of Florida,' Robert Norberg of Arden Insurance in Lantana said. WATCH BELOW: Isaias triggers Florida insurance deductibles that could cost homeowners thousands Hurricane Deductibles in Effect in Florida Hurricane deductibles are common in Florida and are used for hurricane-related claims. They also have a much higher deductible than the usual deductibles on insurance policies. 'Typically, it's 2 to 3 percent of the property's insured value not 2 to 3 percent of the claim so it can be pretty extensive; some people even have 5 or 10 percent deductible,' Norberg said. A 2 percent deductible on a $300,000 home can run about $6,000. And that deductible applies anywhere in the state as long as a hurricane is posted somewhere in Florida. 'Any type of wind damage that causes a claim say you're in Palm Beach County, those people will be subject to the wind deductible,' Norberg said The hurricane deductible, according to state statute, expires 72 hours after the last hurricane warning is lifted. Inspectors also documented detainees being confined in what were described as "small metal enclosures."A separate Government Accountability Office report highlighted concerns about spending and potential waste. The report found Immigration and Customs Enforcement had not finalized a contract or formal agreement with Florida before immigrants began arriving at the facility.Without pre-negotiated rates in place, the state sought reimbursement at significantly higher costs. The GAO found Florida's approved reimbursement rate was $249 per detainee per day, compared with ICE's reported median detention bed rate of $92 per day, a difference of 171%.So far, neither report concludes Florida violated the terms of its FEMA grant. That distinction could prove important.Palermo says federal agencies typically look first at whether grant recipients complied with the specific requirements attached to funding."Just because there is some sort of deviation from the anticipated standard doesn't necessarily mean that any funding will be withheld," Palermo explained.While the grant excludes typical termination language, it requires Florida to provide a detailed cost breakdown and justification for each reimbursement request.He noted that FEMA retains the authority to review spending, conduct audits and potentially challenge reimbursements if costs are deemed unreasonable. "There is always a chance that there could be an audit or even an investigation into reimbursement that was granted that could potentially lead to a reversal," Palermo said.Federal regulations also give agencies avenues to revisit previously issued payments."There is usually a chance under federal regulations for the government to potentially audit, investigate, review funds that have been paid out and make sure that they were reasonable and could potentially claw them back," he said.Gov. Ron DeSantis dismissed the findings in the federal reports and defended the state's handling of the facility.He also told us last month that additional federal funding continues to flow to the state. To date, just over $134 million has been dispersed from the grant according to USAspending.gov.Neither the Governor's office nor Florida's Department of Emergency Management responded to our inquiries about how the federal reports could impact funding for the facility.The detention center is closed. The federal money is still in question. And until federal officials determine whether all reimbursement requests meet grant requirements, Florida taxpayers have no guarantee they won't end up responsible for part of the final bill.

entry.title: Former city manager Nick Mimms found guilty of misconduct charge, not guilty of bid tampering
entry.summary: Former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms was found guilty of a third-degree felony of official misconduct and not guilty of a second-degree felony of bid tampering on Thursday. Mimms was arrested in 2024 on charges of bid tampering and official misconduct. WATCH BELOW: Former Fort Pierce city manager found guilty of official misconduct Former city manager found guilty of official misconduct According to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, Mimms was accused of rigging the bidding process for two vacant parcels of land along Avenue D, adjacent to the Lincoln Theater, in favor of a local nonprofit, Lincoln Park Young Professionals. Among that nonprofit's board was Caleta Scott, Mimms' niece, and also a city employee. The nonprofit had been awarded a $500,000 grant from Allegheny Franciscan Ministries for a community center project, but nothing was ever built. Johnathan Bridges, special assistant state attorney and Brandon White, major crimes attorney for the 19th Circuit, said there was a mountain of evidence, including emails and city documents that incriminated Mimms. 'What we learned is millions of dollars have been wasted by this city hall under the leadership of Nick Mimms, and for too long, it went unchecked, said White. The people of Ft. Pierce deserve better, and I think this verdict shows the corruption that was happening under Nick Mimms. It's about time someone was held accountable.' WPTV pressed Mimms and his attorney for comment as they left the courtroom but did not get a response. Mimms was granted a pre-sentencing investigation and is scheduled to be sentenced on Dec. 11 at the St. Lucie County Courthouse. Prosecutors said he could face a maximum of five years in prison.

entry.title: Palm Beach County firefighters team up with adoptable pets for popular charity calendar fundraiser
entry.summary: Palm Beach County Fire Rescue and Animal Care and Control are joining forces once again to help homeless animals find loving homes through a one-of-a-kind fundraiser. The annual Palm Beach County Fire Rescue calendar brings together firefighters, EMTs and adoptable animals for a photo shoot designed to raise money and awareness for animals in need. Organizers say the calendar has become much more than a collection of photos, helping support local animal welfare efforts while connecting pets with potential adopters. WATCH BELOW: Firefighters team up with adoptable pets for popular charity calendar fundraiser Firefighters, adoptable pets team up for calendar fundraiser in Palm Beach County While posing for the camera may be outside their usual line of work, firefighters say they are happy to step out of their comfort zones for a good cause. 'I am excited but a little nervous, but it's for a great cause,' firefighter Jose Besosa said. The fundraiser began last year and quickly gained momentum. 'Last year we started it, and it kind of took off from there, and it's become a huge event,' said Bryan Brather, Second Legislative Vice President of Local 2928. This year's kickoff event will give the public a chance to help decide which firefighter and dog duo is featured in each month of the calendar. A struggle followed.Reaves shot Raczkowski four times in the back, killing him.For nearly 40 years, Raczkowski's brother, Marc Raczkowski, has lived with the loss."Why? Why?" he said while speaking with WPTV near his brother's gravesite. "It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody." Instead, he wants DeSantis to commute Reaves' death sentence so the now-77-year-old can spend the rest of his life behind bars.Central to his plea is Reaves' history as a decorated Vietnam War veteran and questions raised during decades of appeals about his mental health, substance abuse and legal representation.Court records show Reaves repeatedly challenged his conviction and death sentence, including claims that his trial attorney failed to adequately investigate and present evidence concerning his drug use and mental health."The attorney wasn't an effective attorney for that type of case," Farrington said. "That was his first death row case."At Reaves' sentencing, testimony described him as suffering from what was then called "Vietnam syndrome," rather than post-traumatic stress disorder.Years later, other experts testified that Reaves suffered from PTSD, substance abuse and other impairments.Farrington said none of that excuses the murder."I'm not going to say that his PTSD, his drug use, his being on cocaine and all the other stuff excuses what he did," Farrington said. "I mean, he's being punished by being in prison, and he's 77. The governor can let him stay in prison for the rest of his life, and still he's being punished without killing him and taking another life."Farrington also acknowledges that his family is not the only one carrying grief into Oct. 20.On the other side is Raczkowski's family, which has spent four decades living with the consequences of Reaves' actions."I mean, trying to understand what he feels — there's no way I could do that," Farrington said of Raczkowski's brother.He said he understands why the deputy's family may want the execution to proceed."I know that the family, the officer ... entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire Board continues law firm search in effort to create complaint policy amid hazing fallout - WFLX
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire Board continues law firm search in effort to create complaint policy amid hazing fallout    WFLX
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District has hit a snag in its effort to create a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders as fallout continues from a controversial hazing investigation. During a Fire District Board workshop Wednesday morning, board members had hoped to hear from outside law firms about helping draft a new complaint policy. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said one of the law firms contacted never returned her calls, while another disclosed a potential conflict of interest. “I appreciated her honesty and forthrightness on that issue,” Fowler said of the attorney during the meeting. “That being said, she did provide two references, both on the West Coast.” The board discussed now reaching out to additional law firms in hopes of securing outside legal help ahead of its next meeting Oct. “I think we’d be doing ourselves an injustice if we at least we don’t have a courtesy conversation with these other firms, so that we’re at least prepared just in case these two firms aren’t available, non-responsive,” Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson said. “I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and and I don’t want to delay any further.” The effort follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30 , when members publicly acknowledged what they described as a significant gap in district policy: There is no clear process for independently handling complaints made against some of the district’s own contract employees. “Since this district’s inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves,” Fowler said during that meeting. “They — being those positions — have essentially been able to investigate themselves.” Those positions include the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director. The issue came under increased scrutiny amid fallout from a hazing investigation involving three veteran firefighters. A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing. Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result. Hutchinson and Boudrias previously told WPTV they did not consider the conduct hazing and said there was no intent to hurt anyone. “It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun,” Hutchinson said. “We’re all still friends,” Boudrias said. “Us and the victims, there was no ill intent.” The controversy has also raised questions about how complaints involving district leadership have been handled. Months before the hazing incident came to light, Baldwin and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025. District officials ultimately denied it. Baldwin and Hutchinson later filed additional complaints, including an amended complaint to investigators alleging the hazing investigation and their subsequent terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. Lucie County Fire District told WPTV it is not currently in receipt of any official retaliation complaint from any party involved in this matter. “That’s not a good process,” Fowler previously told WPTV. entry.article_text: Two women in Fort Pierce are accused of animal neglect after a dog died on their watch, according to arrest reports from the Fort Pierce Police Department . FPPD says that Samya Shanice Bryant, 25, and Danielle Amanda Potts, 28, were arrested on Oct. 2 in connection with the neglect and death of a dog at Pine Creek Apartments. Officers found the dog days before on Sept. 29 lying outside an apartment. The dog was severely underweight with visible ribs, infected sores on his paws, and no food or water. Bryant told the officers that the dog was hers, and that he had been sick for weeks after another man allegedly poured boiling water on him. FPPD says that both women who each lived in the apartment had control of the dog but did not get him veterinary treatment. See also: Trump touts West Palm golf club as possible Camp David-style retreat for future presidents Animal Control took the dog for emergency care, but the dog had to be euthanized on Oct. 2 because of injuries, infections and organ failure. Both Bryant and Potts were arrested and are being charged with aggravated animal cruelty and confining/impounding an animal without sufficient food or water.

entry.title: Vero Beach remembers 17-year-old Sulli Bah as family seeks justice - WPTV
entry.summary: Vero Beach remembers 17-year-old Sulli Bah as family seeks justice    WPTV
entry.article_text: Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm & Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman “Sulli” Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. No arrests have been made, and investigators are examining whether the shooting may have involved self-defense. The celebration of life was held at the Vero Beach restaurant where Bah worked. Through tears and memories, those who knew him described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room.As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm & Flame while people who knew Bah stood together to honor his life.Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. “He touched everybody’s heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room,” Rodriguez said.Bah's close friends told WPTV he was focused on his future and enjoyed spending time with the people closest to him.Alex Cortez said he and Bah boxed together, spent time together and shared many memories. “He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future,” Cortez said.Friend Xavi Espinosa remembered Bah as someone who could immediately make others feel welcome. “Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul,” Espinosa said.The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Bah was at a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired. The sheriff's office said investigators are looking into whether the shooting was self-defense. No arrests have been made.Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his entire life ahead of him. She said she wants investigators to consider all the facts as they determine what happened.“I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right,” Godfrey said. “I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail.”During the celebration, people took turns sharing memories of Bah and the impact he had on their lives.Angela Sanders, one of Bah's former sixth grade teachers, remembered his personality and smile. “His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room,” Sanders said.Myan Agosto said Bah was the type of friend who regularly checked on the people around him. “He never failed to make sure everybody was okay,” Agosto said. “He was just a really good friend.”Another friend, Zani Zoutten, remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person.The memories shared Wednesday showed how many people Bah touched during his 17 years.“He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth — look at this room,” another speaker said during the celebration.Bah's funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

entry.summary: Florida officials are urging residents in the Panhandle to finalize their hurricane preparations as Hurricane Isaias strengthens in the Gulf of Mexico and heads toward the state's northwestern coast. During a news briefing Thursday, Gov. Ron DeSantis said the storm is expected to bring impacts as early as Friday afternoon, with landfall projected late Friday night into early Saturday morning. WATCH THE FULL NEWS CONFERENCE BELOW: Gov. Ron DeSantis holds news conference ahead of Hurricane Isaias While forecasters currently expect Isaias to make landfall as a Category 2 hurricane, state officials said they are preparing for a Category 3 storm. 'We're taking it very seriously,' DeSantis said. 'Our assumption is that it's going to hit strong as a probably lower-end Category 3, and then we work off that assumption.' The governor warned that the storm's most dangerous conditions are expected to be on the eastern side of its track, putting much of the Florida Panhandle at risk for storm surge, tornadoes, flooding and damaging winds. Current forecasts show landfall somewhere between Mobile Bay and Navarre, though officials stressed the track could still change. 'There will be impacts all across the Florida Panhandle.' State mobilizes resources Florida's Emergency Operations Center is operating at its highest activation level as agencies across the state prepare for response and recovery efforts. entry.title: 'We are doing everything we can': Martin County works to find solutions after MARTY suspended - WPBF
entry.summary: 'We are doing everything we can': Martin County works to find solutions after MARTY suspended    WPBF
entry.article_text: MARTY public transit service in Martin County came to an abrupt halt Thursday, leaving residents who depend on the transit system without regular transportation as county officials scramble to find a solution. Martin County officials told WPBF's Caleb Califano they were given no advance warning that service would stop Thursday. According to the county, MARTY’s operator, Martin County Transit LLC, had requested a significant increase in its contract. The company says rising insurance, fuel and maintenance costs have led to significant financial losses since it began operating the service in July 2025. Despite negotiations with the county, the two sides were unable to reach an agreement. County officials said the company provided a 180-day notice to terminate its contract approximately two weeks ago. However, Thursday morning, Martin County Transit LLC notified the county that it was immediately discontinuing service. The sudden shutdown has left residents who rely on MARTY to get around the county without their regular transportation option. George Stokus, assistant Martin County administrator, said officials are now exploring both short-term and long-term solutions to restore service. "We are doing everything we can humanly do right now to restore service as soon as we can," Stokus said. "It’s just not an easy operation or switch to turn it back on. It’s going to take some time, and we are working to get to that." In the meantime, county officials say they are working with community partners, including United Way, to help residents impacted by the shutdown. The county has not provided a timeline for when MARTY operations could resume. Officials say they will continue posting updates on social media and will notify residents as soon as a solution is reached. Riders react Leticia Chaclan, of Martin County, waited for the bus in Stuart on Thursday, but it never came. She was unaware that the MARTY bus had been suspended until WPBF's Jasimine Yasmine Julmisse informed her. Chaclain says she's been riding the bus for years and that it's a staple for many members of the community. "We really need the bus," she said. "Especially people within the Hispanic community, who don’t have a driver’s license, and need it to go to places like the clinic, to go to the hospital, and for other things we need. entry.summary: Martin County Public Transit riders left without service after transit provider suspends operations    WFLX
entry.article_text: Martin County officials are scrambling to restore public transportation service after the county's contracted transit provider abruptly canceled its services, leaving Martin County Public Transit (MARTY) riders without transportation effective immediately. In a statement Thursday, Martin County said it is aware that its contracted transit service provider has canceled service and that MARTY transit operations are currently interrupted. "Martin County is actively working to identify solutions to restore transit service as quickly as possible and minimize the impact on our riders," the county said. "Additional information will be provided as it becomes available." Officials did not immediately identify the transit provider or explain why the service was canceled. "We understand the importance of MARTY services to our community and apologize for the disruption," the statement said. In response, United Way of Martin County said it is preparing for an increase in transportation assistance requests through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents. Region Martin County "Transportation isn't a luxury for the people who depend on it. It's how they get to work, receive medical care and put food on the table," said Carol G. Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County. "When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn't disappear with it." United Way officials said the program was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption. The organization is now anticipating an even greater need for transportation assistance. Ashley Capital has committed an initial $2,500 donation to help support Ride United's response to the outage. Since launching in September 2022, Ride United has provided thousands of rides for Martin County residents facing transportation barriers. However, United Way emphasized that the program cannot fully replace MARTY's fixed-route bus and paratransit services and that its response is only a temporary solution dependent on available funding. WPTV reached out to Martin County Transit who responded with this statement: "We understand that this news may feel sudden to riders and residents. As strong advocates for reliable public transportation, we are disappointed that we are unable to continue to operate the MARTY system." Martin County Transit told WPTV that 29 employees will be losing jobs as a result of the contract termination. Residents seeking transportation assistance can call 772-283-4800 or visit https://www.unitedwaymartin.org/rideunited for more information. Martin County said it will continue providing updates as it works to restore public transit service. Information about MARTY can be found on the county's transit website .

entry.summary: Jury convicts former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County jury convicted former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct Thursday, finding he improperly obstructed, delayed or prevented information about a possible felony involving the city from being communicated. Jurors found Mimms not guilty of bid tampering, the first count he faced. But they found him guilty on the official-misconduct count and specifically determined the misconduct involved obstructing, delaying or preventing communication of information related to a possible felony that directly involved or affected the government entity he served. The verdict followed a trial that began Sept. 29 and centered on allegations that Mimms improperly influenced the city’s bidding process for two vacant Lincoln Park-area lots. Prosecutors alleged Mimms steered the process toward Lincoln Park Young Professionals , a nonprofit whose board included his niece and another city employee. The organization sought a lease involving the properties, near the Lincoln Theater. During trial, FDLE Agent Derek Brisky testified about emails, city records and the request-for-proposals process. Prosecutors pointed to communications showing Mimms continued to discuss the RFP’s evaluation criteria and committee after the matter had been referred to the city’s purchasing department. The defense argued the purchasing department controlled the RFP’s publication and administration, and challenged the state’s claim that the process amounted to an improper sole-source arrangement. See also: 4 people arrested after drugs, 26 firearms found at North Palm Beach home Court records show Circuit Judge Michael James Linn denied the state’s request to have Mimms taken into custody pending sentencing. Mimms was allowed to remain free on bond. Sentencing is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Lucie County Circuit Court.

They also have a much higher deductible than the usual deductibles on insurance policies. 'Typically, it's 2 to 3 percent of the property's insured value not 2 to 3 percent of the claim so it can be pretty extensive; some people even have 5 or 10 percent deductibles,' Norberg said. A 2 percent deductible on a $300,000 home can run about $6,000. And that deductible applies anywhere in the state as long as a hurricane is posted somewhere in Florida. entry.summary: The detention center Florida dubbed 'Alligator Alcatraz' may have shut down, but questions remain about who will ultimately pay for it. Last year, the federal government awarded Florida more than $600 million through FEMA to help fund operations at the immigration detention facility built in the Everglades. entry.article_text: The detention center Florida dubbed "Alligator Alcatraz" may have shut down, but questions remain about who will ultimately pay for it.Last year, the federal government awarded Florida more than $600 million through FEMA to help fund operations at the immigration detention facility built in the Everglades. WATCH ALLIGATOR ALCATRAZ, IS FEDERAL FUNDING AT RISK?While state leaders touted the project and President Donald Trump praised it shortly after opening, only a portion of the promised funding has been distributed so far.Now, two federal reports are putting renewed attention on whether that money could be withheld and Florida could face additional scrutiny before receiving the rest of the funds."I think what these reports and the findings in them do is create a potential basis for scrutiny," said Stetson University law professor Anthony Palermo, who specializes in contracts.The questions stem from two separate federal reviews examining the facility's operations.A report from the Department of Homeland Security's Office of Inspector General found the detention center failed to meet several basic standards related to environmental health, safety, medical care, food service and hygiene.According to the report, some detainees reported lacking access to clean drinking water. Inspectors also documented detainees being confined in what were described as "small metal enclosures."A separate Government Accountability Office report highlighted concerns about spending and potential waste. The report found Immigration and Customs Enforcement had not finalized a contract or formal agreement with Florida before immigrants began arriving at the facility.Without pre-negotiated rates in place, the state sought reimbursement at significantly higher costs. The GAO found Florida's approved reimbursement rate was $249 per detainee per day, compared with ICE's reported median detention bed rate of $92 per day, a difference of 171%.So far, neither report concludes Florida violated the terms of its FEMA grant. That distinction could prove important.Palermo says federal agencies typically look first at whether grant recipients complied with the specific requirements attached to funding."Just because there is some sort of deviation from the anticipated standard doesn't necessarily mean that any funding will be withheld," Palermo explained.While the grant excludes typical termination language, it requires Florida to provide a detailed cost breakdown and justification for each reimbursement request.He noted that FEMA retains the authority to review spending, conduct audits and potentially challenge reimbursements if costs are deemed unreasonable. "There is always a chance that there could be an audit or even an investigation into reimbursement that was granted that could potentially lead to a reversal," Palermo said.Federal regulations also give agencies avenues to revisit previously issued payments."There is usually a chance under federal regulations for the government to potentially audit, investigate, review funds that have been paid out and make sure that they were reasonable and could potentially claw them back," he said.Gov. Ron DeSantis dismissed the findings in the federal reports and defended the state's handling of the facility.He also told us last month that additional federal funding continues to flow to the state. To date, just over $134 million has been dispersed from the grant according to USAspending.gov.Neither the Governor's office nor Florida's Department of Emergency Management responded to our inquiries about how the federal reports could impact funding for the facility.The detention center is closed. The federal money is still in question. And until federal officials determine whether all reimbursement requests meet grant requirements, Florida taxpayers have no guarantee they won't end up responsible for part of the final bill.

entry.title: 'I love him': Family of death row inmate William Reaves pleads for clemency ahead of Oct. 20 execution
entry.summary: For the first time, the family of a man set to be executed for the 1986 murder of an Indian River County sheriff's deputy is speaking publicly about their effort to save his life. William Reaves has spent nearly four decades on death row for shooting and killing 29-year-old Deputy Richard Raczkowski. Reaves' execution is scheduled for Oct. 20. WATCH BELOW: As execution nears, Reaves' family asks DeSantis to spare his life As execution nears, Reaves' family asks DeSantis to spare his life Now, with less than two weeks remaining, Reaves' family is asking Gov. Ron DeSantis to grant him clemency and commute his death sentence to life in prison. 'I mean, he's my uncle, and I love him,' Reaves' nephew, Meredith Farrington, told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. Farrington said his family does not dispute the gravity of Reaves' crime or the pain Raczkowski's family has endured. 'I can't be upset. I can't be mad at the governor or the decision,' Farrington said. 'I mean, my uncle did take a life.' But Farrington added, 'I just want the governor to look at the whole picture.' A killing that left decades of grief That story stretches back to Sept. 23, 1986. According to court records, Reaves called 911 from a convenience store in Indian River County after he was unable to get a taxi. Raczkowski responded and was attempting to help Reaves call a cab when a gun fell from Reaves' pants. A struggle followed. Reaves shot Raczkowski four times in the back, killing him. For nearly 40 years, Raczkowski's brother, Marc Raczkowski, has lived with the loss. 'Why? Why?' he said while speaking with WPTV near his brother's gravesite. 'It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody.' A stretch of road near where the deputy was killed now bears Raczkowski's name a memorial to a life taken and a crime that continues to reverberate through two families four decades later. 'The pain will still always be there,' Marc Raczkowski said. Reaves' family asks governor to consider his history DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant Sept. 22, scheduling his execution for Oct. 20. Farrington is not asking the governor to pardon his uncle or release him from prison. Instead, he wants DeSantis to commute Reaves' death sentence so the now-77-year-old can spend the rest of his life behind bars. Central to his plea is Reaves' history as a decorated Vietnam War veteran and questions raised during decades of appeals about his mental health, substance abuse and legal representation. A struggle followed.Reaves shot Raczkowski four times in the back, killing him.For nearly 40 years, Raczkowski's brother, Marc Raczkowski, has lived with the loss."Why? Why?" he said while speaking with WPTV near his brother's gravesite. "It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody." A stretch of road near where the deputy was killed now bears Raczkowski's name — a memorial to a life taken and a crime that continues to reverberate through two families four decades later."The pain will still always be there," Marc Raczkowski said.DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant Sept. 22, scheduling his execution for Oct. 20.Farrington is not asking the governor to pardon his uncle or release him from prison. Instead, he wants DeSantis to commute Reaves' death sentence so the now-77-year-old can spend the rest of his life behind bars.Central to his plea is Reaves' history as a decorated Vietnam War veteran and questions raised during decades of appeals about his mental health, substance abuse and legal representation.Court records show Reaves repeatedly challenged his conviction and death sentence, including claims that his trial attorney failed to adequately investigate and present evidence concerning his drug use and mental health."The attorney wasn't an effective attorney for that type of case," Farrington said. "That was his first death row case."At Reaves' sentencing, testimony described him as suffering from what was then called "Vietnam syndrome," rather than post-traumatic stress disorder.Years later, other experts testified that Reaves suffered from PTSD, substance abuse and other impairments.Farrington said none of that excuses the murder."I'm not going to say that his PTSD, his drug use, his being on cocaine and all the other stuff excuses what he did," Farrington said. "I mean, he's being punished by being in prison, and he's 77. The governor can let him stay in prison for the rest of his life, and still he's being punished without killing him and taking another life."Farrington also acknowledges that his family is not the only one carrying grief into Oct. 20.On the other side is Raczkowski's family, which has spent four decades living with the consequences of Reaves' actions."I mean, trying to understand what he feels — there's no way I could do that," Farrington said of Raczkowski's brother.He said he understands why the deputy's family may want the execution to proceed."I know that the family, the officer ... I would probably want the same thing, and I can't even imagine," Farrington said.For the Raczkowski family, the case is about a life taken nearly 40 years ago.For Reaves' family, it is now about whether another life should end."But we're praying," Farrington said.Reaves has already lost his latest attempt to stop the execution in Indian River County court. He has appealed that decision to the Florida Supreme Court.For now, his execution remains scheduled for Oct. 20 unless a court intervenes or DeSantis grants clemency.If carried out, Reaves' execution will mark the 18th in Florida in 2026.

entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire Board continues law firm search in effort to create complaint policy amid hazing fallout - WPTV
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire Board continues law firm search in effort to create complaint policy amid hazing fallout    WPTV
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District has hit a snag in its effort to create a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders as fallout continues from a controversial hazing investigation. During a Fire District Board workshop Wednesday morning, board members had hoped to hear from outside law firms about helping draft a new complaint policy.WATCH BELOW: Fire district's new complaint policy effort stalls amid hazing falloutInstead, St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said one of the law firms contacted never returned her calls, while another disclosed a potential conflict of interest."I appreciated her honesty and forthrightness on that issue," Fowler said of the attorney during the meeting. "That being said, she did provide two references, both on the West Coast." The board discussed now reaching out to additional law firms in hopes of securing outside legal help ahead of its next meeting Oct. 21."I think we'd be doing ourselves an injustice if we at least we don't have a courtesy conversation with these other firms, so that we're at least prepared just in case these two firms aren't available, non-responsive," Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson said. "I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and and I don't want to delay any further." The effort follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30, when members publicly acknowledged what they described as a significant gap in district policy: There is no clear process for independently handling complaints made against some of the district's own contract employees. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said during that meeting. "They — being those positions — have essentially been able to investigate themselves."Those positions include the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director.The issue came under increased scrutiny amid fallout from a hazing investigation involving three veteran firefighters.A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing.Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result.Hutchinson and Boudrias previously told WPTV they did not consider the conduct hazing and said there was no intent to hurt anyone."It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said."We're all still friends," Boudrias said. "Us and the victims, there was no ill intent."The controversy has also raised questions about how complaints involving district leadership have been handled.Months before the hazing incident came to light, Baldwin and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025. District officials ultimately denied it. Baldwin and Hutchinson later filed additional complaints, including an amended complaint to investigators alleging the hazing investigation and their subsequent terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. Lucie County Fire District told WPTV it is not currently in receipt of any official retaliation complaint from any party involved in this matter."That's not a good process," Fowler previously told WPTV.Sabol submitted her notice of retirement Sept. 30, just minutes after the special board meeting, effective 90 days from her notice. The District stated she will continue to provide services during that 90-day period. Lee previously acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process and told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey that he welcomed outside scrutiny."I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," Lee said, adding that he "welcomes any investigation from any agency."Lee also defended Sabol following her notice of retirement, calling it a "sad day" and saying she had been a "tremendous attorney for the district."Meanwhile, firefighters have been casting ballots in a union vote of no confidence in Lee."It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler previously said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message."Lee previously said he would wait for the results before commenting further on the vote."We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee said. "I came up on the labor side; I've always fought for our men and women on the line."The union is also continuing its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin.During the Sept. 30 meeting, Fowler questioned whether the fire board itself may have the authority to bring the three firefighters back rather than waiting for the arbitration process to play out."I think we might actually," Fowler said at the time.Board members are expected to continue searching for an outside law firm to help develop the new policy before the Fire District Board meets again Oct.

As strong advocates for reliable public transportation, we are disappointed that we are unable to continue to operate the MARTY system," Martin County Transit said.In an afternoon press conference County leaders explained they were in negotiations after the vendor asked for a significant increase in the cost of the contract. Two weeks ago, the company gave notice it planned to leave in 180 days and instead, it walked away Thursday.Jim Gordon, Martin County's Public Works Director, said the county had no warning the cancellation was coming."We were not given advanced notice that they were going to cancel service today," Jim Gordon said.For Joe, a 67-year-old veteran and Martin County resident, losing MARTY service means losing his lifeline. Joe sat at the bus stop Thursday expecting his regular pickup, but no buses came. He relies on the transit system daily."[I use it] to go to work sometimes and to go down to the homeless place, the church that feeds us food," Joe said.Joe said he received no notice before service was cut."No warning at all, nothing, zero." Joe said.Physical limitations make alternative transportation all but impossible for Joe."I've had two broken necks, three broken backs, I can't feel my feet, so I'm not getting anywhere," Joe said.Tony Argudo, a Martin County resident, said the transit company's handling of the shutdown lacked transparency."I don't think letting people go first thing this morning was a good idea. There should have been more transparency and the people should have had some kind of notice so they could have made other plans," Argudo said.George Stokus, Martin County's Assistant County Administrator, said county officials are working urgently to restore service."We're doing everything we can humanly due to restore service as soon as we can," George Stokus said.In the meantime, the United Way of Martin County is stepping in through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents for trips to work, grocery stores, medical appointments and other essential services.The organization said it was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption and is now anticipating even greater need.Carol G. Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County, emphasized the critical importance of transportation access for those who depend on it."Transportation isn't a luxury for the people who depend on it. It's how they get to work, receive medical care and put food on the table. When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn't disappear with it," Houwaart-Diez said.Houwaart-Diez said the United Way is committed to being there for riders during the disruption."This is important for people to be able to get to the doctors to get to wherever they need to go so we want to be there," Houwaart-Diez said.Ashley Capital has committed an initial $2,500 donation to help support the Ride United program's response, alongside a contribution from another donor. Since launching in September 2022, Ride United has provided thousands of rides for Martin County residents facing transportation barriers. However, United Way emphasized that the program cannot fully replace MARTY's fixed-route bus and paratransit services and that its response is only a temporary solution dependent on available funding.Martin County said it will continue providing updates as it works to restore public transit service. entry.title: Ex-CIA agent who stole $194M used $102M to buy Palm Beach, Hobe Sound properties - WPEC
entry.summary: Ex-CIA agent who stole $194M used $102M to buy Palm Beach, Hobe Sound properties    WPEC
entry.article_text: A former CIA agent convicted Tuesday of defrauding the government of $194 million reportedly used the majority of the money to acquire properties in Palm Beach and Hobe Sound. According to CBS Miami , court filings say 49-year-old David J. Rush of Virginia, a former high-ranking federal employee, directed $145 million to a holding company he controlled, and that $102 million was used to purchase four Florida properties: Two Palm Beach homes: $21.9 million and $27 million One Palm Beach parcel: $13.65 million One Hobe Sound parcel: $40 million Prosecutors allege Rush intended to eventually resell the properties for a profit. How the scheme unfolded According to the Department of Justice , Rush, of Ashburn, Virginia, pleaded guilty Tuesday, Oct. 6, to wire fraud in federal court in Alexandria, Virginia. According to prosecutors, Rush used his senior-level government position and "Top Secret" clearance to create fictitious government authorities and obtain federal money for his own benefit. Between November 2025 and March 2026, he directed approximately $145 million to a holding company established at his direction, according to court documents. The money was then used to purchase the properties. The Justice Department says Rush fraudulently obtained approximately $193.6 million in government funds. The South Florida real estate was only part of the alleged scheme. Gold bars Prosecutors say Rush separately created a fake "sensitive government activity" to justify acquiring hundreds of gold bars. On May 19, 2026, FBI agents searched Rush's Virginia home and recovered 298 gold bars, approximately $2.1 million in cash, €104,795, and numerous luxury watches. The gold had cost the government approximately $46 million, according to the Justice Department. Rush has agreed to forfeit the gold bars and cash, the Florida properties, luxury watches, and two 2026 BMW Alpina vehicles as part of his plea agreement. What's next Rush is scheduled to be sentenced Jan. He faces a maximum of 20 years in federal prison, along with possible restitution, forfeiture and a fine. The Justice Department said its investigation is continuing. The Director of National Intelligence has also requested an investigation by the Intelligence Community's inspector general. The allegations and admissions are detailed in federal court documents filed as part of Rush's guilty plea.

entry.title: Jury convicts former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct - WPEC
entry.summary: Jury convicts former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County jury convicted former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct Thursday, finding he improperly obstructed, delayed or prevented information about a possible felony involving the city from being communicated. Jurors found Mimms not guilty of bid tampering, the first count he faced. But they found him guilty on the official-misconduct count and specifically determined the misconduct involved obstructing, delaying or preventing communication of information related to a possible felony that directly involved or affected the government entity he served. The verdict followed a trial that began Sept. 29 and centered on allegations that Mimms improperly influenced the city’s bidding process for two vacant Lincoln Park-area lots. Prosecutors alleged Mimms steered the process toward Lincoln Park Young Professionals , a nonprofit whose board included his niece and another city employee. The organization sought a lease involving the properties, near the Lincoln Theater. During trial, FDLE Agent Derek Brisky testified about emails, city records and the request-for-proposals process. Prosecutors pointed to communications showing Mimms continued to discuss the RFP’s evaluation criteria and committee after the matter had been referred to the city’s purchasing department. The defense argued the purchasing department controlled the RFP’s publication and administration, and challenged the state’s claim that the process amounted to an improper sole-source arrangement. See also: 4 people arrested after drugs, 26 firearms found at North Palm Beach home Court records show Circuit Judge Michael James Linn denied the state’s request to have Mimms taken into custody pending sentencing. Mimms was allowed to remain free on bond. Sentencing is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Lucie County Circuit Court.

A struggle followed.Reaves shot Raczkowski four times in the back, killing him.For nearly 40 years, Raczkowski's brother, Marc Raczkowski, has lived with the loss."Why? Why?" he said while speaking with WPTV near his brother's gravesite. "It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody." Instead, he wants DeSantis to commute Reaves' death sentence so the now-77-year-old can spend the rest of his life behind bars.Central to his plea is Reaves' history as a decorated Vietnam War veteran and questions raised during decades of appeals about his mental health, substance abuse and legal representation.Court records show Reaves repeatedly challenged his conviction and death sentence, including claims that his trial attorney failed to adequately investigate and present evidence concerning his drug use and mental health."The attorney wasn't an effective attorney for that type of case," Farrington said. "That was his first death row case."At Reaves' sentencing, testimony described him as suffering from what was then called "Vietnam syndrome," rather than post-traumatic stress disorder.Years later, other experts testified that Reaves suffered from PTSD, substance abuse and other impairments.Farrington said none of that excuses the murder."I'm not going to say that his PTSD, his drug use, his being on cocaine and all the other stuff excuses what he did," Farrington said. "I mean, he's being punished by being in prison, and he's 77. The governor can let him stay in prison for the rest of his life, and still he's being punished without killing him and taking another life."Farrington also acknowledges that his family is not the only one carrying grief into Oct. 20.On the other side is Raczkowski's family, which has spent four decades living with the consequences of Reaves' actions."I mean, trying to understand what he feels — there's no way I could do that," Farrington said of Raczkowski's brother.He said he understands why the deputy's family may want the execution to proceed."I know that the family, the officer ...
