entry.title: Truffle Smiles brings taste of Italy to West Palm Beach GreenMarket
entry.summary: The West Palm Beach GreenMarket is more than a weekend destination. Its also serving as a launching pad for local entrepreneurs, including several new vendors making their debut this season. For this weeks Saturday Small Business, WPTVs Christy Waite visited Truffle Smiles, one of five new vendors joining the GreenMarket this year. Owner Robert Hurbanek specializes in artisan truffle products imported from Italy. We import artisan truffle products from Italy. If you love to cook, this is the place to stop, Hurbanek said. Visitors to the Truffle Smiles booth can find a variety of products, including oils, pasta, sauces, and truffle chips. Hurbanek recommends the truffle mayonnaise. The mayonnaise! Oh my gosh, if you put that on a burger or a BLT sandwich, it changes everything, he said. With so many options, Hurbanek said one product customers keep coming back for: Parmesan Reggiano. People come back for the Parmesan Reggiano, Hurbanek said. You can put it on mashed potatoes, a burger. I have even made decadent grilled cheese sandwiches. The business also fits into this years GreenMarket theme, The World Right Here, which celebrates the food traditions, people and cultures that make the community unique. Hurbanek said choosing the West Palm Beach GreenMarket was an easy decision because farmers markets give him the opportunity to connect directly with customers and hear how they use his products. I mostly sell at farmers markets. I like interacting with people and listening to peoples recipes, and just being here at the GreenMarket, which is a nice place to be, he said. Truffle Smiles is one of the new businesses shoppers can check out this season at the West Palm Beach GreenMarket in downtown West Palm Beach.

entry.title: 'EXTREMELY ALARMING': Hobe Sound woman buried kittens alive, believing they were demons - WPTV
entry.summary: 'EXTREMELY ALARMING': Hobe Sound woman buried kittens alive, believing they were demons    WPTV
entry.article_text: A Hobe Sound woman is facing multiple animal cruelty charges after deputies say she killed and buried several kittens because she believed they were possessed by demons.The Martin County Sheriff's Office (MCSO) arrested 36-year-old Alba Chavez on Thursday after responding to reports of animal cruelty at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park.WATCH BELOW: Woman buried cats alive, thought they were demons, deputies sayAccording to MCSO Sheriff John Budensiek, three youths living in the home called 911 after they discovered several of their kittens had disappeared. The children told deputies they believed Chavez had killed two kittens earlier in the week and were worried about the remaining animals.Budensiek said the children had attempted to protect three kittens by locking them inside a bedroom before going out to dinner Thursday evening. When they returned, they found the door had been forced open, and the kittens were gone."When deputies arrived, she admitted she thought the kittens had demons and said she didn't want black cats or brown cats in her residence," Budensiek said during a Friday news conference.Investigators said Chavez told deputies she had killed two kittens on Monday, thrown them into the trash, later removed them and buried them in the backyard.Deputies said she then led them to a burial site behind the home and told them to bring gloves, shovels and bags if they wanted to find the missing kittens.Despite heavy rain and lightning, deputies began digging in the backyard."As they were digging, they could hear cries from the kittens," Budensiek said.Deputies rescued two kittens that were buried alive inside a plastic Publix bag. The two kittens killed earlier in the week were also recovered deceased from the burial site.A fifth kitten remains missing. Budensiek said deputies and investigators extensively searched the backyard and mobile home but have not located the animal.The two surviving kittens were rushed to a veterinary emergency clinic, where they are being treated for dehydration and monitored for potential long-term effects from being buried underground."If they survive, they'll eventually be taken to the Humane Society and go through the adoption process," Budensiek said.Chavez was arrested on four counts of animal cruelty involving torture, inflicting pain, serious injury or death to an animal. Authorities said additional charges could follow if the missing kitten is found dead.The arrest marks at least the third animal cruelty or neglect case in Martin County since late July. Asked whether the trend surprised him, Budensiek said reports of violence against animals often mirror broader societal problems."We've seen society kind of going downward and we see more violence with interactions with humans, and then that translates into animals," Budensiek said. "In fact, a lot of times it starts with animals and then moves over to humans. So unfortunately, based on the trends and societal trends that we're seeing, it does not surprise me, but when we see it, it's extremely alarming.Budensiek said Chavez is being held without bond at the Martin County Jail and is also subject to an immigration hold. The sheriff identified her as a Venezuelan national who he said is in the United States illegally.According to the sheriff, deputies had previously responded to the home for incidents involving Chavez's mental health but had never received complaints related to animal cruelty.When asked about Chavez's motive, Budensiek said investigators still aren't certain whether mental health issues played a role."She said they were demonic. She said she didn't want those cats in her house," Budensiek said. "I don't know whether it was a mental health issue or she just didn't like the cats."Budensiek said the three youths who reported the incident were emotional but showed courage by contacting law enforcement."I applaud them for reaching out, calling 911 and letting us save the two kittens," he said.The children were taken into the custody of the Florida Department of Children and Families before being turned over to their father, who lives locally, according to investigators.Other adult cats found at the home were examined by animal services and determined to be healthy.Budensiek called the case "extremely alarming" and praised the responding deputies for their efforts to rescue the buried animals."We're going to aggressively pursue criminal charges on her to make sure she pays for the damage that she did to these animals," he said.

entry.title: Jury convicts former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct - WPEC
entry.summary: Jury convicts former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County jury convicted former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct Thursday, finding he improperly obstructed, delayed or prevented information about a possible felony involving the city from being communicated. Jurors found Mimms not guilty of bid tampering, the first count he faced. But they found him guilty on the official-misconduct count and specifically determined the misconduct involved obstructing, delaying or preventing communication of information related to a possible felony that directly involved or affected the government entity he served. The verdict followed a trial that began Sept. 29 and centered on allegations that Mimms improperly influenced the city’s bidding process for two vacant Lincoln Park-area lots. Prosecutors alleged Mimms steered the process toward Lincoln Park Young Professionals , a nonprofit whose board included his niece and another city employee. The organization sought a lease involving the properties, near the Lincoln Theater. During trial, FDLE Agent Derek Brisky testified about emails, city records and the request-for-proposals process. Prosecutors pointed to communications showing Mimms continued to discuss the RFP’s evaluation criteria and committee after the matter had been referred to the city’s purchasing department. The defense argued the purchasing department controlled the RFP’s publication and administration, and challenged the state’s claim that the process amounted to an improper sole-source arrangement. See also: 4 people arrested after drugs, 26 firearms found at North Palm Beach home Court records show Circuit Judge Michael James Linn denied the state’s request to have Mimms taken into custody pending sentencing. Mimms was allowed to remain free on bond. Sentencing is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Lucie County Circuit Court.

In a second video, Simmons said the other victim, a man, died from a generator that was not properly ventilated. The sheriff said that four other people were inside the same home and had to be hospitalized. "What I saw was both from the structural perspective, I think our structures handled the storm very well," DeSantis said. "The problem is that the storm knocked over a lot of trees."State officials confirmed two storm-related deaths. One person in Escambia County was killed when a tree fell on a home. Another person died after operating a generator inside a garage, highlighting ongoing safety concerns as residents cope with power outages.Emergency crews have completed roughly 180 missions through the Florida Division of Emergency Management, according to the governor. State officials said nearly 10,000 power accounts have already been restored, but approximately 430,000 customers remained without electricity Saturday morning. About 325,000 of those outages are within Florida Power & Light's service area.Officials said debris removal remains one of the biggest challenges slowing restoration efforts."The folks have been out since daylight," DeSantis said. "Some of it is that you've got to get the debris out of the way before the linemen can connect it."The Florida Department of Transportation began clearing roads and bridges before sunrise, while the Florida Highway Patrol has completed dozens of debris-clearing missions. State officials said 85 traffic signals have been restored using generators.Northwest Florida Beaches International Airport has reopened to commercial air traffic, while airports in Pensacola and Fort Walton Beach remained closed Saturday but were expected to resume operations soon.Florida Division of Emergency Management Executive Director Jared Perdue said more than 16,000 utility workers have been mobilized to restore power throughout the region.Perdue also warned residents that flooding risks remain even after the storm's passage. Several rivers, including the Shoal River in Okaloosa County, are still rising and are not expected to crest for several days."We want to make sure we keep enough resources on hand in case search and rescue is needed," Perdue said.State leaders urged residents to avoid flooded roads and standing water, warning that even shallow water can quickly become dangerous.Meanwhile, Attorney General James Uthmeier said a small number of price-gouging complaints had already been reported. Residents who believe businesses are overcharging for essentials such as fuel, food or other emergency supplies are encouraged to file complaints through the attorney general's office.Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia also warned residents about post-storm scams, including unlicensed contractors and fraudulent roofers targeting homeowners.Officials urged residents not to sign contracts or provide deposits before verifying a contractor's credentials. The state also plans to establish insurance assistance hubs in impacted areas within the next 48 hours to help residents file claims and meet with insurance representatives.Businesses affected by the storm can report damage through the state's business damage assessment survey at FloridaDisaster.biz. State officials said the information will help expedite recovery assistance and assess losses.DeSantis said recovery efforts will continue across the Panhandle, where damage stretches from the Alabama state line to the eastern Panhandle.The governor cautioned that additional flooding could develop in the coming days as rivers continue rising but said Florida has water rescue teams and emergency assets positioned throughout the region."We're going to get through this," DeSantis said. "There's damage, and that's going to be difficult for people whose property was damaged, but I also feel like this is very surmountable for us if we all just work together and get the job done."

entry.summary: Hurricane Isaias became the first hurricane to make direct landfall in the United States in more than two years when it came ashore late Friday as a Category 2 storm. By Saturday morning, Isaias had weakened into a post-tropical cyclone as it moved across Alabama. While no longer a hurricane, its remnants were expected to bring heavy rain and gusty winds across parts of the South on Saturday before spreading into the Great Lakes and Northeast on Sunday. As of 2 p.m. CT Saturday, more than 700,000 customers were without power. More than 400,000 outages were reported in Florida's Panhandle, while Alabama reported more than 180,000 outages and Georgia reported about 40,000. At its peak, nearly 900,000 customers were without power. 2 dead as Hurricane Isaias weakens over the South The storm also caused significant wind damage in the Pensacola area, where a hotel lost its roof as Isaias made landfall. RELATED STORY | Study: Super-sized El Nio could cause more than 450,000 heat deaths by February The hurricane pushed storm surge onto coastal roadways across the Florida Panhandle. Escambia County Sheriff Chip W. Simmons confirmed one person died during the storm. He added that some roads were impassable due to downed trees and power lines. Away from the coast, a death was reported in Birmingham, Alabama, due to a fallen tree limb. Isaias marked a departure from what had been one of the quietest Atlantic hurricane seasons in recent years. It was also the first hurricane to form in the Atlantic basin in 2026. Forecasters had predicted a below-normal season because of a strong El Nio, which typically creates upper-level winds that can disrupt tropical cyclone development. Although Isaias was the ninth named storm of the season, all previous systems had peaked at tropical-storm strength. The same upper-level winds that limited hurricane activity this year also contributed to Isaias weakening before landfall. The storm maintained Category 3 strength for much of Friday before being downgraded to a Category 2 hurricane just hours before reaching the coast. RELATED STORY | El Nino keeps Atlantic hurricane season historically calm Behind Isaias, the National Hurricane Center said it was not tracking any additional systems. The Atlantic hurricane season typically peaks around Sept. 10 and begins to wind down by mid-October before ending Nov. 30. Since 2013, only two hurricanes have made U.S. landfall after Oct. 15. The most recent was Hurricane Nicole in 2022.

entry.title: Martin County employee rescues 3 girls caught in rip current at Bob Graham Beach - WFLX
entry.summary: Martin County employee rescues 3 girls caught in rip current at Bob Graham Beach    WFLX
entry.article_text: A Martin County employee helped rescue three girls who were struggling in a rip current Thursday afternoon at Bob Graham Beach near Jensen Beach. Amy Offenbach said she arrived at the beach around 2 p.m. to surf when she noticed three girls about 25 yards offshore holding onto the same surfboard. Watch report: Offenbach, who works in Martin County's Growth and Development Department and is an avid surfer, said something about the situation immediately caught her attention. "The ocean could be very gentle and calm, but it can also be very heavy and crash very hard," Offenbach said. Offenbach said she became concerned when one of the girls appeared distressed. "That kind of struck me as strange," she said. "The other one seemed a little agitated." Moments later, a girl on the beach told Offenbach she believed her friends needed help. "By that time the girls were waving in the water like they needed help, so immediately I just went into rescue mode," Offenbach said. Offenbach and a friend went into the water and paddled toward the girls. When Offenbach reached the group, she said one of the girls appeared to be in serious distress. "I looked at her, and she seemed kind of dazed and confused," Offenbach said. "I said, 'Get up on the board.'" Offenbach said she gave the surfboard she was riding to two of the girls and instructed them to hold on and kick toward shore. She then placed the third girl on her soft-top surfboard and paddled her back to the beach. Offenbach said she has some lifeguard training and quickly recognized the girl needed medical attention after they returned to shore. "The girl that I rescued said that she blacked out under the water," Offenbach said. "She inhaled water, and she had a severe headache." Because Bob Graham Beach is unguarded, Offenbach said she drove the girl to a nearby lifeguard station, where an ambulance was called. Offenbach hopes the rescue serves as a reminder for beachgoers to understand ocean conditions before entering the water. She encourages people to swim at guarded beaches when possible, check rip current forecasts and use flotation devices or boards when appropriate. "I'm just really happy that I was in the right place at the right time," Offenbach said. Offenbach said she has not been able to reconnect with the girl she rescued or learn more about her condition. While she enjoys spending time in the ocean, Offenbach said it is important to remember the dangers it can present. "It can be very treacherous. entry.title: Deputies hear cries underground, rescue 2 kittens buried alive in Hobe Sound - WPEC
entry.summary: Deputies hear cries underground, rescue 2 kittens buried alive in Hobe Sound    WPEC
entry.article_text: Deputies digging through a rain-soaked backyard in Martin County heard the cries of kittens buried up to 3 feet underground, leading to the rescue of two animals while two others were found dead, the sheriff revealed Friday. During a news conference, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek provided new details about the arrest of 36-year-old Alba Chavez, who is accused of killing two kittens and burying two others alive at a mobile home park in Hobe Sound. According to the sheriff's office, deputies responded to the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park on Thursday night after several minors inside the home called 911 to report that Chavez had allegedly killed two kittens Monday, placed them in the trash and later buried them in the backyard. The children, who feared for the safety of three remaining kittens, attempted to protect them by locking them inside a bedroom before leaving for dinner Thursday night. Budensiek said that when the children returned home, they discovered the bedroom door had been forced open and the kittens were missing. The children then called law enforcement to report the incident. When deputies arrived, Chavez was standing in the roadway and reportedly admitted to killing the two kittens. While speaking with deputies, Chavez said she believed the kittens had demons, described them as ugly and said she did not want black or brown cats inside the home. Chavez then led deputies to the backyard, where the kittens had allegedly been buried. "She took them to the backyard where our deputies started digging frantically trying to recover what they believed to be three live kittens and two dead kittens," Budensiek said. See also: Hurricane Isaias strengthens into major Category 3 storm near Florida Panhandle As deputies dug through the backyard, they heard cries coming from underground. Two kittens were recovered alive, while the two kittens Chavez allegedly killed Monday were found dead. A fifth kitten remains missing despite repeated searches of the property. Budensiek said the two surviving kittens were immediately taken to an emergency veterinary facility, where they were being treated for dehydration. The sheriff said veterinarians were also concerned about possible injuries caused by a lack of oxygen while the kittens were buried. Despite being rescued, the kittens could still die from their injuries. Chavez was arrested and charged with four counts of animal torture involving pain, serious injury or death, according to the sheriff's office. The four charges correspond to the two kittens found dead and the two rescued alive. The sheriff said Chavez was being held without bond at the Martin County Jail and also had an immigration hold. Investigators have not determined exactly how the first two kittens died. The sheriff said Chavez initially cooperated with deputies and led them to the burial site but later stopped answering questions about how the animals were killed. Authorities also have not determined her motive. Budensiek said deputies had previously responded to calls involving Chavez's mental health but had received no prior animal cruelty complaints at the residence. Additional charges could be filed if the fifth kitten is found dead, according to the sheriff. Following the incident, the Florida Department of Children and Families became involved, and the children were later released to their father, who lives locally. Officials said resources were available to help the children cope with what happened.

entry.title: Explosion inside Port St. Lucie home leaves family with little to salvage - WPBF
entry.summary: Explosion inside Port St. Lucie home leaves family with little to salvage    WPBF
entry.article_text: An explosion inside a Port St. Lucie home destroyed almost everything owned by a family of four. Lucie County Fire District, the initial call came in at 1:24 p.m. for a fire at a home in the 100 block of Carmelite Street Friday afternoon. Neighbors called 911 after noticing the home was on fire. "I looked, and there was all kinds of smoke going through the yard," said neighbor Rob Roadman. "I was outside in the backyard, and then I see very heavy smoke," said Marina Cheong, who lives a few doors down. Cheong said she ran toward the home to help but was stopped by the explosion. "And then there was explosion, very loud, loud explosion, and debris started flying everywhere," she said. "I heard a huge explosion. At first, I thought maybe it's a transformer or something, but it was much, much, much louder than that," Roadman said. Neighbors said the man who lives in the home told them he had been cooking when a grease fire started in the garage, where the propane tank was located. The explosion sent the propane tank flying out of the garage, across the street, and into the garage of a neighbor's home. "I thought it was an air raid. It was not a casual thing. My house shook," Roadman said. "I thought that the whole house had exploded. It was very loud," Cheong added. Roadman said he spoke to the man shortly after the explosion. "I asked the dad if he was OK, and he goes, 'Yeah.' But you could tell he wasn't. Who wouldn't be?" Roadman said. The man was briefly hospitalized but returned to the house a few hours later to join family and friends in going through the debris to see what could be salvaged. They said there wasn’t much left. However, a family member told WPBF 25 News that they consider themselves lucky that nobody was seriously injured. She said the family has a strong community and a strong church to help them persevere. The family has set up a GoFundMe account for donations. entry.title: Vero Beach remembers 17-year-old Sulli Bah as family seeks justice - WFLX
entry.summary: Vero Beach remembers 17-year-old Sulli Bah as family seeks justice    WFLX
entry.article_text: Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman “Sulli” Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week, according to the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office. No arrests have been made, and investigators are examining whether the shooting may have involved self-defense. The celebration of life was held at the Vero Beach restaurant where Bah worked. Through tears and memories, those who knew him described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room. As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm Flame while people who knew Bah stood together to honor his life. Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. “He touched everybody’s heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room,” Rodriguez said. Bah’s close friends told WPTV he was focused on his future and enjoyed spending time with the people closest to him. Alex Cortez said he and Bah boxed together, spent time together and shared many memories. “He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future,” Cortez said. Friend Xavi Espinosa remembered Bah as someone who could immediately make others feel welcome. “Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul,” Espinosa said. The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office said Bah was at a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired. The sheriff’s office said investigators are looking into whether the shooting was self-defense . No arrests have been made. Bah’s mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his entire life ahead of him. She said she wants investigators to consider all the facts as they determine what happened. “I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right,” Godfrey said. “I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail.” During the celebration, people took turns sharing memories of Bah and the impact he had on their lives. Angela Sanders, one of Bah’s former sixth grade teachers, remembered his personality and smile. “His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room,” Sanders said. Myan Agosto said Bah was the type of friend who regularly checked on the people around him. “He never failed to make sure everybody was okay,” Agosto said. “He was just a really good friend.” Another friend, Zani Zoutten, remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person. The memories shared Wednesday showed how many people Bah touched during his 17 years. “He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth — look at this room,” another speaker said during the celebration. Bah’s funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

entry.title: Jury convicts former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct - cw34.com
entry.summary: Jury convicts former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie County jury convicted former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct Thursday, finding he improperly obstructed, delayed or prevented information about a possible felony involving the city from being communicated. Jurors found Mimms not guilty of bid tampering, the first count he faced. But they found him guilty on the official-misconduct count and specifically determined the misconduct involved obstructing, delaying or preventing communication of information related to a possible felony that directly involved or affected the government entity he served. The verdict followed a trial that began Sept. 29 and centered on allegations that Mimms improperly influenced the city’s bidding process for two vacant Lincoln Park-area lots. Prosecutors alleged Mimms steered the process toward Lincoln Park Young Professionals , a nonprofit whose board included his niece and another city employee. The organization sought a lease involving the properties, near the Lincoln Theater. During trial, FDLE Agent Derek Brisky testified about emails, city records and the request-for-proposals process. Prosecutors pointed to communications showing Mimms continued to discuss the RFP’s evaluation criteria and committee after the matter had been referred to the city’s purchasing department. The defense argued the purchasing department controlled the RFP’s publication and administration, and challenged the state’s claim that the process amounted to an improper sole-source arrangement. See also: 4 people arrested after drugs, 26 firearms found at North Palm Beach home Court records show Circuit Judge Michael James Linn denied the state’s request to have Mimms taken into custody pending sentencing. Mimms was allowed to remain free on bond. Sentencing is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Lucie County Circuit Court.

entry.title: Martin County's MARTY bus transit abruptly shuts down, leaving riders stranded and 29 workers jobless - WFLX
entry.summary: Martin County's MARTY bus transit abruptly shuts down, leaving riders stranded and 29 workers jobless    WFLX
entry.article_text: Martin County’s contracted transit provider walked away from its agreement Thursday, halting all MARTY bus service and laying off 29 employees with no warning to riders or county leaders. Martin County issued an official statement acknowledging the disruption and pledging to work toward a solution. “Martin County is actively working to identify solutions to restore transit service as quickly as possible and minimize the impact on our riders,” Martin County officials said in the statement. Martin County Transit, the company contracted to operate the MARTY system, blamed rising operating costs for the decision. In a statement, CEO Karen Deigl said, “we entered this contract in good faith and made every effort to find a path forward. We understand how important MARTY is to its riders and the community, and this decision was not made lightly.” Martin County Transit also acknowledged the abruptness of the shutdown. “We understand that this news may feel sudden to riders and residents. As strong advocates for reliable public transportation, we are disappointed that we are unable to continue to operate the MARTY system,” Martin County Transit said. In an afternoon press conference, county leaders explained they were in negotiations after the vendor asked for a significant increase in the cost of the contract. Two weeks ago, the company gave notice it planned to leave in 180 days and instead, it walked away Thursday, according to the county. Jim Gordon, Martin County’s Public Works Director, said the county had no warning the cancellation was coming. “We were not given advanced notice that they were going to cancel service today,” Gordon said. For Joe, a 67-year-old veteran and Martin County resident, losing MARTY service means losing his lifeline. Joe sat at the bus stop Thursday expecting his regular pickup, but no buses came. He relies on the transit system daily. “[I use it] to go to work sometimes and to go down to the homeless place, the church that feeds us food,” Joe said. Joe said he received no notice before service was cut. “No warning at all, nothing, zero.” Joe said. Physical limitations make alternative transportation all but impossible for Joe. “I’ve had two broken necks, three broken backs, I can’t feel my feet, so I’m not getting anywhere,” Joe said. Tony Argudo, a Martin County resident, said the transit company’s handling of the shutdown lacked transparency. “I don’t think letting people go first thing this morning was a good idea. There should have been more transparency and the people should have had some kind of notice so they could have made other plans,” Argudo said. George Stokus, Martin County’s Assistant County Administrator, said county officials are working urgently to restore service. “We’re doing everything we can humanly due to restore service as soon as we can,” George Stokus said. In the meantime, the United Way of Martin County is stepping in through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents for trips to work, grocery stores, medical appointments and other essential services. The organization said it was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption and is now anticipating even greater need. Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County, emphasized the critical importance of transportation access for those who depend on it. “Transportation isn’t a luxury for the people who depend on it. It’s how they get to work, receive medical care and put food on the table. When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn’t disappear with it,” Houwaart-Diez said. Region Martin County Houwaart-Diez said the United Way is committed to being there for riders during the disruption. “This is important for people to be able to get to the doctor’s, to get to wherever they need to go so we want to be there,” Houwaart-Diez said. Ashley Capital has committed an initial $2,500 donation to help support the Ride United program’s response, alongside a contribution from another donor. Since launching in September 2022, Ride United has provided thousands of rides for Martin County residents facing transportation barriers. However, United Way emphasized that the program cannot fully replace MARTY’s fixed-route bus and paratransit services and that its response is only a temporary solution dependent on available funding. Martin County said it will continue providing updates as it works to restore public transit service. Information about MARTY can be found on the county’s transit website . Residents seeking transportation assistance can call the United Way of Martin County at 772-283-4800 or click here to visit their website. entry.summary: Port St. Lucie assisted-living project raises contamination concerns    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A proposed 150-unit assisted-living facility in Port St. Lucie is moving through the development process as nearby residents question whether enough is known about the environmental history of a neighboring property with petroleum contamination. The project, known as PSL Westmoreland ALF , is planned for 7.1 acres within the Rivella planned unit development, along Southeast Morningside Boulevard near Southeast Westmoreland Boulevard. The three-story facility would include assisted-living units and a memory care component. Lucie City Council approved the project’s major site plan on Sept. Construction has not begun, and the developer must still submit construction plans for technical review and additional agency reviews. A group of residents opposes the project, citing concerns about the neighboring property’s contamination history and the potential implications for people who could eventually live at the facility. See also: 'It's not safe': Treasure Coast neighbors raise concerns after teen hit walking to school It’s not about what is being built there, resident David Lipps said, arguing that nearby businesses and other facilities could also be affected by environmental concerns. Resident Charlie D’Agata said residents have raised objections at City Council meetings for about two years. He questioned why a developer would be allowed to build near a property he described as contaminated. Residents say they have contacted outside organizations, including the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Florida Department of Health , in an effort to get answers about the site. An engineering letter provides some context for their concerns. In a letter discussing a March 2026 meeting with environmental officials about the neighboring property, BTEX Engineering said the proposed remediation approach should be changed because of concerns about surrounding properties, including the planned assisted-living facility. The letter said vapors would need to be captured during remediation. The environmental history of the neighboring property and the extent of any potential impact on surrounding land remain central questions for residents seeking more information. The city has approved the major site plan, but the project must clear additional steps before construction can begin. The developer is expected to submit construction plans for technical review, followed by reviews involving the South Florida Water Management District and other agencies. Residents say they want clearer answers about the neighboring property’s environmental history and how any potential risks would be addressed as the project advances

entry.article_text: A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student died Friday after being struck by a vehicle while walking to school in Port St. Lucie on Wednesday morning. Lucie Police Department said the crash occurred near the intersection of Southwest Port St. Lucie Boulevard and Southwest Squirrel Avenue. An updated news release dated 8 p.m. Friday from Chief Leo Niemczyk, said: "14-YEAR-OLD PEDESTRIAN SUCCUMBS TO INJURIES FOLLOWING CRASH." "The Port St. Lucie Police Department extends its deepest condolences to the student's family, friends, classmates, and all those affected by this heartbreaking loss. Our thoughts are with them during this incredibly difficult time," the department said in a statement. The preliminary investigation revealed the freshman was walking northbound along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near the edge of the roadway when he was struck from behind by a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man. The investigation remains ongoing as detectives continue to examine the circumstances surrounding the crash. Investigators said the vehicle involved was a 2002 Ford Excursion. According to police, the driver initially believed he had struck a construction barrel and did not realize he had hit a person. The driver later made a U-turn at the next safe location, returned to the scene, activated his hazard lights and found the teenager unconscious on the side of the roadway. entry.title: Treasure Coast families invited to watch and try dog sports at kennel club's Pirate Cluster - WFLX
entry.summary: Treasure Coast families invited to watch and try dog sports at kennel club's Pirate Cluster    WFLX
entry.article_text: Dog lovers from across South Florida are heading to Fort Pierce this weekend for the Treasure Coast Kennel Club’s Pirate Cluster, a four-day event featuring dock diving, FastCAT racing, agility, frisbee competitions, and other canine sports. The event is taking place Oct. Lucie County Fairgrounds, where visitors can watch trained canine athletes compete or give their own dogs an opportunity to try several activities. According to Treasure Coast Kennel Club President Lisa Root, many of the events offer same-day participation. “It has to do with all kinds of sporting events that we do with our dogs, so dock diving, FastCAT, agility, UpDog (frisbee catching). The Pirate Cluster features activities for beginners and experienced competitors alike. Visitors can watch dogs leap into a pool during dock-diving competitions, sprint down a FastCAT course while chasing a lure, navigate agility obstacles, and participate in frisbee events. Root said the event is designed to be welcoming for both dog owners and spectators. “It’s a really family day. Admission and parking are free for spectators. Fees apply for participants entering dogs into individual events. One of the most popular attractions is dock diving, where dogs run down a platform and launch themselves into a pool in pursuit of a toy. Competitors say many dogs recognize the venue before they even leave the vehicle. “Once they start competing, they know what this dock means,” said dock-diving participant Janet. “You’ll see them when they start coming in. They just roll past the dock, and they’ll start barking in the cars and stuff because they know that they get to get up here and just jump.” Organizers say the excitement surrounding dock diving often becomes contagious for owners and spectators alike. In addition to the sporting events, the Pirate Cluster includes vendors, raffles and opportunities for families to spend time with fellow dog lovers. The event highlights the growing popularity of dog sports as a way for owners to stay active, build stronger relationships with their pets and connect with others in the community. Whether someone owns a highly trained competitor or simply wants to learn more about canine activities, organizers say the weekend provides an opportunity to see what these sports are all about. entry.title: 'A strong support system': Community helps injured father after Port St. Lucie house fire - cw34.com
entry.summary: 'A strong support system': Community helps injured father after Port St. Lucie house fire    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A fire that spread through the garage of a Port St. Lucie home Friday afternoon left a father injured and displaced a family, while neighbors and church members rallied to help them begin the cleanup process. The fire happened on Carmelite Street in the Northport Village neighborhood near St. According to the family, the fire started in the kitchen before spreading through the garage. They say a propane tank later exploded, causing additional damage and impacting a neighbor's garage doors across the street. Lucie County Fire District responded to the home around 1:30 p.m. Crews arrived to find heavy fire coming from the garage. When firefighters extinguished the flames, significant damage was left behind, including a charred garage door, blackened walls and belongings covered in soot. Renter Nigel Laidlow was inside the home when the fire broke out. He suffered burns to his legs and was transported for medical treatment. "I don't even know how to describe it. It was really surreal," Laidlow said. "I would've never thought a little fire would turn into this." By Saturday, family photos, furniture and other belongings were spread across the front yard as loved ones worked to salvage what they could. Members of the Fort Pierce Seventh-day Adventist Church spent the day helping move and sort through damaged items. "We have a really strong support system, especially from my church," Laidlow said. Despite the loss, Laidlow said he is grateful his family survived. "This right here is something not anybody would like to deal with. Not in a lifetime," he said. See also: MCSO warns scam emails may trick development applicants into wiring money The family is now focused on recovering and determining its next steps. The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

Residents should avoid driving through flooded roadways and be prepared for rapidly changing conditions through Thursday night.

entry.summary: Martin County's MARTY bus transit abruptly shuts down, leaving riders stranded and 29 workers jobless    WFLX
entry.article_text: Martin County’s contracted transit provider walked away from its agreement Thursday, halting all MARTY bus service and laying off 29 employees with no warning to riders or county leaders. Martin County issued an official statement acknowledging the disruption and pledging to work toward a solution. “Martin County is actively working to identify solutions to restore transit service as quickly as possible and minimize the impact on our riders,” Martin County officials said in the statement. Martin County Transit, the company contracted to operate the MARTY system, blamed rising operating costs for the decision. In a statement, CEO Karen Deigl said, “we entered this contract in good faith and made every effort to find a path forward. We understand how important MARTY is to its riders and the community, and this decision was not made lightly.” Martin County Transit also acknowledged the abruptness of the shutdown. “We understand that this news may feel sudden to riders and residents. As strong advocates for reliable public transportation, we are disappointed that we are unable to continue to operate the MARTY system,” Martin County Transit said. In an afternoon press conference, county leaders explained they were in negotiations after the vendor asked for a significant increase in the cost of the contract. Two weeks ago, the company gave notice it planned to leave in 180 days and instead, it walked away Thursday, according to the county. Jim Gordon, Martin County’s Public Works Director, said the county had no warning the cancellation was coming. “We were not given advanced notice that they were going to cancel service today,” Gordon said. For Joe, a 67-year-old veteran and Martin County resident, losing MARTY service means losing his lifeline. Joe sat at the bus stop Thursday expecting his regular pickup, but no buses came. He relies on the transit system daily. “[I use it] to go to work sometimes and to go down to the homeless place, the church that feeds us food,” Joe said. Joe said he received no notice before service was cut. “No warning at all, nothing, zero.” Joe said. Physical limitations make alternative transportation all but impossible for Joe. “I’ve had two broken necks, three broken backs, I can’t feel my feet, so I’m not getting anywhere,” Joe said. Tony Argudo, a Martin County resident, said the transit company’s handling of the shutdown lacked transparency. “I don’t think letting people go first thing this morning was a good idea. There should have been more transparency and the people should have had some kind of notice so they could have made other plans,” Argudo said. George Stokus, Martin County’s Assistant County Administrator, said county officials are working urgently to restore service. “We’re doing everything we can humanly due to restore service as soon as we can,” George Stokus said. In the meantime, the United Way of Martin County is stepping in through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents for trips to work, grocery stores, medical appointments and other essential services. The organization said it was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption and is now anticipating even greater need. Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County, emphasized the critical importance of transportation access for those who depend on it. “Transportation isn’t a luxury for the people who depend on it. It’s how they get to work, receive medical care and put food on the table. When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn’t disappear with it,” Houwaart-Diez said. Region Martin County Houwaart-Diez said the United Way is committed to being there for riders during the disruption. “This is important for people to be able to get to the doctor’s, to get to wherever they need to go so we want to be there,” Houwaart-Diez said. Ashley Capital has committed an initial $2,500 donation to help support the Ride United program’s response, alongside a contribution from another donor. Since launching in September 2022, Ride United has provided thousands of rides for Martin County residents facing transportation barriers. However, United Way emphasized that the program cannot fully replace MARTY’s fixed-route bus and paratransit services and that its response is only a temporary solution dependent on available funding. Martin County said it will continue providing updates as it works to restore public transit service. Information about MARTY can be found on the county’s transit website . Residents seeking transportation assistance can call the United Way of Martin County at 772-283-4800 or click here to visit their website. entry.article_text: A Hobe Sound woman is facing multiple animal cruelty charges after deputies say she killed and buried several kittens because she believed they were possessed by demons.The Martin County Sheriff's Office (MCSO) arrested 36-year-old Alba Chavez on Thursday after responding to reports of animal cruelty at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park.WATCH BELOW: Woman buried cats alive, thought they were demons, deputies sayAccording to MCSO Sheriff John Budensiek, three youths living in the home called 911 after they discovered several of their kittens had disappeared. The children told deputies they believed Chavez had killed two kittens earlier in the week and were worried about the remaining animals.Budensiek said the children had attempted to protect three kittens by locking them inside a bedroom before going out to dinner Thursday evening. When they returned, they found the door had been forced open, and the kittens were gone."When deputies arrived, she admitted she thought the kittens had demons and said she didn't want black cats or brown cats in her residence," Budensiek said during a Friday news conference.Investigators said Chavez told deputies she had killed two kittens on Monday, thrown them into the trash, later removed them and buried them in the backyard.Deputies said she then led them to a burial site behind the home and told them to bring gloves, shovels and bags if they wanted to find the missing kittens.Despite heavy rain and lightning, deputies began digging in the backyard."As they were digging, they could hear cries from the kittens," Budensiek said.Deputies rescued two kittens that were buried alive inside a plastic Publix bag. The two kittens killed earlier in the week were also recovered deceased from the burial site.A fifth kitten remains missing. Budensiek said deputies and investigators extensively searched the backyard and mobile home but have not located the animal.The two surviving kittens were rushed to a veterinary emergency clinic, where they are being treated for dehydration and monitored for potential long-term effects from being buried underground."If they survive, they'll eventually be taken to the Humane Society and go through the adoption process," Budensiek said.Chavez was arrested on four counts of animal cruelty involving torture, inflicting pain, serious injury or death to an animal. Authorities said additional charges could follow if the missing kitten is found dead.The arrest marks at least the third animal cruelty or neglect case in Martin County since late July. Asked whether the trend surprised him, Budensiek said reports of violence against animals often mirror broader societal problems."We've seen society kind of going downward and we see more violence with interactions with humans, and then that translates into animals," Budensiek said. "In fact, a lot of times it starts with animals and then moves over to humans. So unfortunately, based on the trends and societal trends that we're seeing, it does not surprise me, but when we see it, it's extremely alarming.Budensiek said Chavez is being held without bond at the Martin County Jail and is also subject to an immigration hold. The sheriff identified her as a Venezuelan national who he said is in the United States illegally.According to the sheriff, deputies had previously responded to the home for incidents involving Chavez's mental health but had never received complaints related to animal cruelty.When asked about Chavez's motive, Budensiek said investigators still aren't certain whether mental health issues played a role."She said they were demonic. She said she didn't want those cats in her house," Budensiek said. "I don't know whether it was a mental health issue or she just didn't like the cats."Budensiek said the three youths who reported the incident were emotional but showed courage by contacting law enforcement."I applaud them for reaching out, calling 911 and letting us save the two kittens," he said.The children were taken into the custody of the Florida Department of Children and Families before being turned over to their father, who lives locally, according to investigators.Other adult cats found at the home were examined by animal services and determined to be healthy.Budensiek called the case "extremely alarming" and praised the responding deputies for their efforts to rescue the buried animals."We're going to aggressively pursue criminal charges on her to make sure she pays for the damage that she did to these animals," he said.

entry.title: Martin County employee rescues girl from rip current at Stuart beach - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County employee rescues girl from rip current at Stuart beach    WPBF
entry.article_text: A Martin County employee is being praised for her quick actions after rescuing a girl from drowning at Bob Graham Beach in Stuart on Thursday afternoon. Amy Offenbach, who came to the beach to surf, said the day took an unexpected turn. "It was just by chance that we were here and thank God that we were at the right time," Offenbach said. Offenbach, who has years of lifeguard training, said her instincts kicked in when she saw three girls struggling in the water. "I took off my clothes, grabbed the board, and started paddling," she said. "I immediately went into rescue mode." Authorities said one of the girls was choking on water, and the beach had no lifeguards on duty. Offenbach rushed in to help, using a surfboard to stabilize the girl. "Once she was on the board, she was kind of limp. Her body wasn't doing anything else," Offenbach said. Offenbach said the girl's forehead felt cold, prompting her to rush the child to the nearest lifeguard stand down the road. The girl was then taken to the hospital with minor drowning injuries. "I'm just really thankful that her parents have their child," Offenbach said. Offenbach, a Martin County employee, said she doesn’t feel the need for recognition. While some are calling her a hero, Offenbach said she was simply acting on her instincts as a mother. "I have a 14-year-old son myself, and I can't imagine him not coming back from hanging out at the beach with his friends," she said. The incident serves as a reminder to exercise caution at the beach, especially in areas without lifeguards. entry.title: Vero Beach remembers 17-year-old Sulli Bah as family seeks justice - WPTV
entry.summary: Vero Beach remembers 17-year-old Sulli Bah as family seeks justice    WPTV
entry.article_text: Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm & Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman “Sulli” Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. No arrests have been made, and investigators are examining whether the shooting may have involved self-defense. The celebration of life was held at the Vero Beach restaurant where Bah worked. Through tears and memories, those who knew him described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room.As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm & Flame while people who knew Bah stood together to honor his life.Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. “He touched everybody’s heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room,” Rodriguez said.Bah's close friends told WPTV he was focused on his future and enjoyed spending time with the people closest to him.Alex Cortez said he and Bah boxed together, spent time together and shared many memories. “He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future,” Cortez said.Friend Xavi Espinosa remembered Bah as someone who could immediately make others feel welcome. “Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul,” Espinosa said.The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Bah was at a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired. The sheriff's office said investigators are looking into whether the shooting was self-defense. No arrests have been made.Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his entire life ahead of him. She said she wants investigators to consider all the facts as they determine what happened.“I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right,” Godfrey said. “I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail.”During the celebration, people took turns sharing memories of Bah and the impact he had on their lives.Angela Sanders, one of Bah's former sixth grade teachers, remembered his personality and smile. “His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room,” Sanders said.Myan Agosto said Bah was the type of friend who regularly checked on the people around him. “He never failed to make sure everybody was okay,” Agosto said. “He was just a really good friend.”Another friend, Zani Zoutten, remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person.The memories shared Wednesday showed how many people Bah touched during his 17 years.“He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth — look at this room,” another speaker said during the celebration.Bah's funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

entry.title: Palm Beach Atlantic University celebrates Hispanic heritage through art, music festival
entry.summary: Palm Beach Atlantic University wrapped up its three-day Hispanic Heritage Festival on Saturday, celebrating Hispanic art, culture and music during Hispanic Heritage Month in South Florida. The annual festival featured a contemporary art exhibition and a series of musical performances designed to showcase the cultural contributions and artistic traditions of the Hispanic world. Organizers say the event continues to grow as it enters its 17th year. In a region with a large Hispanic population, organizers say the festival provides an opportunity for students and community members to engage with artists and musicians while learning more about the diversity of Hispanic cultures. Artists from across the Hispanic world The festival began Thursday with an art exhibition featuring artists representing more than 10 countries. Visitors viewed a wide range of artistic styles and mediums, including oil paintings, photography and metalwork. Among the featured artists was Franco Sotillo, a visual artist originally from Lima, Peru, who said his work combines mixed media and reflects both his heritage and personal experiences. 'I'm a visual artist and came from Lima, Peru,' Sotillo said. 'I moved to this country 12 years ago.' Sotillo said his work incorporates materials including oils, paper and other raw elements. He said sharing his art allows him to introduce audiences to Peruvian artistic expression. 'I'm an immigrant, but also bringing my culture to the states to show people how Peruvian art is expressed,' Sotillo said. Festival expands music offerings Festival Director Michael O'Connor said the event continues to evolve each year. 'We're expanding every year,' O'Connor said. O'Connor said this year's festival marked the first time organizers expanded programming beyond art and classical music to also include popular music from Hispanic cultures. 'What we want to do is we want to celebrate the Hispanic artistic heritage, because here in South Florida, especially, we have a very, very large Hispanic population,' O'Connor said. Inspiring students and the community Organizers said they hope attendees leave with a deeper appreciation for Hispanic artistic traditions and the people behind them. 'We hope they'll be inspired too to see the artworks here at the exhibition and to see how the Hispanic world makes itself known through visual arts,' O'Connor said. He said sharing his art allows him to introduce audiences to Peruvian artistic expression."I'm an immigrant, but also bringing my culture to the states to show people how Peruvian art is expressed," Sotillo said.Festival Director Michael O'Connor said the event continues to evolve each year."We're expanding every year," O'Connor said.O'Connor said this year's festival marked the first time organizers expanded programming beyond art and classical music to also include popular music from Hispanic cultures."What we want to do is we want to celebrate the Hispanic artistic heritage, because here in South Florida, especially, we have a very, very large Hispanic population," O'Connor said.Organizers said they hope attendees leave with a deeper appreciation for Hispanic artistic traditions and the people behind them."We hope they'll be inspired too to see the artworks here at the exhibition and to see how the Hispanic world makes itself known through visual arts," O'Connor said. "Not just the art is Hispanic, but also the artists are Hispanic."The festival concluded Saturday with performances featuring both classical and popular Hispanic music.Organizers say they hope the festival continues for many years to come as it celebrates the art, music and cultural heritage that help shape South Florida's diverse communities.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Martin County employee rescues 3 girls caught in rip current at Bob Graham Beach - WFLX
entry.summary: Martin County employee rescues 3 girls caught in rip current at Bob Graham Beach    WFLX
entry.article_text: A Martin County employee helped rescue three girls who were struggling in a rip current Thursday afternoon at Bob Graham Beach near Jensen Beach. Amy Offenbach said she arrived at the beach around 2 p.m. to surf when she noticed three girls about 25 yards offshore holding onto the same surfboard. Watch report: Offenbach, who works in Martin County's Growth and Development Department and is an avid surfer, said something about the situation immediately caught her attention. "The ocean could be very gentle and calm, but it can also be very heavy and crash very hard," Offenbach said. Offenbach said she became concerned when one of the girls appeared distressed. "That kind of struck me as strange," she said. "The other one seemed a little agitated." Moments later, a girl on the beach told Offenbach she believed her friends needed help. "By that time the girls were waving in the water like they needed help, so immediately I just went into rescue mode," Offenbach said. Offenbach and a friend went into the water and paddled toward the girls. When Offenbach reached the group, she said one of the girls appeared to be in serious distress. "I looked at her, and she seemed kind of dazed and confused," Offenbach said. "I said, 'Get up on the board.'" Offenbach said she gave the surfboard she was riding to two of the girls and instructed them to hold on and kick toward shore. She then placed the third girl on her soft-top surfboard and paddled her back to the beach. Offenbach said she has some lifeguard training and quickly recognized the girl needed medical attention after they returned to shore. "The girl that I rescued said that she blacked out under the water," Offenbach said. "She inhaled water, and she had a severe headache." Because Bob Graham Beach is unguarded, Offenbach said she drove the girl to a nearby lifeguard station, where an ambulance was called. Offenbach hopes the rescue serves as a reminder for beachgoers to understand ocean conditions before entering the water. She encourages people to swim at guarded beaches when possible, check rip current forecasts and use flotation devices or boards when appropriate. "I'm just really happy that I was in the right place at the right time," Offenbach said. Offenbach said she has not been able to reconnect with the girl she rescued or learn more about her condition. While she enjoys spending time in the ocean, Offenbach said it is important to remember the dangers it can present. "It can be very treacherous. entry.title: Port St. Lucie assisted-living project raises contamination concerns - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie assisted-living project raises contamination concerns    WPEC
entry.article_text: A proposed 150-unit assisted-living facility in Port St. Lucie is moving through the development process as nearby residents question whether enough is known about the environmental history of a neighboring property with petroleum contamination. The project, known as PSL Westmoreland ALF , is planned for 7.1 acres within the Rivella planned unit development, along Southeast Morningside Boulevard near Southeast Westmoreland Boulevard. The three-story facility would include assisted-living units and a memory care component. Lucie City Council approved the project’s major site plan on Sept. Construction has not begun, and the developer must still submit construction plans for technical review and additional agency reviews. A group of residents opposes the project, citing concerns about the neighboring property’s contamination history and the potential implications for people who could eventually live at the facility. See also: 'It's not safe': Treasure Coast neighbors raise concerns after teen hit walking to school It’s not about what is being built there, resident David Lipps said, arguing that nearby businesses and other facilities could also be affected by environmental concerns. Resident Charlie D’Agata said residents have raised objections at City Council meetings for about two years. He questioned why a developer would be allowed to build near a property he described as contaminated. Residents say they have contacted outside organizations, including the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Florida Department of Health , in an effort to get answers about the site. An engineering letter provides some context for their concerns. In a letter discussing a March 2026 meeting with environmental officials about the neighboring property, BTEX Engineering said the proposed remediation approach should be changed because of concerns about surrounding properties, including the planned assisted-living facility. The letter said vapors would need to be captured during remediation. The environmental history of the neighboring property and the extent of any potential impact on surrounding land remain central questions for residents seeking more information. The city has approved the major site plan, but the project must clear additional steps before construction can begin. The developer is expected to submit construction plans for technical review, followed by reviews involving the South Florida Water Management District and other agencies. Residents say they want clearer answers about the neighboring property’s environmental history and how any potential risks would be addressed as the project advances

entry.summary: Port St. Lucie police confirmed that a man found unconscious in the roadway with severe head injuries early Friday morning was the victim of a hit-and-run crash. WATCH BELOW: Police seek driver after man found unconscious in Port St. Lucie The victim has been identified as a 63-year-old Port St. Lucie resident, police said. The incident occurred at about 12:56 a.m. near the intersection of NW University Boulevard and NW California Boulevard. The 63-year-old man was unconscious and suffering from severe head trauma and significant bleeding, police said. He was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for medical treatment and remains in critical condition. Police said detectives obtained surveillance video from a nearby business that captured the incident and are continuing to collect and evaluate additional video footage as they work to determine the circumstances surrounding the crash and identify the vehicle and driver involved. Authorities are asking anyone who was driving in the area around the time of the crash, may have witnessed the incident, or has dashcam or other video footage from the area to come forward. Even information that may seem insignificant could assist investigators in identifying the driver and bringing this investigation to a resolution. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000. The investigation remains active and ongoing.

entry.article_text: A fire that spread through the garage of a Port St. Lucie home Friday afternoon left a father injured and displaced a family, while neighbors and church members rallied to help them begin the cleanup process. The fire happened on Carmelite Street in the Northport Village neighborhood near St. According to the family, the fire started in the kitchen before spreading through the garage. They say a propane tank later exploded, causing additional damage and impacting a neighbor's garage doors across the street. Lucie County Fire District responded to the home around 1:30 p.m. Crews arrived to find heavy fire coming from the garage. When firefighters extinguished the flames, significant damage was left behind, including a charred garage door, blackened walls and belongings covered in soot. Renter Nigel Laidlow was inside the home when the fire broke out. He suffered burns to his legs and was transported for medical treatment. "I don't even know how to describe it. It was really surreal," Laidlow said. "I would've never thought a little fire would turn into this." By Saturday, family photos, furniture and other belongings were spread across the front yard as loved ones worked to salvage what they could. Members of the Fort Pierce Seventh-day Adventist Church spent the day helping move and sort through damaged items. "We have a really strong support system, especially from my church," Laidlow said. Despite the loss, Laidlow said he is grateful his family survived. "This right here is something not anybody would like to deal with. Not in a lifetime," he said. See also: MCSO warns scam emails may trick development applicants into wiring money The family is now focused on recovering and determining its next steps. The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

entry.title: Treasure Coast High School freshman dies after being hit by car while walking to school
entry.summary: A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student who was hit by a vehicle while walking to school last week has died from his injuries, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department. Police said the crash happened the morning of Oct. 7 near the intersection of Southwest Port St. Lucie Boulevard and Southwest Squirrel Avenue. According to police, the freshman was walking northbound along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near the edge of the roadway when he was struck from behind by a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man. The teen suffered critical injuries and was transported to a local hospital. Police said he was pronounced clinically deceased on Oct. 9 shortly after 4 p.m. Investigators said the crash remains under investigation as detectives continue to examine the circumstances surrounding what happened. Amid the tragedy, the student's family made the decision to donate his organs in hopes of helping others and honoring their son's memory. 'In the midst of their grief, their decision offers the possibility of hope and healing for other families and individuals whose lives may be changed through this extraordinary gift,' police said in a statement. Treasure Coast High School will provide grief counseling services for students and staff as the school community copes with the loss. The Port St. Lucie Police Department extended its condolences to the student's family, friends, classmates and the entire Treasure Coast High School community. 'We recognize that no words can ease the pain of losing a child, and our thoughts remain with everyone affected by this heartbreaking tragedy,' the department said.

entry.title: No lawyer, no law degree: Port St. Lucie man takes on Flock cameras in federal court - WPEC
entry.summary: No lawyer, no law degree: Port St. Lucie man takes on Flock cameras in federal court    WPEC
entry.article_text: A former surgeon turned Wall Street analyst is taking on his city, its mayor and surveillance technology company Flock Safety in federal court. He has no lawyer and wants the city's license plate cameras gone for good. Steven Greer filed the lawsuit in August against Port St. Lucie, Mayor Shannon Martin and Flock Safety, arguing the technology police use to track criminals also threatens Americans' constitutional rights from privacy to gun ownership. "I was appalled at what I learned," Greer told the CBS12 News I-Team. Greer said he spent much of August researching Flock's technology and preparing the federal lawsuit himself. While he has no formal legal training, he says his years working as a surgeon and later on Wall Street prepared him for the technical research and writing involved in representing himself. Flock's automated license plate readers photograph passing vehicles, recording identifying information along with the time and location. Police can search those records to help identify vehicles connected to crimes, but Greer argues the technology also allows officers to reconstruct someone's movements without obtaining a warrant. His amended complaint alleges Port St. Lucie operated 53 Flock cameras and another 73 Axon license plate readers, for a combined network of 126 devices. See also: Brevard County sheriff’s agent killed in wrong-way crash while responding to shooting Greer argues the collection and sharing of that information violates the Fourth Amendment, which protects against unreasonable searches and seizures. The CBS12 News I-Team has been reporting on Flock cameras since last year, examining how the technology is used by law enforcement and more recently, allegations of misuse. In Fort Pierce, Officer Josepher Crutchfield was arrested after investigators accused him of searching his ex-girlfriend's vehicle 382 times. In another case, a woman was arrested and jailed after investigators mistakenly linked her vehicle to a deadly hit-and-run crash. The charges against her were later dropped. Greer cites both cases in his complaint, but argues the larger problem is the surveillance system itself. During their interview, CBS12 I-Team reporter Katie Bente asked Greer about people who aren't concerned about surveillance because they have nothing to hide. "A lot of people say, you know, 'I'm not doing anything wrong. So what does it really matter?'" Bente asked. "Those are the people who don't deserve freedoms. It's just sheer ignorance. They don't even understand why we have a Fourth Amendment," Greer responded. Law enforcement agencies, however, defend license plate readers as valuable investigative tools, crediting the technology with helping identify suspects, recover stolen vehicles and solve crimes. "I know that police have always argued these Flock cameras really help solve crimes. What would be your response to that?" Bente asked. "That's their number one defense. It's not true," Greer said. His assertion is disputed by law enforcement agencies that have documented cases in which license plate reader information helped investigators. Whether the technology is useful in solving crimes is a separate question from whether particular searches are constitutional. Greer's lawsuit also raises an argument not typically associated with traffic cameras: the right to bear arms. He points to Flock cameras reportedly installed at the entrance to the Ocala Shooting Range, a public gun range in Marion County. Greer argues that recording who visits a shooting range could discourage people from exercising their Second Amendment rights. "When I saw that case where they have Flock cameras in gun ranges, I said, 'Whoa, that's a Second Amendment violation,'" Greer told the I-Team. The key buzzword is chilling. You know, if they scare you away from using your gun rights that's a violation." The complaint also challenges the city's handling of public records requests, alleging officials withheld information about camera locations and system audit logs. It includes claims under Florida's constitutional privacy protections and questions the legality of public spending on the network. Greer has also raised First Amendment concerns following a Sept. Lucie City Council meeting. He told the I-Team that the number of police officers present made him feel intimidated and could discourage residents from speaking out. I'm looking around, I see police officers all over the place," Greer said. Meanwhile, the legal debate over Flock is playing out across the country. In Oklahoma, a federal judge ruled Oct. 1 that a warrantless search of approximately a month of license plate location records violated the Fourth Amendment, suppressing evidence obtained following the search. The ruling concerned the specific circumstances of that case and did not establish that all Flock searches are unconstitutional. Law enforcement agencies have continued to defend the technology, while privacy advocates argue that large networks of searchable cameras allow police to monitor ordinary drivers on a scale that wasn't previously possible. Florida is already seeing changes. The Florida Department of Transportation revoked permits for automated license plate readers on state highway rights-of-way, requiring their removal from those locations. Lucie also voted to remove 18 of its 53 Flock cameras. But for Greer, taking down some cameras isn't enough. When Bente pointed out that Port St. Lucie was already removing cameras, Greer argued that voluntary decisions can be reversed by future administrations. "The end result is to get a consent decree, where the city and Flock agrees to pull the cameras forever," he said. His amended lawsuit seeks a declaration that the city's surveillance program violates constitutional protections and an injunction restricting operation of the network or national data sharing without a warrant supported by probable cause. It also seeks disputed public records, statutory damages under federal privacy law and litigation costs. Greer told the I-Team that his primary goal is a binding court order, not a financial payout. "I'm not running for office. I'm not seeking attention," he said. "It's my way of doing something." The lawsuit still faces significant legal hurdles, including potential motions to dismiss. A federal judge has not ruled that Port St. Lucie's camera program violates the Constitution. Greer says he's willing to accept help from an attorney, but for now, he's prepared to continue the fight himself. "You cannot have this technology and not violate the Fourth Amendment. There's no way around it," he said. "You've got to get rid of it.
