WPTV reporter Christy Waite connected with AmeriCorps Program Director for Martin County Boys and Girls Club, Russell Lamberti."We want to serve 575 students, and we want to see an increase of 65% growth, and that can be in vocabulary, fluency and grammar," AmeriCorps Program Director Russell Lamberti said.AmeriCorps volunteers will work one-on-one and in small groups with kindergarten through fifth-grade students at four Boys & Girls Club locations, with an emphasis on literacy.For AmeriCorps Volunteer Experience Specialist Abelard Cesar, the mission also has a personal connection."I am a Haitian American. I learned English at 13 years old, and I had mentors that helped me grow," Cesar said.The Boys & Girls Clubs says the program delivered significant academic results during its previous six-year run. In some cases, as many as eight in 10 participating students moved their reading from Level 1 to Level 4. About the same percentage maintained or improved their English Language Arts grades, according to the organization.The organization said students also showed improvements in literacy rates, assessment scores, school attendance and behavioral patterns.AmeriCorps members' work previously extended beyond the classroom. According to the Boys & Girls Clubs, volunteers completed nearly 50 service projects in Martin County and contributed more than 60,000 hours to community cleanup efforts and other acts of service.The return comes as literacy remains a focus across the county. Earlier this year, the Martin County School District reported that local kindergarten students tied for fourth place statewide in readiness scores and literacy assessments.The AmeriCorps program is part of a broader academic effort by the Boys & Girls Clubs of Martin County, which serves more than 1,000 members ages 6 to 18 in its daily programs. The organization also provides after-school academic assistance through certified teachers.Beyond its Clubs, the organization runs or manages several programs serving local children, including Reading Buddies, Character Counts!, career training using virtual reality technology, culinary programs and skilled-trades programs.With AmeriCorps volunteers returning, the Boys & Girls Clubs says it hopes to build on the program's previous results while giving more Martin County students the individual attention and support they need.

Commissioner Gregg Weiss, who represents the district where the hotel will stand, cast the only dissenting vote, the lawsuit states.Under the deal, the county will advance $26 million from its General Fund reserves to a Related Ross affiliate as construction deposits, acquire the completed hotel at 940 South Rosemary Avenue, West Palm Beach, and lease it back to Related Ross for up to 97 years. The project is an 18-story, 400-room hotel replacing a surface parking lot approximately 45 feet from neighboring townhomes.The lawsuit claims the county gave the public no reasonable notice before voting on the deal. County officials placed the proposed transaction on an "add-on" agenda item just six days before the Sept. 29 vote, invoking a procedure the Board's own rules reserve for emergency circumstances. The complaint says no emergency existed.The full 715-page transaction file was not made available to the public until 8 a.m. 29, ninety minutes before the meeting began. Commissioners themselves received approximately 600 pages of the agreements just five days before the vote.Margaret Frazzini, president of both plaintiff organizations, spoke at the Sept. 29 meeting."Not enough time for us to assemble the people who had something to say," Frazzini said.She also told the Board the process left residents feeling "unheard and invisible."WATCH BELOW: Residents question Related Ross ties on Downtown Development Authority boardAt least one Grandview Heights resident who had participated in previous city hearings on the hotel said he could not rearrange his work schedule on six days' notice to attend the county vote.The county administrator, Joseph Abruzzo, later acknowledged the county had "verbally agreed" with Related to bring the transaction to a vote in September, and that the timing was set in part to accommodate Related's goal to break ground by the end of that month, the lawsuit states.At the meeting, the county attorney told the Board that "the law only requires us to provide a minimum of 24 hours" and that five days' notice was "consistent with our agenda processes."The lawsuit argues that six days' notice — and 90 minutes to read 715 pages of documents — does not constitute reasonable notice of a $26 million, 97-year commitment of public funds and public land. The complaint argues action taken without reasonable notice is "void ab initio," meaning invalid from its inception.The plaintiffs' members live in and around the Grandview Heights Historic District, a neighborhood listed on the National Register of Historic Places on July 8, 1999. The neighborhood's one- and two-story homes, built between 1910 and 1948, sit one block south of the hotel site, across L Street.The hotel is planned for an approximately 1.8-acre parcel at 940 South Rosemary Avenue. The nearest townhomes are approximately 45 feet from the hotel's planned pool deck. The structure would rise 204 feet and include a pool deck and ballroom terrace facing south toward the historic neighborhood.The developer is Related Ross, controlled by billionaire Stephen M. A Related Ross executive told an audience of real estate professionals in 2026 that the company's pipeline in Palm Beach County exceeds $10 billion. Ross sat in the front row of the Commission Chambers during the Sept. 29 vote, according to the complaint.WATCH BELOW: West Palm Beach residents push for transparency on downtown redevelopmentResidents said they have raised concerns about the project for years, according to the complaint. 18, 2025 meeting with Related, Grandview Heights residents objected to valet safety hazards and to noise, lighting, and privacy impacts from the planned pool deck and ballroom terrace. The Grandview Heights Neighborhood Association submitted a 14-page written objection to the City's Development Services Director on June 14, 2026.At a City Planning Board hearing on June 16, 2026, plaintiffs' members opposed the hotel, citing traffic congestion, pedestrian safety, and noise and light pollution from the planned pool deck and ballroom terrace. A pedestrian counter installed at the intersection of L Street and South Rosemary Avenue in May 2026 recorded more than 600 pedestrians per day during the low season. The association estimated the count will exceed 1,000 per day "in season."On Aug. 31, 2026, the West Palm Beach City Commission authorized the 18-story, 400-room hotel by adopting Ordinance No. 5179-26 and related resolutions. The approved hotel received three development waivers, including one that reduced required ground-level frontage along L Street from 20% to 9.5%.The county will lease the completed hotel back to Related for an initial 33-year term, with renewal options totaling a potential 97-year lease. Base rent begins at $1,117,000 per year with 3% annual increases, with the first nine months of rent deferred, the lawsuit states.The county's own consultant, BAE Urban Economics, valued the property-tax benefit that county ownership gives Related at approximately $2.5 million annually and approximately $1.3 billion over the potential lease term. The county also agreed to commit 590 spaces in the county's public Convention Center parking garage to the two hotels, releasing Related from a prior obligation to construct a parking garage on the hotel site.The complaint also notes that two independent appraisals valued the land at approximately $42.7 million and $43 million, while the Palm Beach County Property Appraiser places the market value of the parcel at $8.8 million. The county agreed to pay $26 million for the land and the completed hotel.The lawsuit further notes that, according to the county's own financial consultant, all projected payments to the county over 97 years carry a present value of approximately $275 million — roughly 3% of the headline figure of nearly $8.5 billion cited by officials.The plaintiffs seek a declaration that the Sept. 29 approval is void and a temporary and permanent injunction barring the county from executing, recording, or funding the transaction until the Board considers it at a properly noticed public meeting, with the full transaction documents made available to the public in advance."The residents of Grandview Heights and the others affected by this program deserve that much," the complaint states.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Crash involving 7 vehicles blocks southbound Florida's Turnpike in Delray Beach
entry.summary: A multi-vehicle crash on Florida's Turnpike in Delray Beach shut down all southbound lanes Thursday and left two people with serious injuries, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. Troopers responded to a seven-vehicle crash on the southbound lanes of State Road 91 (Florida's Turnpike) at Atlantic Avenue (SR 806). According to FHP, the vehicles were traveling southbound in multiple lanes when, for reasons still under investigation, one vehicle caused a chain-reaction crash involving seven vehicles. Palm Beach County Fire Rescue says the accident spanned across 300 yards of roadway (PBCFR). All southbound traffic was diverted off the Turnpike at the Atlantic Avenue exit, while crews worked at the scene. All lanes have since reopened. According to PBCFR, eight total drivers were taken to the hospital, and FHP says two drivers were classified as trauma alerts with serious injuries. The State Warning Point has been notified, according to FHP. No additional information has been released, and the investigation remains ongoing.

entry.title: Florida ordered license plate readers off state roads. Why does Palm Beach County still have them?
entry.summary: The Palm Beach County Sheriffs Office says it has received an exemption allowing the agency to continue using license plate reader cameras on state roads, despite a statewide push to remove the technology from those roads. Sheriff Ric Bradshaw told WPTV's Michael Hoffman the exemption is connected to the agencys role in protecting President Donald Trump when he is in Palm Beach County. WATCH: Why PBSO can keep license plate readers on state roads Florida ordered license plate readers off state roads. Why does Palm Beach Co. still have them? The cameras, often referred to as Flock-type cameras or automated license plate readers, capture license plate information that law enforcement can use to help locate vehicles and people. PBSO has used the technology for years, including in searches for criminal suspects and endangered people. entry.article_text: The Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office says it has received an exemption allowing the agency to continue using license plate reader cameras on state roads, despite a statewide push to remove the technology from those roads.Sheriff Ric Bradshaw told WPTV's Michael Hoffman the exemption is connected to the agency’s role in protecting President Donald Trump when he is in Palm Beach County.WATCH: Why PBSO can keep license plate readers on state roadsThe cameras, often referred to as Flock-type cameras or automated license plate readers, capture license plate information that law enforcement can use to help locate vehicles and people.PBSO has used the technology for years, including in searches for criminal suspects and endangered people.“The thing that I want people to understand is this: It’s a very good tool to find people that we’re looking for in a law enforcement capacity,” Bradshaw said. “Not just for the heck of it.”The technology has also played a role in several high-profile investigations.PBSO used license plate reader technology during the search for Ryan Routh after the apparent assassination attempt against Trump at Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach.Most recently, the sheriff’s office said the cameras were used Tuesday while deputies tracked a robbery suspect. That incident ultimately ended in a deputy-involved shooting.But the continued presence of the cameras on state roads comes after Gov. Ron DeSantis directed the Florida Department of Transportation in August to take action to remove them from state roads.Bradshaw said Palm Beach County’s situation is different.“We filed a brief with the Department of Highway Safety up there in Tallahassee that, along with the Secret Service, and says, ‘Hey, this is why we can’t take them down,’ and they granted us that exemption,” Bradshaw said.That raised another question: If the exemption is connected to protecting the president, why can PBSO use those cameras for unrelated law enforcement investigations?WPTV’s Michael Hoffman put that question directly to Bradshaw.“There were some people who reached out to me and said, ‘Well, if they have an exemption to protect the president, why are they using it for other law enforcement activities?’ How would you respond to somebody with that concern?” Hoffman asked.“Well, because the law enforcement activities came first, the president came second,” Bradshaw responded. “We’ve been using them for six years, so he just became part of the system.”The cameras have also faced scrutiny over privacy and the potential for law enforcement misuse.Hoffman asked Bradshaw what safeguards PBSO has in place to prevent its system from being abused.“If you have the right guardrails, you have the right policies and procedures, you can stop that from happening,” Bradshaw said.“You can’t just put the information in there and say, ‘Gee, I’d like to see where my girlfriend was yesterday.’ This has to be a bona fide law enforcement investigation,” he added.Bradshaw said somebody audits the agency’s use of the system every week.The sheriff also pushed back against broader concerns that license plate readers amount to surveillance.“They call them surveillance. It’s not surveillance,” Bradshaw said. “Surveillance is when I think you committed a crime, and we’re going to follow you 24 hours a day, wherever you go. We’re going to be there watching you. This is just a snapshot of a particular point in time.”Bradshaw also argued there is no expectation of privacy when a person is traveling in public.Hoffman asked, "is there any scenario in which you you would take down these cameras?" "No," Sheriff Bradshaw said"Why is that?" Hoffman followed up. Because they're legal," he said. "They're a great investigative tool. We help the public with them, and it's a crime prevention tool that we use to solve cases."The sheriff said PBSO has license plate reader cameras on county roads in addition to those it has been allowed to keep on state roads.

entry.title: Celebrities tee off for a cause at Par for the Culture golf tournament in Greenacres
entry.summary: Golf, celebrities and community impact will come together on Monday, Oct. 19, as Par for the Culture celebrity golf tournament takes over Palm Beach National Golf Country Club, raising awareness and support for people experiencing homelessness in Palm Beach County. The event, organized by Darren Wingate, will bring together professional athletes, celebrities, influencers and community leaders for a day of golf with a purpose. WATCH BELOW: Golf tournament tees up support for The Lord's Place Par For the Culture Proceeds from the tournament will benefit The Lord's Place, a Palm Beach County nonprofit organization that provides housing assistance, supportive services and programs designed to help individuals and families experiencing homelessness rebuild their lives. For Wingate, the mission goes beyond the golf course. The tournament is designed to use the influence of sports and entertainment to bring attention to affordable housing, homelessness and the importance of community involvement. The event also aims to introduce new audiences to golf while creating opportunities for people from different backgrounds to connect through a shared cause. The Lord's Place works to address homelessness through services that include street outreach, housing support, employment training and programs that help people achieve greater independence. Organizers hope the tournament will encourage athletes and community leaders to use their platforms to support housing initiatives, not just in Palm Beach County, but in communities across the country. entry.title: Spookyville and Fright Nights return to the South Florida Fairgrounds this October
entry.summary: Whether your idea of Halloween involves collecting candy with the kids or screaming your way through a haunted house, the South Florida Fairgrounds has an event designed for you. This October, the fairgrounds once again become home to two popular seasonal attractions: Spookyville, a family-friendly Halloween celebration at Yesteryear Village, and Fright Nights, a nighttime attraction featuring haunted houses, scare zones, rides, and entertainment. Family-Friendly Fun at Spookyville Spookyville transforms historic Yesteryear Village into a Halloween destination geared toward children and families. Guests can enjoy safe trick-or-treating throughout the village, costume parades, live entertainment, food vendors, and plenty of opportunities for festive family photos. The attraction's historic buildings are decorated with pumpkins, spider webs, fall decorations, and Halloween displays. Visitors can also enjoy rides, a petting zoo, balloon artists, and special performances. Among this year's entertainers is Wizard Aloysius, who brings magic tricks and family-friendly entertainment to the event on select dates. Spookyville runs Oct. 17-18, 23-25 and 30-31. Looking for a Good Scare? When the sun goes down, the atmosphere changes dramatically. Fright Nights returns to the South Florida Fairgrounds with four haunted attractions, roaming scare actors, carnival rides, live entertainment, food vendors, and a midway designed to test visitors' courage. The event has become a Halloween tradition for thrill-seekers across South Florida and offers an alternative to traveling to larger attractions outside the area. During a behind-the-scenes visit, WPTV's T.A. Walker got a firsthand look at what it takes to become one of the monsters responsible for scaring guests. After receiving scare training, costume, and makeup, he attempted life as a Fright Nights scare actor under the pirate persona 'Captain Arby's.' The results were mixed. While a few guests played along, many walked by unfazed, proving that creating a memorable scare is much harder than it looks. Fright Nights runs October 15-17, 22-24, and 29-30. Captain Arbys attempts to scare Fright Nights guestsTwo Experiences, One Destination The South Florida Fairgrounds offers Halloween fans two distinctly different experiences throughout October. Families looking for safe seasonal fun can enjoy Spookyville during the day and evening, while older guests seeking thrills can test their nerves at Fright Nights after dark. Whethe

entry.title: Ex-Florida congressman Matt Gaetz among defendants named in newly filed civil lawsuit
entry.summary: Former Florida Republican U.S. Congressman Matt Gaetz is among the defendants named in a new federal civil lawsuit filed on behalf of two women identified as Jane Doe 1 and Jane Doe 2. The complaint also names former Seminole County Tax Collector Joel Greenberg and several other defendants. WATCH BELOW: Ex-Rep. Matt Gaetz among defendants named in newly filed civil lawsuit Ex-US Rep. Matt Gaetz of Florida named in civil lawsuit West Palm Beach attorney Spencer Kuvin, who represents the plaintiffs, said the lengthy complaint was intentionally detailed. 'We wanted the courts to understand the full breadth of this operation,' Kuvin told WPTV. In the lawsuit, the plaintiffs allege from 2017 through January of 2019, 'that Gaetz and Greenberg coordinated recruitment, payments, drugs, and travel to obtain commercial sexual acts' Gaetz left Congress in 2024. He has previously denied wrongdoing connected to allegations investigated by the House Ethics Committee. Greenberg, the former Seminole County tax collector, is currently serving federal prison time following his conviction in a separate criminal case. Kuvin told WPTV that attorneys for the plaintiffs believe communications and other evidence, text messages in particular, referenced in the complaint support their allegations. 'The text messages we have we believe are incredibly damaging to Mr. Gaetz and Mr. Greenberg,' Kuvin said. The allegations contained in a civil complaint are claims made by the plaintiffs and have not been proven in court. WPTV's Ashley Glass reached out to Gaetz, Greenberg and others named in the lawsuit after it was filed. Below is the statement we received from Gaetz: I look forward to taking the plaintiffs depositions because much of the conduct alleged against me is false. entry.title: St. Lucie County voters to decide on sales tax renewal, mosquito control expansion - WPBF
entry.summary: St. Lucie County voters to decide on sales tax renewal, mosquito control expansion    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie County voters will decide in November on two ballot questions aimed at addressing the county's growing population and its impact on infrastructure and services. The first question asks voters to renew the half-cent sales tax, originally approved in 2018, which is set to expire in two years. County leaders are seeking to extend the tax for another decade. This is not a new tax but would keep the total sales tax rate at 7%, with the half-cent portion funding infrastructure projects such as road improvements, sidewalks, stormwater drainage, and major projects like widening St. "Now we're seeing that impact, you know, the delayed maintenance and the increased growth we've seen picked up, we're starting to have to play catch-up with those infrastructure projects and the needs are still there," said Erick Gill, communications director for St. The second question focuses on expanding the mosquito control district to include the Tradition and southwestern areas of the county, which have grown beyond the current service boundaries. Currently, mosquito control services cover about half of the county's 600 square miles. If voters approve the expansion, affected property owners would pay about $28 more annually in taxes to fund fogging, spraying, and mosquito surveillance. Both measures will appear on the November ballot, addressing different needs as St. Lucie County continues to grow. Voters are encouraged to review their sample ballots to determine which questions apply to them before voting on Nov. entry.title: Treasure Coast water tank in the running for a national award - WPBF
entry.summary: Treasure Coast water tank in the running for a national award    WPBF
entry.article_text: A water tank at Jaycee Park has been transformed into a colorful tribute to Florida’s native wildlife thanks to Stuart-born and raised artist Christian Stanley and his wife, Jessica. "We keep an eye on the happenings that are going on here in Fort Pierce and saw that there was an open call to artists and put together a design that we thought was a strong submission and submitted it, and we're fortunately selected to come out here and paint the tank," said Stanley, co-owner of C. The decades-old, 22-foot-tall tank that can hold a million gallons of water is owned by Fort Pierce Utilities Authority. It was once a bright shade of white; now it features colorful paintings of manatees, dolphins, turtles, fish and pelicans, along with a sunset. "The great joy that I get out of being of mural artist is taking stuff from the ocean, from the forest, whatever, and bringing it out to the streets for people to see in a much larger-than-life fashion," he said. "So, when I knew the call was interested in being kind of native Florida wildlife, I knew that we could really bring something together that would be really impactful for the community." On Tuesday, Stanley and his wife traveled from Central Florida to the Treasure Coast to apply a UV clear coat to help protect the artwork against the harsh environment of the shore. The two originally began painting the tank in August, completing the mural within a month. He said they then decided to enter their work into Tnemec Company, Inc.'s 2026 Tank of the Year, not expecting much. But became the only South Florida water tank in the running against dozens across the state and the country. "We're so excited," Stanley said.

entry.article_text: WPTV has been reporting extensively on the growth at the Vero Beach Regional Airport when it comes to flights.But on Tuesday, Vero Beach City Council approved a lease agreement to bring a four-story, 116-room Marriott hotel to the airport."We've been in negotiations with this for the last three years,” Brian Dembeck, interim airport director, said. "This is something that is going to dramatically improve the passenger experience."Dembeck took WPTV to the site, which sits just outside the gates of the terminal along Aviation Boulevard."They're going to have a hotel right next door that they can come, they can stay, wait for their flight, and then go right over to the terminal."But the lodging is more than just for passengers.Brian Cartland, vice-president of economic development for the Indian River County Chamber of Commerce, said the hotel could attract more businesses to the city of Vero Beach and beyond."The hotel is going to serve multiple purposes,” said Cartland. "This hotel is going to help target industry growth by giving those companies that are looking at the area some additional alternatives for some great high-end options."While the hotel is close to the airport, Chad Maxey, senior vice president of Diversified Companies, the developer of the project, said one big need for the extra lodging is just down the street at the Jackie Robinson Training Complex."We feel this is a great location to have a hotel that's going to be able to provide amenities to the airport and also to the families and kids that are going to play baseball,” Maxey said.Maxey said the hotel will also feature a “homerun dugout amenity” for families."Kids can play virtual baseball in the hotel as they're getting ready to go across the street and actually hit the diamond over there and play with the Major League Baseball players,” Maxey said.Developers said the hotel will break ground next year and is expected to be completed by the end of 2028.

entry.title: How to find your polling place in Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast
entry.summary: Before heading to the polls for Florida's 2026 general election, voters should confirm where they are assigned to vote. Polling places can change between election cycles, and election officials recommend checking your polling location well before Election Day. Voters in Palm Beach County, St. Lucie County, Martin County, Indian River County and Okeechobee County can visit their local supervisor of elections website to verify registration information, view their sample ballot and locate their assigned polling place. How do I find my polling place? Most county election offices offer online voter lookup tools that allow voters to: Verify voter registration status View a sample ballot Find their precinct Locate their Election Day polling site Confirm district assignments Can I vote at any polling place? On Election Day, voters must generally cast a ballot at their assigned polling location. During early voting, voters may use any authorized early voting location within their county. What should I bring? Voters should bring a valid photo ID with a signature. Those who arrive without acceptable identification may be eligible to cast a provisional ballot.

Reservations are available through Avelo Airlines .

entry.title: Indian River, Okeechobee county sheriffs announce apprehension of suspect
entry.summary: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers and Okeechobee County Chief Deputy Michael Hazellief announced the apprehension of wanted suspect on Oct. 15, 2026 in Vero Beach. Earl D. Wadlington III, 35, was arrested by deputies. He has over 800 felonies in his criminal background, sheriffs said. WATCH BELOW: Sheriffs announce arrest of wanted suspect Indian River, Okeechobee sheriffs announce apprehension of suspect This is a developing story.
entry.article_text: A welfare check on an 88-year-old Okeechobee County veteran led to the discovery of a homicide and the arrest of the victim's grandson following an early-morning police chase in Indian River County, Sheriff Eric Flowers and Chief Deputy Michael Hazellief.WATCH BELOW: Sheriffs announce arrest of wanted suspectPaul Eugene Baker, a longtime Okeechobee County resident and veteran, was found dead on his property after his daughter-in-law called for a welfare check. His grandson, 35-year-old Earl Douglas Wadlington III, was taken into custody after deputies pursued him through a Walmart parking lot at approximately 4 a.m."What started off as a simple welfare check of an 88-year-old veteran in our county has turned into a tragedy and a family tragedy," Chief Hazzellief said.Baker's daughter-in-law had not seen or heard from him in several days. She went to his residence and found the house in disarray, which investigators said was highly unusual."She hadn't seen him or talked to him in several days. She went by to check on the residence. She found the house in disarray, became concerned, and it was highly unusual for him to not be around or for the house to be in this manner," Hazzellief said.Law enforcement obtained and executed a search warrant for the property. Baker was found dead on the property. Investigators said the manner and location of his death made it immediately evident that it was a homicide.Baker's only vehicle was also missing from the residence, along with other property. Investigators learned that Wadlington had recently been living with Baker.The daughter-in-law told investigators that Wadlington had a history with the criminal justice system and that no other family member would allow him to live with them. Wadlington has over 800 felonies in his criminal background, sheriffs said."The daughter-in-law also explained to us that he had been in and out of prison, that he had challenges that nobody else in the family would allow him to live with him, but the grandfather had allowed him to stay there," Hazzellief said.Because the daughter-in-law also held power of attorney for Baker, law enforcement was able to enter the missing vehicle into the ALPR system — a license plate reader network connected to partner agencies across the Treasure Coast area — as stolen. The vehicle was flagged as connected to a homicide suspect. Investigators tracked the vehicle leaving the area but chose not to issue a public alert."We didn't put anything out publicly at that time because we did not want to startle. We wanted the suspect to stay in the vehicle. Quite honestly, we wanted to keep driving," Hazzellief said.Investigators noted that while the agency was required this past month to remove Flock cameras from state roads and permitted locations per a state DOT order, cameras in other qualifying locations remained operational and allowed investigators to move forward with the case."To be specific with the language, we still have them in place in places that don't meet that criteria, and because of that, we were able to really move forward with this case," Hazzellief said.Senior detective Ashley Rojas and her team led the investigation.The stolen vehicle was detected by Indian River County's Flock camera system this morning, leading investigators to the suspect's location.Indian River County Sheriff Flowers described the early-morning pursuit caught on video, in which Wadlington fled from deputies through a Walmart parking lot."One of the particular things that's interesting is it's 4 o'clock in the morning. He's running from our deputies. He's running through the Walmart parking lot. You see that our deputies were able to deploy stop sticks. The reason that he ultimately stopped and got out and ran is because his truck was going to stop working. That stolen vehicle is going to stop working," Flowers said.Sebastian Police Department also responded and assisted Indian River County deputies throughout the pursuit."Doesn't matter if the uniform is green or blue, doesn't matter what color it is. We're all going to go after the bad guys," Flowers said.Flowers praised the Flock camera system and said the county will continue using it despite public criticism."For all the naysayers and all the people who don't like flock and who don't like it, we're going to continue to use it. We're going to continue to put bad guys in jail because of it," Flowers said.Flowers noted that Indian River County cameras not covered by the state DOT order remain in operation. He said the Flock system has aided in other cases, including one involving a missing elderly woman.Wadlington was arrested on fleeding and eluding charges, deputies said, in addition to driving a stolen a vehicle. Both agencies said they are working very closely with the state attorney's office to obtain a warrant for his arrest for the homicide very soon.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

entry.title: 'We need help': Martin County transit cuts put strain on United Way's Ride United program
entry.summary: The United Way of Martin County is calling on the community for support as transit services for residents face mounting challenges. The organization says the MARTY bus shutdown last week was just the tip of the iceberg. The United Way has been seeing an increased need for transit services following state budget cuts earlier this year. WATCH BELOW: United Way's Ride United program strained by surge in transit requests United Way's Ride United program strained by surge in transit requests Henry Hayden relies on community transit services to get to and from work. As an adult on the autism spectrum, he and his mom, Leigh Hayden, say his job gives him purpose. 'It feels like I'm independent. I can do stuff on my own,' Henry Hayden said. 'I like working because I like to talk to people. I like to get some knowledge.' 'The gifts that come with having Henry employed they're so huge,' Leigh Hayden said. In August, state budget cuts reduced funding for Community Coach, a program that helps disabled people like Henry get around. The cuts meant any disabled riders under age 70 had to find a new means of transportation. 'I said I don't know what to do,' Henry Hayden said. 'It was like having the bottom drop out. This is our lifeline, and until you know that, you really don't understand how important something like transportation is,' Leigh Hayden said. Carol Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of the United Way of Martin County, says many turned to the organization's 'Ride United' program following the Community Coach cuts. It is the same program that Martin County residents are now using amid the MARTY Bus shutdown. 'When that closed, everything fell on the United Way. It's just really put a strain on us financially,' Houwaart-Diez said. Last year alone, 'Ride United' provided over 7,600 trips. In the last three and a half months, the organization says it has already completed over 2,800 trips. 'We need help, we need people to really start looking at how we can get that funding restored because we shouldn't be the only solution,' Houwaart-Diez said. Without services like 'Ride United,' people like Henry Hayden would lose their independence. 'I'm eternally grateful,' Henry Hayden said. 'Transportation is the piece of the puzzle that hooks to self-esteem to groceries to purpose to his character,' Leigh Hayden said. The United Way is calling on the community for help to support the increased need for community transit services. This story was reported on-air by a journalist

entry.title: City council approves lease agreement to bring hotel to Vero Beach Regional Airport area - WPTV
entry.summary: City council approves lease agreement to bring hotel to Vero Beach Regional Airport area    WPTV
entry.article_text: WPTV has been reporting extensively on the growth at the Vero Beach Regional Airport when it comes to flights.But on Tuesday, Vero Beach City Council approved a lease agreement to bring a four-story, 116-room Marriott hotel to the airport."We've been in negotiations with this for the last three years,” Brian Dembeck, interim airport director, said. "This is something that is going to dramatically improve the passenger experience."Dembeck took WPTV to the site, which sits just outside the gates of the terminal along Aviation Boulevard."They're going to have a hotel right next door that they can come, they can stay, wait for their flight, and then go right over to the terminal."But the lodging is more than just for passengers.Brian Cartland, vice-president of economic development for the Indian River County Chamber of Commerce, said the hotel could attract more businesses to the city of Vero Beach and beyond."The hotel is going to serve multiple purposes,” said Cartland. "This hotel is going to help target industry growth by giving those companies that are looking at the area some additional alternatives for some great high-end options."While the hotel is close to the airport, Chad Maxey, senior vice president of Diversified Companies, the developer of the project, said one big need for the extra lodging is just down the street at the Jackie Robinson Training Complex."We feel this is a great location to have a hotel that's going to be able to provide amenities to the airport and also to the families and kids that are going to play baseball,” Maxey said.Maxey said the hotel will also feature a “homerun dugout amenity” for families."Kids can play virtual baseball in the hotel as they're getting ready to go across the street and actually hit the diamond over there and play with the Major League Baseball players,” Maxey said.Developers said the hotel will break ground next year and is expected to be completed by the end of 2028.

entry.title: Policyholder advocates warn Florida homeowners of insurance challenges after Hurricane Isaias
entry.summary: As homeowners in Florida's Panhandle begin navigating insurance claims after Hurricane Isaias , policyholder advocates are sounding a warning. 'The storm after the storm is already on the way,' says Doug Quinn of the American Policyholder Association. 'An insurance system that charges more, covers less, and too often fails homeowners when they need it most.' WATCH BELOW: 'Storm after the storm': Advocates warn homeowners about insurance claims Advocates warn Florida homeowners about insurance claims after Hurricane Isaias Quinn's organization, along with Rebuild: The National Disaster Survivors Association, says insurance companies may leave many homeowners with denied claims and reduced benefits. 'America is facing a home insurance affordability crisis, and Florida families are on the front line,' said Quinn, who is currently in the Panhandle to assist homeowners. The insurance industry responded to the comments by strongly denying them. 'Bottom line is legitimate claims are not being denied,' Mark Friedlander of the Insurance Information Institute said. 'If a storm loss is covered by your wind storm coverage in your home insurance policy, those claims are covered.' Leaders in Tallahassee and insurance executives insist the insurance landscape in Florida is improving with lower rates as more insurers enter the market after litigation reforms. A poll released by the University of North Florida in September revealed that 63% of Floridians are more concerned about insurance costs than property taxes.

entry.title: Palm Beach County schools celebrate academic honors as teachers raise concerns over pay, staffing cuts
entry.summary: The School District of Palm Beach County spent part of Tuesday night celebrating new academic recognition from the state. But as district leaders highlighted student achievement and school performance, teachers and employees used public comment to raise concerns about salary freezes, staffing cuts and growing pressures inside schools. The contrast unfolded during a school board meeting where Superintendent Mike Burke announced Palm Beach County had been named one of Florida's academically high-performing districts. According to Burke, Palm Beach County was one of just 18 of Florida's 67 school districts to receive the distinction. The designation is based on multiple factors, including district and school grades, compliance with class-size requirements and financial audit reviews. But as district leaders highlighted student achievement and school performance, teachers and employees used public comment to raise concerns about salary freezes, staffing cuts and growing pressures inside schools.The contrast unfolded during a school board meeting where Superintendent Mike Burke announced Palm Beach County had been named one of Florida's academically high-performing districts.WATCH BELOW: Teachers raise pay concerns amid academic honors"We are proud to say we are one of those academically high-performing districts," Burke told board members.According to Burke, Palm Beach County was one of just 18 of Florida's 67 school districts to receive the distinction. The designation is based on multiple factors, including district and school grades, compliance with class-size requirements and financial audit reviews."We hit all three criteria, and we are maintaining not just our A rating but this status as an academically high-performing school district," Burke said.The district also received another major recognition from the Florida State Board of Education. Burke announced that 45 Palm Beach County schools were named Schools of Excellence, including 23 elementary schools, 12 middle schools, seven high schools and three K-8 or combination schools.To qualify, schools must rank in the top 20% statewide in performance for at least two of the previous three years."So congratulations to our 45 schools of excellence," Burke said. "We put a lot on their plates as a school district. I want them to know how thankful we are and this board is in their commitment to their schools and their students."The accolades come as district leaders continue promoting Palm Beach County's educational offerings and encouraging families to explore the district's growing number of choice programs.But while school leaders celebrated the recognition, several educators who addressed the board argued that employees responsible for those achievements are facing significant challenges of their own."We see billboards proudly boasting Palm Beach County as the A-rated school district," Jaqueline Major, a teacher with the School District of Palm Beach County, said during public comment. "But please remember it's on the backs of the teachers not in the boardroom that that occurs."The comments come amid ongoing concern over district finances.Earlier this year, district officials warned that declining enrollment has significantly reduced state funding. The district has said enrollment losses resulted in roughly $60 million less in state funding and forced officials to make difficult budget decisions. The district has also eliminated 1,173 positions, although many affected employees were reassigned to other jobs.It has left some employees frustrated that discussions about potential salary freezes are happening at the same time the district is celebrating academic success."We did the heavy lifting, but how are we rewarded with a salary freeze and people forced to work second and third jobs to make ends meet," Major told the board, questioning district priorities."Protect your teachers, show your worth," Major said, adding: "Instead, we're left stranded on the island of financial disparity."The criticism extended beyond compensation. Some speakers raised concerns about staffing reductions, resource limitations and changes affecting school libraries.One longtime educator challenged school board members to spend time working inside schools to better understand what teachers face every day."If you want to run the district effectively, you need information based on reality, not PR," he said. "I have dedicated 45 years to this profession and I'm challenging you to spend one week in our shoes."While educators voiced their concerns, district leaders did not directly address the ongoing salary negotiations during the meeting.Burke did, however, emphasize the importance of reapproving a one-mill property tax referendum that appears on the November ballot. The superintendent said the referendum helps fund teacher supplements, choice programs and school safety initiatives."This is the tax levy that allows us to pay our teachers more," Burke said.Burke said the referendum provides additional pay based on experience and helps support hundreds of teaching positions across the district.WPTV has learned that, at this point, raises and potential salary freezes have not been finalized.The district and teachers union remain in negotiations and are expected to continue discussions this week.WPTV has reached out to Superintendent Mike Burke for additional comment and is working to hear back.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: High inflation and the Iran war put pressure on Republicans ahead of the midterm elections
entry.summary: With less than 20 days until the midterm elections, new data from the Department of Labor shows the price of gasoline is contributing to rising inflation and higher prices. The numbers show the Consumer Price Index spiked over half a percentage point in just one month and is up 3.7% from a year ago. A 9.1% increase in the price of gas between August and September is driving those numbers as the ongoing war with Iran continues to put pressure on wallets. Despite the higher prices, the Social Security Administration on Wednesday projected a 3.6% cost of living increase in benefits for 2027, meaning roughly $75 a month more for the nearly 72 million Americans receiving Social Security. However, some seniors worry even that increase might not be enough to offset higher prices. RELATED STORY | Social Security checks are getting their biggest raise since 2023. Inflation may eat it anyway Republicans and President Trump have been forced to defend the higher prices on the campaign trail. In Arizona Wednesday, Trump pledged a swift end to the war with Iran. 'The prices are all coming down, but when this war ends it's going to end very soon by the way, very soon,' Trump said. 'But when the war ends, the prices are going to they should be much lower.' Despite a growing number of calls for the Trump Administration to end the war, it's not clear when the conflict will end, or how the president plans to bring it to a close. The war and higher costs are a major liability for Republicans in the final days of the midterm election campaign, with Democrats frequently invoking the issue of affordability a top concern for voters on the campaign trail.

Election workers generally provide written instructions before voters leave the polling location. Why should I check? entry.title: Florida voter ID requirements for the 2026 election
entry.summary: Florida voters are required to present identification when voting in person. The identification must include a photo and signature. Acceptable Forms of Identification Examples include: Florida driver's license Florida identification card U.S. passport Military ID Student ID Retirement center ID Public assistance ID What if I forget my ID? Voters who do not present an approved ID may cast a provisional ballot. Election officials will review that ballot after Election Day to determine eligibility. What if my photo ID doesn't include a signature? Voters may be asked to provide a secondary form of identification containing a signature.

entry.article_text: A welfare check on an 88-year-old Okeechobee County veteran led to the discovery of a homicide and the arrest of the victim's grandson following an early-morning police chase in Indian River County, Sheriff Eric Flowers and Chief Deputy Michael Hazellief said Thursday during a press conference.WATCH BELOW: Sheriffs announce arrest of wanted suspectPaul Eugene Baker, a longtime Okeechobee County resident and veteran, was found dead on his property after his daughter-in-law called for a welfare check. His grandson, 35-year-old Earl Douglas Wadlington III, was taken into custody after deputies pursued him through a Walmart parking lot at approximately 4 a.m."What started off as a simple welfare check of an 88-year-old veteran in our county has turned into a tragedy and a family tragedy," Hazellief said.Baker's daughter-in-law had not seen or heard from him in several days. She went to his residence and found the house in disarray, which investigators said was highly unusual."She hadn't seen him or talked to him in several days. She went by to check on the residence. She found the house in disarray, became concerned, and it was highly unusual for him to not be around or for the house to be in this manner," Hazellief said.Law enforcement obtained and executed a search warrant for the property. Baker was found dead on the property. Investigators said the manner and location of his death made it immediately evident that it was a homicide.Baker's only vehicle was also missing from the residence, along with other property. Investigators learned that Wadlington had recently been living with Baker.The daughter-in-law told investigators that Wadlington had a history with the criminal justice system and that no other family member would allow him to live with them. Wadlington has over 800 felonies in his criminal background, the chief deputy said."The daughter-in-law also explained to us that he had been in and out of prison, that he had challenges that nobody else in the family would allow him to live with him, but the grandfather had allowed him to stay there," Hazellief said.Because the daughter-in-law also held power of attorney for Baker, law enforcement was able to enter the missing vehicle into the ALPR system — a license plate reader network connected to partner agencies across the Treasure Coast area — as stolen. The vehicle was flagged as connected to a homicide suspect. Investigators tracked the vehicle leaving the area but chose not to issue a public alert."We didn't put anything out publicly at that time because we did not want to startle. We wanted the suspect to stay in the vehicle. Quite honestly, we wanted to keep driving," Hazellief said.WATCH BELOW: Dashcam video of chase, bodycam video of arrest in Indian River CountyInvestigators noted that while the agency was required this past month to remove Flock cameras from state roads and permitted locations per a state DOT order, cameras in other qualifying locations remained operational and allowed investigators to move forward with the case."To be specific with the language, we still have them in place in places that don't meet that criteria, and because of that, we were able to really move forward with this case," Hazellief said.Senior detective Ashley Rojas and her team led the investigation, the chief deputy said.The stolen vehicle was detected by Indian River County's Flock camera system this morning, leading investigators to the suspect's location.Indian River County Sheriff Flowers described the early-morning pursuit caught on video, in which Wadlington fled from deputies through a Walmart parking lot."One of the particular things that's interesting is it's 4 o'clock in the morning. He's running from our deputies. He's running through the Walmart parking lot. You see that our deputies were able to deploy stop sticks. The reason that he ultimately stopped and got out and ran is because his truck was going to stop working. That stolen vehicle is going to stop working," Flowers said.Sebastian Police Department also responded and assisted Indian River County deputies throughout the pursuit."Doesn't matter if the uniform is green or blue, doesn't matter what color it is. We're all going to go after the bad guys," Flowers said.Flowers praised the Flock camera system and said the county will continue using it despite public criticism."For all the naysayers and all the people who don't like flock and who don't like it, we're going to continue to use it. We're going to continue to put bad guys in jail because of it," Flowers said.Flowers noted that Indian River County cameras not covered by the state DOT order remain in operation. entry.article_text: A shooting in the Banner Lake area of Hobe Sound on Wednesday night left one person dead, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. Deputies responded to the scene along Southeast Citrus Way and spent hours investigating. Authorities said one person was detained for questioning. Harriet Ford Greg, who said the victim was her grandson, shared that he lived with her. She recalled hearing three gunshots while she was in bed and immediately worrying about him, knowing he was out that night. When she stepped outside, she said she saw him on the ground as first responders tried to save him. " laying on the ground out there and the police officer was reviving him," Greg said. "I thought that he's not going to make it. Somebody shot him." Greg said she is trying to stay strong for her family but admitted she cannot bring herself to walk into the room where her grandson stayed, saying none of this feels real. The sheriff’s office is expected to release more information Thursday afternoon. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

entry.article_text: Two West Palm Beach neighborhood associations filed a lawsuit in Palm Beach County circuit court challenging the county's approval of a $26 million deal for a second convention center hotel, claiming commissioners violated Florida's open meetings law when they voted on the transaction with limited public notice.WATCH BELOW: Palm Beach County approves second hotel next to convention centerThe Grandview Heights Neighborhood Association and the West Palm Beach Neighborhood Alliance filed the complaint October 14 in the 15th Judicial Circuit. The suit names Palm Beach County, Related Ross affiliates CityPlace South Tower II, LLC, CityPlace Hotel, LLC, The Related Companies, L.P., and CityPlace Retail, L.L.C., along with the CityPlace Community Development District, the City of West Palm Beach, and the City of West Palm Beach Community Redevelopment Agency as defendants.The Palm Beach County Board of County Commissioners approved the 34-part transaction on Sept. Commissioner Gregg Weiss, who represents the district where the hotel will stand, cast the only dissenting vote, the lawsuit states.Under the deal, the county will advance $26 million from its General Fund reserves to a Related Ross affiliate as construction deposits, acquire the completed hotel at 940 South Rosemary Avenue, West Palm Beach, and lease it back to Related Ross for up to 97 years. The project is an 18-story, 400-room hotel replacing a surface parking lot approximately 45 feet from neighboring townhomes.The lawsuit claims the county gave the public no reasonable notice before voting on the deal. County officials placed the proposed transaction on an "add-on" agenda item just six days before the Sept. 29 vote, invoking a procedure the Board's own rules reserve for emergency circumstances. The complaint says no emergency existed.“Plaintiffs believe the County cannot use an emergency procedure to avoid accountability. The approval process is not an obscure procedural matter; it is designed to protect their rights to a meaningful voice in the process,” said William A. Brewer III, partner at Brewer, Attorneys & Counselors—lead counsel to the coalition. “The West Palm Beach community should not have to fight to ensure its public servants follow the rules. Residents deserve transparency, accountability, and a meaningful opportunity to understand how decisions affecting their community are made—and that is precisely what we intend to fight for."The full 715-page transaction file was not made available to the public until 8 a.m. 29, ninety minutes before the meeting began. Commissioners themselves received approximately 600 pages of the agreements just five days before the vote.Margaret Frazzini, president of both plaintiff organizations, spoke at the Sept. 29 meeting."Not enough time for us to assemble the people who had something to say," Frazzini said.She also told the Board the process left residents feeling "unheard and invisible."Frazzini of the West Palm Beach Neighborhood Alliance sent WPTV the following statement:WATCH BELOW: Residents question Related Ross ties on Downtown Development Authority boardAt least one Grandview Heights resident who had participated in previous city hearings on the hotel said he could not rearrange his work schedule on six days' notice to attend the county vote.The county administrator, Joseph Abruzzo, later acknowledged the county had "verbally agreed" with Related to bring the transaction to a vote in September, and that the timing was set in part to accommodate Related's goal to break ground by the end of that month, the lawsuit states.At the meeting, the county attorney told the Board that "the law only requires us to provide a minimum of 24 hours" and that five days' notice was "consistent with our agenda processes."The lawsuit argues that six days' notice — and 90 minutes to read 715 pages of documents — does not constitute reasonable notice of a $26 million, 97-year commitment of public funds and public land. The complaint argues action taken without reasonable notice is "void ab initio," meaning invalid from its inception.The plaintiffs' members live in and around the Grandview Heights Historic District, a neighborhood listed on the National Register of Historic Places on July 8, 1999. The neighborhood's one- and two-story homes, built between 1910 and 1948, sit one block south of the hotel site, across L Street.The hotel is planned for an approximately 1.8-acre parcel at 940 South Rosemary Avenue. The nearest townhomes are approximately 45 feet from the hotel's planned pool deck. The structure would rise 204 feet and include a pool deck and ballroom terrace facing south toward the historic neighborhood.The developer is Related Ross, controlled by billionaire Stephen M. A Related Ross executive told an audience of real estate professionals in 2026 that the company's pipeline in Palm Beach County exceeds $10 billion. Ross sat in the front row of the Commission Chambers during the Sept. 29 vote, according to the complaint.WATCH BELOW: West Palm Beach residents push for transparency on downtown redevelopmentWPTV received the response below from Related Ross regarding the lawsuit:Residents said they have raised concerns about the project for years, according to the complaint. 18, 2025 meeting with Related, Grandview Heights residents objected to valet safety hazards and to noise, lighting, and privacy impacts from the planned pool deck and ballroom terrace. The Grandview Heights Neighborhood Association submitted a 14-page written objection to the City's Development Services Director on June 14, 2026.At a City Planning Board hearing on June 16, 2026, plaintiffs' members opposed the hotel, citing traffic congestion, pedestrian safety, and noise and light pollution from the planned pool deck and ballroom terrace. A pedestrian counter installed at the intersection of L Street and South Rosemary Avenue in May 2026 recorded more than 600 pedestrians per day during the low season. The association estimated the count will exceed 1,000 per day "in season."On Aug. 31, 2026, the West Palm Beach City Commission authorized the 18-story, 400-room hotel by adopting Ordinance No. 5179-26 and related resolutions. The approved hotel received three development waivers, including one that reduced required ground-level frontage along L Street from 20% to 9.5%.The county will lease the completed hotel back to Related for an initial 33-year term, with renewal options totaling a potential 97-year lease. Base rent begins at $1,117,000 per year with 3% annual increases, with the first nine months of rent deferred, the lawsuit states.The county's own consultant, BAE Urban Economics, valued the property-tax benefit that county ownership gives Related at approximately $2.5 million annually and approximately $1.3 billion over the potential lease term. The county also agreed to commit 590 spaces in the county's public Convention Center parking garage to the two hotels, releasing Related from a prior obligation to construct a parking garage on the hotel site.The complaint also notes that two independent appraisals valued the land at approximately $42.7 million and $43 million, while the Palm Beach County Property Appraiser places the market value of the parcel at $8.8 million. The county agreed to pay $26 million for the land and the completed hotel.The lawsuit further notes that, according to the county's own financial consultant, all projected payments to the county over 97 years carry a present value of approximately $275 million — roughly 3% of the headline figure of nearly $8.5 billion cited by officials.The plaintiffs seek a declaration that the Sept. 29 approval is void and a temporary and permanent injunction barring the county from executing, recording, or funding the transaction until the Board considers it at a properly noticed public meeting, with the full transaction documents made available to the public in advance."The residents of Grandview Heights and the others affected by this program deserve that much," the complaint states.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: AmeriCorps returns to Martin County with renewed focus on boosting students' reading skills - WFLX
entry.summary: AmeriCorps returns to Martin County with renewed focus on boosting students' reading skills    WFLX
entry.article_text: A program that has worked with thousands of Martin County children is returning after a brief hiatus, with a renewed focus on helping young students strengthen their reading skills. The Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County is celebrating the return of its AmeriCorps program, which places volunteers directly with students to provide individualized and small-group academic support. WATCH BELOW: Literacy program returns to Martin County after hiatus “We missed it. It was an extremely important piece to our success and moving the district forward,” Martin County Schools Superintendent Michael Maine said. The Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County first introduced the federal mentorship program to the area in 2019. For six years, AmeriCorps volunteers worked with thousands of local students before federal funding shortfalls forced the program to pause. Now, program leaders have set new goals for its return. WPTV reporter Christy Waite connected with AmeriCorps Program Director for Martin County Boys and Girls Club, Russell Lamberti. “We want to serve 575 students, and we want to see an increase of 65% growth, and that can be in vocabulary, fluency and grammar,” AmeriCorps Program Director Russell Lamberti said. AmeriCorps volunteers will work one-on-one and in small groups with kindergarten through fifth-grade students at four Boys Girls Club locations, with an emphasis on literacy. For AmeriCorps Volunteer Experience Specialist Abelard Cesar, the mission also has a personal connection. I learned English at 13 years old, and I had mentors that helped me grow,” Cesar said. The Boys Girls Clubs says the program delivered significant academic results during its previous six-year run. In some cases, as many as eight in 10 participating students moved their reading from Level 1 to Level 4. About the same percentage maintained or improved their English Language Arts grades, according to the organization. The organization said students also showed improvements in literacy rates, assessment scores, school attendance and behavioral patterns. AmeriCorps members’ work previously extended beyond the classroom. According to the Boys Girls Clubs, volunteers completed nearly 50 service projects in Martin County and contributed more than 60,000 hours to community cleanup efforts and other acts of service. The return comes as literacy remains a focus across the county. Earlier this year, the Martin County School District reported that local kindergarten students tied for fourth place statewide in readiness scores and literacy assessments. The AmeriCorps program is part of a broader academic effort by the Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County, which serves more than 1,000 members ages 6 to 18 in its daily programs. The organization also provides after-school academic assistance through certified teachers. Beyond its Clubs, the organization runs or manages several programs serving local children, including Reading Buddies, Character Counts!, career training using virtual reality technology, culinary programs and skilled-trades programs. With AmeriCorps volunteers returning, the Boys Girls Clubs says it hopes to build on the program’s previous results while giving more Martin County students the individual attention and support they need.

entry.title: Death sentence handed down for 67-year-old Otto Lenke in Fort Pierce killing case - WPEC
entry.summary: Death sentence handed down for 67-year-old Otto Lenke in Fort Pierce killing case    WPEC
entry.article_text: Otto Lenke, convicted of killing Fort Pierce motorcycle shop owner Richard Benson, was sentenced to death Wednesday. "The court's independent evaluation of this case herein leads to the conclusion that the death sentence is appropriate and a just sentence for the murder of Richard Benson. Therefore, Otto Lenke, I hereby sentence you to death for the first-degree murder of Richard Benson," said Circuit Court Judge Michael Linn. Lenke sat motionless as he learned his fate. "He did a horrific act he's going to pay the price. And up until the day that he dies, he's going to be in solitary confinement. For years, this case has been pending and today, the family of Richard Benson got justice. So, I'm very, very relieved for that," said Brandon White, Asst. "We're relieved and the judge's decision is, we respect it and that's what we were hoping for in this case and we're glad that justice could be served," said Justin Cormier, Asst. Lenke, 67, was found guilty of first-degree murder and arson in May 2026 for Benson’s 2021 death. See also: Man fatally shot by PBSO deputy after Boynton Beach pursuit identified Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson at Fast Frank’s Custom Cycle Components, then poured denatured alcohol on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. The crime happened just down the street from the Fort Pierce Police Department. Investigators say the motive stemmed from a personal relationship. According to prosecutors, Benson had been dating a woman who previously had a relationship with Lenke. During the murder trial, prosecutors argued that the murder was fueled by jealousy, claiming that Lenke could not accept that Benson was dating someone from his past. The prosecutor says Lenke carefully planned the murder and used a car that day that belonged to his daughter, a car which people would not associate him with and he cut up the gun and disposed of it in pieces. Lenke is a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter. A close friend of Richard Benson, who attended every day of the trial, had this to say about the sentence Lenke received. "I like that he got the death penalty. I don't like the fact that we may be back here two or three more times on the appeals," said Skip Thompson, a friend who helped Benson in his motorcycle repair shop. Lenke did not testify in his own defense during the trial. Florida law requires the State Supreme Court to review every death sentence. So Lenke still has a legal path to challenge his conviction and sentence. That process could take years.

entry.title: Martin County Sheriff's Office investigates deadly Hobe Sound shooting among friends
entry.summary: A 21-year-old man was fatally shot by a man investigators say was his friend on SE Citrus Way in the Banner Lake neighborhood of Hobe Sound. The Martin County Sheriff's Office is now working to determine whether the shooting qualifies as a Stand Your Ground case. The victim has been identified as Jarvis Preston. No one has been arrested. The Martin County Sheriff is still weighing whether the facts point to a homicide charge or a Stand Your Ground defense. The sheriff's office says the two men had been drinking together Wednesday afternoon. Detectives believe Preston continued to drink into the evening, then attempted to rob his friend, who investigators have not publicly identified. The friend got away, but investigators say Preston followed him home and threatened him. 'The deceased starts to pull out a handgun. Shooter pulls his AR-15, acts a rifle, shoots him three times in the chest, and he drops right there,' John Budensiek of the Martin County Sheriff's Office said. After the shooting, Prestons friend allegedly dropped his weapon, unarmed Preston, and started to render aid until deputies arrived. Investigators are searching for surveillance video and speaking with several witnesses to determine whether Florida's Stand Your Ground law applies. 'We're really not ready to make that determination. But I want to make sure we do it the right way to send the right messages to the right people, so this doesn't happen again,' Budensiek said. The shooting has shaken the tight-knit Banner Lake community. Neighbor Stephanie Rose described the loss. 'It's just sad, really sad,' Stephanie Rose said. Rose said she knew both men. 'They were good kids, I mean they got a long perfect, I mean they were friends. I don't know what happened,' Rose said. As Preston's family and neighbors grieve, the community is coming to terms with the loss of a young life. 'Unbelievable and it's just sad. I was just on my way to give them my condolences,' Rose said. 1 hospitalized with life-threatening injuries after shooting in Hobe SoundThis story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Palm Beach Royals ambassadors bring pickleball to the Boys & Girls Clubs of Palm Beach County
entry.summary: The fastest-growing sport in the world just got more players. This week, the middle and high school students in Palm Beach County got to try pickleball for the first time. On Wednesday, the Palm Beach Royals , South Florida's Major League Pickleball team, brought the sport to Boys Girls Clubs across the county. WATCH BELOW: Palm Beach Royals bring pickleball to Boys Girls Clubs Palm Beach Royals bring pickleball to Boys Girls Clubs 'It's always fun to try new sports,' 10th grader Lucas Phazekas said. 'I think it's pretty nice. I like it,' eighth grader Quinton Lynum said. During the first practice, Palm Beach Royals ambassadors were on the court helping coach the students. Quinton jumped on the court for his introductory lesson. 'It's pretty complicated, but the more you do it, the easier it is,' Lynum said. The ambassadors helped Lynum with technique and taught him the basics of the game. 'Well, they taught me how to hold a paddle, and when they taught me how to hold it, it kind of helped me. And when they taught me not to hit it so hard, it kind of helped me hit it more in bounds and get more points,' Lynum said. Lucas Phazekas said pickleball is like a mix of sports. 'Tennis, but if it was like ping pong,' Phazekas said. Phazekas said after one practice, he is starting to get the hang of it. 'I mean, I got it down somewhat at least,' Phazekas said. New paddles were also donated to the Boys Girls Clubs of Palm Beach County by Transworld Business Advisors. 'I hope the kids get to learn a new sport and get to be active and not be on their screens maybe for a few minutes and learning teamwork and learning new skills,' Andy Cagnetta said. 'We know the Boys and Girls Clubs are always worried about their budgets and where they're going to get equipment. And so we're happy as the business community to help that.' Terrance Johnson with the Boys Girls Clubs of Palm Beach County said the equipment will be put to good use, and any friendly activity to get students up and active is a huge benefit. 'It helps us save some money and keep some money in our pockets, and they can interact with the equipment for free. It's enough for multiple people to use at once,' Terrance Johnson said. After just one hour of playing pickleball, Lynum said all kids should give it a try. 'I think if you have anything on your mind, this is the type of thing that will kind of get things off your mind and have a lot of fun,' Lynum said.

entry.title: Celebrities tee off for a cause at Par for the Culture golf tournament in Greenacres
entry.summary: Golf, celebrities and community impact will come together on Monday, Oct. 19, as Par for the Culture celebrity golf tournament takes over Palm Beach National Golf Country Club, raising awareness and support for people experiencing homelessness in Palm Beach County. The event, organized by Darren Wingate, will bring together professional athletes, celebrities, influencers and community leaders for a day of golf with a purpose. WATCH BELOW: Golf tournament tees up support for The Lord's Place Par For the Culture Proceeds from the tournament will benefit The Lord's Place, a Palm Beach County nonprofit organization that provides housing assistance, supportive services and programs designed to help individuals and families experiencing homelessness rebuild their lives. For Wingate, the mission goes beyond the golf course. The tournament is designed to use the influence of sports and entertainment to bring attention to affordable housing, homelessness and the importance of community involvement. The event also aims to introduce new audiences to golf while creating opportunities for people from different backgrounds to connect through a shared cause. The Lord's Place works to address homelessness through services that include street outreach, housing support, employment training and programs that help people achieve greater independence. Organizers hope the tournament will encourage athletes and community leaders to use their platforms to support housing initiatives, not just in Palm Beach County, but in communities across the country. Event Details: Par for the Culture Celebrity Golf Tournament Monday, Oct. 19 at Palm Beach National Golf Country Club, Greenacres, Florida. Hosted by Miami Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis. entry.article_text: The person shot during a shooting in Hobe Sound died Thursday, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. The victim's mother identifies the shooting victim as Jarvis Preston, 21, of Hobe Sound. She says her son was shot by his best friend. She says she does not know what led to the shooting. She says Preston was not married, and he was the father of a small child. "It's just, it's dreadful, like, I can't, I can't understand what, why it expired to the way it did, because they, best friends. What escalated this to happen when it did?" said Ebony Preston, the mother of the shooting victim. The sheriff’s office began investigating the shooting Wednesday after it happened on Southeast Citrus Way, off Florida Avenue, in the Banner Lake neighborhood. Neighbors said they heard three gunshots around 8 p.m. Sheriff's Officials say Preston was armed with a handgun with a 30-clip magazine, which was recovered at the scene of the shooting Wednesday night. And they say Preston was shot and killed by his friend, who shot him from 10 feet away with an AR15 assault rifle. Now, what I gotta do, what? I gotta, like, it's horrible," Ebony Preston said. Preston's stepfather also wants answers. That's what I don't understand how it come about, 'cause they best friends," said Rodney Clemon, the victim's stepfather. Sheriff John Budensiek, Preston and his friend had been drinking earlier in the day, and Preston tried to rob his friend near their homes. "Multiple witnesses have now told us that he made threats to all kinds of people out on the street. He was yelling loudly, was extremely intoxicated, acting belligerent," Sheriff Budensiek said. The friend, who was armed with an AR15 assault rifle, came out of his house twice with his girlfriend. The second time, the friend and Jarvis Preston--who was armed with a handgun-- got into a confrontation that ended in gunfire. "The deceased (Preston) starts to pull out a handgun. Actually, it's a rifle, shoots him three times in the chest and he (Preston) drops right there," Sheriff Budensiek explained. Mary’s Medical Center in West Palm Beach and did not survive. Sheriff Budensiek says they have not determined yet if the shooting was self-defense or a murder. The victim's mother says it's devastating. "It's lot of unanswered questions. But my son is dead, so how do we go from there?" Ebony Preston said. See also: Funding for schools in Palm Beach County on your November ballot No one has been arrested. The Sheriff says they're working carefully with the State Attorney's Office to determine if anyone will be charged in this shooting or if it was a case of stand your ground, and if the shooter acted in self-defense. He says the individual who shot Preston attempted to render aid to the victim and remained at the scene following the shooting. The name of the shooter has not been released because the matter is still under investigation.
